sections.body:
Lifestyle modification is not a soft prelude to real treatment — it is the only intervention that addresses the upstream causes of hypertension. At best, lifestyle changes alone can reduce systolic BP by 20 mmHg, avoid lifelong medication in Grade 1 hypertension, and enhance the efficacy of every antihypertensive drug prescribed.

## Salt (sodium) restriction — the most evidence-based lifestyle change

Dietary sodium is the most directly linked dietary factor to blood pressure. The relationship is dose-dependent: each 1 g reduction in daily sodium chloride reduces systolic BP by approximately 3–5 mmHg (more in salt-sensitive individuals: elderly, Black populations, CKD patients). Current recommendations:

- ESC 2018 target: <5 g NaCl per day (= <2 g sodium per day)
- Global average intake: approximately 9–12 g NaCl/day — 2× the recommended amount
- DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension): reduced sodium + high fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy + reduced saturated fat → systolic BP reduction of 8–14 mmHg in RCTs

Indonesian context: Indonesian sodium context: The average Indonesian diet is very high in sodium — driven by fermented sauces (kecap asin/manis), instant noodles (mi instan, one serving contains 800–1,200 mg sodium), salted fish (ikan asin), and shrimp paste (terasi). Practical advice for Indonesian patients: (1) reduce consumption of instant noodles from daily to ≤2× per week; (2) use less kecap asin and replace with kecap manis (sweeter, less sodium) where possible; (3) reduce ikan asin portion sizes; (4) use herbs and lime juice for flavouring rather than salt or MSG. High potassium foods that help counteract sodium: bananas (pisang), potatoes (kentang), sweet potato (ubi), spinach (bayam).

## Weight loss — each kilogram reduces BP by ~1 mmHg systolic

Obesity drives hypertension through multiple mechanisms: ↑ RAAS activation (adipose tissue produces angiotensinogen), ↑ sympathetic nervous system tone (hyperleptinemia → central sympathoexcitation), physical compression of the kidneys (abdominal obesity), sleep apnoea (intermittent hypoxia → sympathetic activation), and insulin resistance. Weight loss reverses these mechanisms. Evidence: every 1 kg of weight loss reduces SBP by approximately 1 mmHg. A 10 kg weight loss can reduce SBP by 8–10 mmHg — equivalent to a first antihypertensive drug. Target: BMI 20–25 kg/m² (or waist circumference <94 cm in men, <80 cm in women using European criteria; Asian-Pacific: <90 cm in men, <80 cm in women).

## Physical activity — exercise as antihypertensive therapy

- Aerobic exercise: the most evidence-based form. 150–300 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (brisk walking, cycling, swimming) reduces SBP by 5–8 mmHg in hypertensive patients. Mechanisms: improved endothelial NO release, ↓ sympathetic tone, ↓ body weight, ↓ insulin resistance.
- Resistance training: additional benefit; 2–3 sessions/week of dynamic resistance exercise (not static isometric) reduces SBP by 2–3 mmHg independently of aerobic exercise.
- Important: hypertensive patients do NOT need to be excluded from exercise. Uncontrolled Grade 3 hypertension (>180/110): defer vigorous exercise until BP is controlled. Grade 1–2: encourage exercise — the BP reduction from regular exercise exceeds the transient rise during exercise sessions.

## Alcohol restriction

Alcohol has a dose-dependent, direct pressor effect: ethanol increases sympathetic activity, impairs baroreceptor sensitivity, and has direct vasoconstrictive effects. Even modest reductions in alcohol intake significantly lower BP. Recommendations:

- Men: ≤14 units per week (≤2 units/day), avoid binge drinking
- Women: ≤8 units per week (≤1 unit/day)
- One unit = 10 mL of pure alcohol = 330 mL of beer (5%) = 100 mL of wine (12%)
- Reducing from heavy (6+ drinks/day) to moderate: SBP reduction 5–7 mmHg

## Smoking cessation — CV risk, not BP

Smoking does NOT chronically elevate blood pressure in the same way as other factors listed here — in fact, chronic smokers often have lower resting BP than non-smokers (nicotine causes acute BP rises during each cigarette but chronic effects on resting BP are modest). However, smoking is a powerful and independent cardiovascular risk factor and dramatically multiplies the risk attributable to hypertension. Patients with hypertension who smoke must stop smoking — not because stopping will lower their BP significantly, but because the combination of hypertension + smoking creates multiplicative CV risk. Varenicline (first-line, EAGLES trial confirmed CV safety) or NRT are the recommended cessation aids.

## Potassium supplementation

High dietary potassium (3.5–5 g/day from food) blunts the sodium pressor effect and lowers BP through: enhanced natriuresis, direct vasodilation, and reduced peripheral resistance. Potassium-rich foods: bananas, sweet potatoes, spinach, legumes, avocado. Potassium supplementation via tablets is not routinely recommended (risk of hyperkalaemia in CKD patients on RAAS blockers) — obtain potassium through diet.

## Expected BP reductions from lifestyle changes — summary

| Intervention | Expected SBP reduction | Evidence quality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium restriction (<5 g NaCl/day) | 3–5 mmHg (up to 7 mmHg in salt-sensitive) | High |
| Weight loss (5–10 kg) | 5–10 mmHg | High |
| Aerobic exercise (150+ min/week) | 5–8 mmHg | High |
| Alcohol restriction (heavy → moderate) | 5–7 mmHg | High |
| DASH diet (full pattern) | 8–14 mmHg | High (in controlled settings) |
| Smoking cessation | Minimal acute BP effect | Large CV risk reduction |
| Caffeine restriction | 1–2 mmHg (non-habitual users) | Low-moderate |

sections.body:
Five drug classes form the evidence-based backbone of antihypertensive therapy: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide-like diuretics, and beta-blockers. Each acts through a distinct mechanism, has a distinct adverse effect profile, and a distinct set of compelling or potentially harmful indications. Knowing these inside-out is foundational to rational prescribing.

## ACE inhibitors (ACEi)

Drug: Ramipril, perindopril, enalapril, captopril, lisinopril
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Ramipril | 2.5–10 mg OD (start 2.5 mg) |
| Perindopril | 4–8 mg OD |
| Enalapril | 5–20 mg BD |
| Captopril | 12.5–50 mg BD–TDS |
| Lisinopril | 5–40 mg OD |

Mechanism: block angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II → vasodilation + reduced aldosterone → ↓ SVR + ↓ sodium retention. Also ↑ bradykinin (beneficial vasodilation, but causes cough).

Evidence base: HOPE (ramipril reduced MI, stroke, CV death by 22% in high-risk non-hypertensive patients — confirming RAAS blockade benefit beyond BP). PROGRESS (perindopril ± indapamide reduced recurrent stroke by 28%).

Compelling indications: all HFrEF (Class I), post-MI LV dysfunction, DM with nephropathy/proteinuria, CKD with proteinuria, high-risk ASCVD, stroke secondary prevention (PROGRESS).

Adverse effects: dry persistent cough (10–20% of patients, up to 30–40% in Southeast Asians — due to bradykinin accumulation; class effect, dose-independent, not resolved by dose reduction → switch to ARB); angioedema (rare, ~0.1%, potentially life-threatening — tongue/laryngeal oedema; more common in Black populations; absolute contraindication to re-use ACEi → switch to ARB); hyperkalaemia (especially with CKD, MRA, NSAIDs); AKI on initiation in bilateral renal artery stenosis or severe volume depletion.

Contraindications: pregnancy (all trimesters — teratogenic), bilateral renal artery stenosis (↓ efferent dilation → ↓ GFR → acute kidney failure), prior angioedema from ACEi, concurrent use with aliskiren in DM/CKD.

## Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)

Drug: Losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan, olmesartan
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Losartan | 25–100 mg OD |
| Valsartan | 80–320 mg OD |
| Candesartan | 4–32 mg OD |
| Irbesartan | 150–300 mg OD |
| Telmisartan | 20–80 mg OD |

Mechanism: block AT1 receptor directly → same downstream effects as ACEi (vasodilation, ↓ aldosterone) but WITHOUT bradykinin accumulation → no cough. AT2 receptor is unblocked → may have additional cardioprotective effects via AT2 stimulation.

Evidence base: LIFE (losartan > atenolol for stroke and LVH regression at equivalent BP); RENAAL (losartan reduced ESRD in DM2 nephropathy); IRMA-2/IDNT (irbesartan renoprotection in DM2); VALUE (valsartan vs amlodipine — similar CV outcomes).

Use: same as ACEi; preferred when ACEi causes cough or angioedema. Candesartan/valsartan have Class I HFrEF indication (Val-HeFT, CHARM). NOT interchangeable with ACEi in the same patient — do NOT use ACEi + ARB together (ONTARGET: dual RAAS blockade → no additional benefit, increased AKI + hyperkalaemia).

Adverse effects: similar to ACEi except NO cough. Angioedema occurs rarely with ARBs (~0.1%) but is less severe — if ACEi angioedema was life-threatening, ARB introduction requires caution.

## Calcium channel blockers (CCBs)

### Dihydropyridines (DHP)

Drug: Amlodipine, nifedipine (SR/LA), felodipine, lercanidipine, nitrendipine
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Amlodipine | 2.5–10 mg OD (long half-life, once daily) |
| Nifedipine LA | 20–90 mg OD |
| Felodipine | 2.5–10 mg OD |

Mechanism: block L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation → ↓ SVR → ↓ BP. Minimal cardiac effect at antihypertensive doses (peripheral selectivity). Amlodipine is the preferred DHP — longest half-life (36–48h), minimal reflex tachycardia, excellent tolerability.

Evidence: ALLHAT (amlodipine non-inferior to chlorthalidone and lisinopril for primary CV prevention); ASCOT (amlodipine + perindopril superior to atenolol + thiazide for stroke and CV outcomes).

Compelling indications: elderly patients (especially isolated systolic hypertension), angina (DHP reduce coronary vasospasm), patients of African descent (renin-low hypertension responds better to CCB/diuretics). Safe in asthma/COPD.

Adverse effects: peripheral oedema (dose-related, not sodium-related — combining with RAAS blocker [ACEi/ARB] largely eliminates this by reducing postcapillary venodilation); flushing; headache; reflex tachycardia (especially short-acting nifedipine — avoid short-acting nifedipine in hypertension). Amlodipine has the least side effects of the DHP class.

### Non-dihydropyridines (non-DHP)

Drug: Diltiazem (rate-limiting CCB), verapamil (rate-limiting CCB)
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Diltiazem SR | 120–360 mg OD or BD |
| Verapamil SR | 120–360 mg OD |

Block both vascular AND cardiac calcium channels → vasodilation + ↓ HR + ↓ AV nodal conduction. Useful for hypertension with rate-requiring conditions (AF with rapid ventricular response, effort angina with tachycardia). Absolutely contraindicated in HFrEF (negative inotrope → decompensation) and in combinations with beta-blockers (dangerous bradycardia/AV block). Preferred in coronary vasospasm (Chapter 95 in tryout).

## Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics

Drug: Indapamide (preferred), chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ)
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Indapamide | 1.5 mg (SR) or 2.5 mg OD |
| Chlorthalidone | 12.5–25 mg OD |
| HCTZ | 12.5–50 mg OD |

Mechanism: block NaCl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule → natriuresis → reduced plasma volume and reduced preload → ↓ CO initially → chronic: ↓ TPR (possibly from reduced intracellular sodium in vascular smooth muscle). The BP effect continues even when the diuretic effect is minimal (at low doses) — the BP reduction is largely from vascular mechanisms at maintenance doses.

Drug comparison: indapamide and chlorthalidone are preferred over HCTZ because they have longer half-lives, greater 24-hour BP reduction, and better outcome data (ALLHAT used chlorthalidone; HYVET used indapamide). HCTZ at 12.5 mg provides less BP reduction than indicated in its original dose range — often subtherapeutic at doses used in practice.

Adverse effects: hypokalaemia (dose-dependent; add K⁺ supplement or combine with K⁺-sparing diuretic/MRA); hyperuricaemia (precipitates gout — avoid in active gout); hyperglycaemia (modest; diabetogenic in combination with beta-blockers — avoid this combination); hyponatraemia (particularly in elderly women — can be severe and fatal); dyslipidaemia (mild, transient elevation of TG and LDL — less with low doses); erectile dysfunction; calcium conservation (thiazides reduce urinary calcium — beneficial in osteoporosis).

## Beta-blockers

Drug: Bisoprolol, atenolol, metoprolol, carvedilol (non-selective + α1), nebivolol (vasodilating beta-blocker)
| Drug | Usual dose |
| --- | --- |
| Bisoprolol | 2.5–10 mg OD |
| Atenolol | 25–100 mg OD |
| Metoprolol succinate | 25–200 mg OD |
| Carvedilol | 3.125–25 mg BD |
| Nebivolol | 2.5–10 mg OD |

Mechanism: block β1-adrenergic receptors → ↓ HR + ↓ cardiac contractility → ↓ CO → ↓ BP. Also reduce renin release (β1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells). Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, carvedilol) also block β2 receptors (bronchospasm in COPD/asthma, vasoconstriction of peripheral arteries, masking of hypoglycaemia symptoms).

Role in hypertension: ESC 2018 downgraded beta-blockers from first-line in uncomplicated hypertension because they are inferior to other classes for stroke prevention (especially atenolol) and increase new-onset diabetes risk (when combined with thiazides). However, beta-blockers have compelling indications where they are the preferred or only appropriate antihypertensive:

- HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate — Class I, mortality benefit)
- Post-MI (reduce recurrent MI and sudden death)
- Effort angina (reduce myocardial O₂ demand)
- AF rate control (slows AV nodal conduction)
- Hypertension in pregnancy (labetalol IV for acute control; oral metoprolol/labetalol for maintenance)

Contraindications: asthma (bronchospasm — use non-selective agents only with great caution; cardioselective beta-blockers acceptable in mild-moderate COPD), sick sinus syndrome, high-degree AV block (without pacemaker), severe bradycardia, acute decompensated HF (can initiate if haemodynamically stable).

Exam tip: The preferred initial drug combination (ESC 2018):
RAAS blocker (ACEi or ARB) + CCB (amlodipine) — most patients
RAAS blocker + thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) — if CCB not tolerated or oedema
Triple therapy if needed: RAAS blocker + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic
What to AVOID as initial combination: ACEi + ARB (ONTARGET — no benefit, more AKI/hyperkalaemia); beta-blocker + thiazide (increased diabetes risk, inferior outcomes); non-DHP CCB + beta-blocker (severe bradycardia/AV block risk). Beta-blockers are not first-line in uncomplicated hypertension — they are added if there is a compelling indication beyond hypertension itself.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
The question is not simply "what BP target should we aim for?" but "which drugs, in what combination, and titrated how aggressively, will achieve that target safely for this patient?" The single pill combination strategy, the treat-to-target approach, and the modern evidence for intensive BP control are the pillars of contemporary hypertension management.

## Blood pressure treatment targets — ESC 2018

| Patient group | On-treatment SBP target | DBP target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General population (18–64 years) | <130 mmHg (if tolerated) | <80 mmHg |
| Elderly (65–79 years) | 130–139 mmHg (target range) | <80 mmHg |
| Very elderly (≥80 years) | 130–139 mmHg (if tolerated; accept ≤150 if not tolerated) | <80 mmHg |
| Diabetes mellitus | <130 mmHg (if tolerated) | <80 mmHg |
| CKD (non-proteinuric) | <140 mmHg | <80 mmHg |
| CKD with proteinuria | <130 mmHg | <80 mmHg |
| Established CVD (CAD, stroke, PAD) | <130 mmHg (if tolerated); ≥120 mmHg (J-curve caution in elderly with CAD) | <80 mmHg |

Key concept: The J-curve phenomenon: BP that is too low may be as harmful as BP that is too high — particularly for coronary events in the elderly with established CAD
Multiple observational studies and post-hoc analyses show a J-shaped relationship between DBP and coronary events — particularly in elderly patients with stiff, non-compliant arteries (isolated systolic hypertension): when DBP falls below 70 mmHg, coronary perfusion (which occurs during diastole) may be compromised → increased risk of MI. The INVEST trial: in CAD patients on intensive BP control, DBP <70 mmHg was associated with increased MI risk. Therefore: for elderly patients with established CAD, avoid aggressive lowering of DBP below 70 mmHg. The general SBP target of <130 mmHg in CAD patients should be pursued cautiously, ensuring DBP does not fall below 70 mmHg.

## SPRINT trial — the case for intensive SBP control

SPRINT (Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial, 2015, NEJM): 9,361 adults with SBP ≥130 mmHg and high CV risk (but WITHOUT diabetes) randomised to intensive (SBP target <120 mmHg) vs standard (<140 mmHg) treatment. Results: intensive arm → 25% reduction in MACE (HR 0.75), 27% reduction in all-cause mortality, 38% reduction in HF. Trial stopped early for benefit. However: the intensive arm required an average of 3 drugs vs 1.8 drugs, and had more adverse events (hypotension, syncope, AKI, electrolyte abnormalities). ESC 2018 compromise: target <130 mmHg in most patients aged <80 years — more intensive than before SPRINT but not as aggressive as <120 mmHg (which required more drugs and caused more side effects without proportionally greater benefit in the real-world outpatient setting).

## The single pill combination (SPC) strategy

Evidence consistently shows that treatment adherence is the biggest driver of poor BP control globally. Single pill combinations — two or three antihypertensive agents in one tablet taken once daily — dramatically improve adherence (by eliminating pill burden) and BP control (by providing complementary mechanisms in one convenient dose).

Mental model: The modern ESC treatment algorithm — simplified:
Step 1 (Initial therapy): Start with a 2-drug SPC (ACEi/ARB + CCB or ACEi/ARB + thiazide-like diuretic) in most patients with confirmed hypertension. Monotherapy is appropriate only for: Grade 1 at low risk, elderly/frail patients (start low, go slow), or patients with very high baseline creatinine (where a gentle start is needed).
Step 2 (If target not reached at 2–4 weeks): Switch to a 3-drug SPC (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic).
Step 3 (Resistant hypertension — BP above target on optimal 3-drug therapy): Add spironolactone 25–50 mg OD (PATHWAY-2 — the evidence-based 4th agent). Alternatively: doxazosin, bisoprolol, or methyldopa.
Key principle: at each step, add a complementary drug class — do not switch drugs repeatedly. Each class addresses a different mechanism. A patient on RAAS + CCB + thiazide has their RAAS, vascular calcium channels, and renal sodium handling all targeted — adding spironolactone as 4th agent adds aldosterone blockade (the residual driver in most resistant cases).

## Compelling indications — which drug is preferred in which condition

| Condition | Preferred agent(s) | Agents to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HFrEF | ACEi/ARB/ARNi + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i | Non-DHP CCB (verapamil, diltiazem), avoid DHP CCB for HTN management (can use for angina) |
| Post-MI | Beta-blocker + ACEi/ARB (± MRA) | Short-acting DHP CCBs (reflex tachycardia) |
| Diabetes mellitus | ACEi or ARB (renoprotection); SGLT2i (CV/renal benefit) | Beta-blocker + thiazide (diabetogenic combination) |
| CKD with proteinuria | ACEi or ARB (reduce intraglomerular pressure + proteinuria) | ACEi + ARB together (ONTARGET) |
| Stroke (secondary prevention) | ACEi + thiazide-like diuretic (PROGRESS: perindopril + indapamide) | Alpha-blockers (orthostatic hypotension risk) |
| Stable angina | Beta-blocker + DHP-CCB (anti-anginal + antihypertensive) | Non-DHP + beta-blocker (dangerous bradycardia) |
| Pregnancy | Methyldopa, labetalol, long-acting nifedipine | ACEi, ARBs, SGLT2i, MRAs |
| Atrial fibrillation | Non-DHP CCB (rate control) or beta-blocker; RAAS for prevention | DHP-CCBs (no rate control), monotherapy beta-blocker (inferior stroke prevention) |
| OSA-associated hypertension | CPAP first (treats root cause); then standard antihypertensives | Sedating agents (worsen OSA) |
| LVH regression | ARB (LIFE: losartan > atenolol for LVH regression) | Atenolol (inferior for LVH regression) |

title: Treatment strategy and blood pressure targets

sections.body:
Treating hypertension in elderly patients demands equal parts evidence and caution. The absolute cardiovascular benefit of treatment is greatest in the elderly — because their baseline risk is highest — yet the absolute risk of adverse drug effects is also greatest. The goal is intensive enough treatment to reduce events without causing falls, AKI, or excessive dizziness.

## Physiology of ageing and blood pressure

With ageing: large elastic arteries (aorta, common carotid) progressively stiffen from collagen deposition and elastin fragmentation → reduced compliance → wider pulse pressure (SBP rises, DBP falls or stays flat → isolated systolic hypertension). Isolated systolic hypertension (ISH) — SBP ≥140 mmHg with DBP <90 mmHg — is the dominant form of hypertension in those ≥65 years and is a stronger predictor of CV events in the elderly than diastolic BP elevation.

Ageing also causes: ↓ baroreceptor sensitivity → increased BP variability and higher risk of orthostatic hypotension; ↓ renal function → electrolyte vulnerability; ↓ cardiac reserve; polypharmacy → drug interaction and over-treatment risk.

## Key trials in elderly hypertension

### HYVET (>80 years, SBP >160 mmHg)

3,845 patients aged ≥80 with SBP ≥160 mmHg → indapamide ± perindopril vs placebo. Results: 30% reduction in stroke (primary endpoint), 39% reduction in stroke death, 21% reduction in all-cause mortality. Stopped early for benefit. Proved that even the very elderly benefit from antihypertensive treatment for high BP. Target in HYVET: SBP <150 mmHg. This confirmed that an SBP of 150 mmHg is an acceptable target for patients ≥80 years (current ESC guideline: target 130–139 mmHg if tolerated, but accept ≤150 if not).

### SPRINT (65–79 years subgroup)

The SPRINT elderly subgroup (age ≥75) showed even greater benefit from intensive SBP target (<120 mmHg) than the overall population — the absolute risk reduction was larger due to higher baseline risk. This supported more intensive treatment in fit elderly patients aged 65–79 years. Frail elderly patients with multiple comorbidities were excluded from SPRINT, so these data do not apply to the frailest patients.

## Frailty assessment before treatment decisions

Frailty — defined as a clinical syndrome of diminished physiological reserve and resistance to stressors — profoundly influences the risk-benefit ratio of intensive antihypertensive treatment. Frail elderly patients are at higher risk of: orthostatic hypotension (falls → hip fracture → disability), hyponatraemia (from diuretics), AKI (from RAAS blockers in dehydration), and drug interactions. Simple frailty tools: FRAIL scale (Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illness, Loss of weight), Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). In very frail patients: a SBP target of 140–150 mmHg may be more appropriate than 130 mmHg, and fewer drugs are preferred.

## Drug choice in the elderly

- Preferred first-line: thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide 1.5 mg SR — well-tolerated, effective for isolated systolic HTN) and DHP CCBs (amlodipine 2.5–5 mg — effective, well-tolerated, no orthostatic hypotension).
- ACEi/ARBs: effective and appropriate in elderly with CKD or proteinuria; monitor K⁺ and creatinine carefully (reduced GFR reserve).
- Beta-blockers: not preferred as first-line in elderly hypertension without a compelling indication (post-MI, AF rate control, HFrEF) — can worsen fatigue, cause bradycardia, and mask hypoglycaemia in diabetic elderly.
- Alpha-blockers: particularly avoid as antihypertensive in elderly — high orthostatic hypotension risk → falls.
- Start low, go slow: initiate at the lowest available dose and titrate over 4–6 weeks. Orthostatic BP check (supine-to-standing at 1 and 3 minutes) at each visit.

## Orthostatic hypotension — definition and management

Orthostatic hypotension (OH): fall in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. In elderly hypertensives, OH occurs in 15–25% — and is dramatically exacerbated by antihypertensive drugs, dehydration, and autonomic dysfunction. OH increases fall risk by 2× and is associated with ischaemic stroke (nocturnal orthostasis with arterial hypoperfusion). Management: ensure adequate hydration, avoid high doses of diuretics and alpha-blockers, consider dose reduction if symptomatic, use compression stockings, rise slowly from chair/bed.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Hypertension rarely exists in isolation. Diabetes, CKD, established CAD, heart failure, stroke, and atrial fibrillation each alter both the BP target and the drug of first choice. Matching the right drug to both the hypertension and the comorbidity is the core skill of rational antihypertensive prescribing.

## Hypertension + Diabetes mellitus

DM + hypertension is the highest-risk combination in primary prevention — multiplicative, not merely additive. Approximately 70% of patients with T2DM have hypertension.

- BP target: SBP <130 mmHg (if tolerated); DBP <80 mmHg. ESC 2021 DM guidelines: SBP 120–129 mmHg in younger patients who tolerate it without orthostatic symptoms.
- Preferred drugs: ACEi or ARB — first choice in DM with any albuminuria (UACR >30 mg/g) or CKD. RAAS blockade provides renoprotection beyond BP lowering by reducing intraglomerular hypertension (HOPE-MICRO, RENAAL, IDNT). Add SGLT2i (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) — reduces HF hospitalisations, CV mortality, and CKD progression in DM with established CVD or high risk (EMPA-REG, DECLARE, CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD).
- Combination: ACEi/ARB + CCB (preferred) or ACEi/ARB + indapamide. Avoid beta-blocker + thiazide as the initial combination in DM (worsens insulin resistance, promotes new-onset T2DM, masks hypoglycaemia symptoms).

## Hypertension + CKD

- BP target: SBP <130 mmHg (proteinuric CKD) or <140 mmHg (non-proteinuric CKD).
- Preferred drug: ACEi or ARB — mandatory if proteinuria is present (UACR >30 mg/g). Reduces glomerular hypertension, reduces proteinuria, slows CKD progression independent of BP lowering. Monitor: K⁺ and creatinine at 1–2 weeks after initiation (acceptable: creatinine rise <30% from baseline, K⁺ <5.5 mmol/L). An acute creatinine rise >30% on RAAS blocker initiation → rule out bilateral RAS or severe volume depletion before labelling as ACEi-induced AKI.
- Loop diuretics vs thiazides in CKD: thiazide diuretics lose efficacy as eGFR falls below 30 mL/min (insufficient tubular secretion). For oedema and volume management in CKD stage 4–5: switch to furosemide (loop diuretic) or torsemide.
- ACEi + ARB combination: DO NOT use — ONTARGET (telmisartan + ramipril vs either alone): no additional renal or CV benefit, significantly more hyperkalaemia and AKI.
- Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA, FIDELIO/FIGARO trials in DM+CKD): reduces CKD progression and CV events in T2DM with CKD + proteinuria, on background ACEi/ARB. Less hyperkalaemia than spironolactone. ESC 2023 DM guideline: Class I.

## Hypertension + established CAD (stable angina, post-MI)

- BP target: SBP <130 mmHg (if tolerated); careful not to reduce DBP <70 mmHg in elderly (J-curve for coronary perfusion).
- Preferred drugs: beta-blocker (first-line — reduces angina symptoms + post-MI mortality) + ACEi/ARB (LV protection, especially if EF is reduced or DM is present). DHP-CCB (amlodipine) can be added for angina or additional BP control.
- After MI: beta-blocker + ACEi/ARB ± MRA (if EF ≤40% or DM: EPHESUS trial — eplerenone post-MI).

## Hypertension + HFrEF

- Preferred: ACEi/ARBs, beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin), sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi — replaces ACEi). These four/five drug classes simultaneously treat both hypertension and HFrEF, making them the only antihypertensives with dual indication in this setting.
- Avoid: non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil — negative inotropes → decompensation); centrally acting agents (methyldopa, clonidine — worsen HF symptoms); hydralazine + nitrate as antihypertensive in non-Black patients (reserved for Black patients intolerant of RAAS — A-HeFT trial).
- DHP CCBs: amlodipine and felodipine are vasodilatory CCBs that do NOT worsen HFrEF mortality (PRAISE-1, V-HeFT) — can be used cautiously for additional BP control if needed in HFrEF.

## Hypertension + stroke (secondary prevention)

- Key trial: PROGRESS (2001, Lancet): 6,105 patients with prior stroke or TIA → perindopril ± indapamide vs placebo. Result: combination reduced recurrent stroke by 43% (both normotensive and hypertensive patients benefited). Perindopril alone reduced stroke by 5% (non-significant); the diuretic combination was essential for the full effect.
- Timing after acute ischaemic stroke: initiate or reinitiate antihypertensives at 24–48 hours after stroke (earlier if BP extremely high — specifically >220 mmHg, treat with IV labetalol to <185 mmHg for tPA eligibility).
- BP target after stroke: <130/80 mmHg (ESC 2018, supported by PROGRESS). For lacunar stroke (small vessel, deep white matter): aggressive BP control to <130 mmHg may be particularly important (SPS3 trial: target <130 mmHg reduced haemorrhagic stroke vs target 130–149 mmHg).

## Hypertension + atrial fibrillation

- Hypertension is the most common modifiable risk factor for AF (30–50% of AF patients have hypertension as the underlying cause). RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARBs) reduce atrial fibrosis and atrial stretch → may prevent new-onset AF (CHARM, Val-HeFT, LIFE) — modest but consistent effect.
- For rate control in hypertensive patients with AF: beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) — these have the dual benefit of rate control + antihypertensive effect. DHP-CCBs (amlodipine) do NOT control ventricular rate in AF.
- Always anticoagulate AF based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc score — hypertension itself contributes 1 point to the score.

sections.body:
The cardiovascular examination begins before you touch the patient. The moment you walk into the room, you are already assessing respiratory rate, posture, distress, skin colour, and the presence of lines, monitors, or oxygen. A structured inspection takes less than 60 seconds and can yield the diagnosis before auscultation begins.

## The structured approach — never skip a step

A consistent, ordered approach prevents omissions. The sequence: General inspection → Hands → Face → Neck → Precordium → Lung bases → Abdomen → Legs. In an examination setting, narrate each finding aloud even if normal — "the hands show no clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis, no splinter haemorrhages" demonstrates systematic thoroughness.

## General inspection — what to assess at the bedside

- Dyspnoea and respiratory effort: is the patient using accessory muscles? Sitting bolt upright (orthopnoea from pulmonary oedema)? Tripod position? Count RR before speaking to the patient — any interaction changes it.
- Central cyanosis: bluish discolouration of the lips, tongue, and oral mucosa. Indicates reduced oxygen saturation (<85% to be visually detectable). Central cyanosis is never normal. Compare with peripheral cyanosis (cold extremities only — due to increased oxygen extraction in low-flow states).
- Pallor: conjunctival pallor (pull down lower lid) and palmar crease pallor are more reliable than overall skin pallor. Anaemia → high-output states → functional murmurs + tachycardia + bounding pulse.
- Jaundice: scleral icterus (yellow sclera) in right heart failure from hepatic congestion. Also in haemolysis (prosthetic valve haemolysis, infective endocarditis).
- Cachexia: loss of muscle bulk + fat wasting, particularly in the temporal fossae and interosseous muscles. Cardiac cachexia from advanced heart failure (tumour necrosis factor, inflammatory cytokines drive catabolism) — a sign of severe, advanced disease.
- Distress and posture: severe aortic stenosis → effort syncope → posture during the examination may reveal orthostasis. Pericarditis → leaning forward to relieve pain.

## The hands — a rich source of cardiovascular findings

Sign: Clubbing
Definition: loss of the normal angle between the nail and nail bed (Lovibond angle >180°); increased nail bed sponginess; increased curvature of the nail. Schamroth's window test: place the dorsal surfaces of matching fingers together — normally a diamond-shaped window is visible; with clubbing, the window is obliterated. Cardiovascular causes: cyanotic congenital heart disease (TOF, Eisenmenger, TGA, TAPVD), infective endocarditis (subacute), atrial myxoma. Not caused by: rheumatic heart disease, hypertension, or most common adult heart diseases.

Sign: Splinter haemorrhages
Linear reddish-brown streaks in the distal nail bed (longitudinal, not transverse), caused by microemboli lodging in the distal nail capillaries. Classic sign of infective endocarditis — but more commonly caused by trauma in manual workers. Clinically significant when: multiple splinters in a patient not doing manual labour, associated with other IE signs (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, clubbing, new murmur, fever). Osler nodes: tender raised lesions on finger pads (immune complex deposition). Janeway lesions: non-tender haemorrhagic macules on palms/soles (septic emboli).

Sign: Peripheral cyanosis
Bluish discolouration of the fingertips, nail beds, and peripheries with normal oral mucosa. Due to increased oxygen extraction in a low-flow, vasoconstricted state. Causes: heart failure (↓CO → ↑peripheral extraction), Raynaud's phenomenon, exposure to cold, hypovolaemia. Distinguish from central cyanosis: press on the fingertip — peripheral cyanosis blanches and refills slowly; check the tongue — if the tongue is pink, it is peripheral cyanosis only.

Sign: Xanthomata
Yellowish plaques or nodules of lipid-laden macrophages deposited in tendons (tendon xanthomata, especially Achilles and extensor tendons of hand) or skin (xanthelasma around the eyes, tuberous xanthomata over joints). Tendon xanthomata are pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH). Xanthelasma is non-specific (may occur in FH or normolipidaemia). Palmar xanthomata (yellow creases in the palmar skin folds) suggest Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia (dysbetalipoproteinaemia).

## The face — cardiac diagnoses on first glance

- Malar flush (mitral facies): bilateral high rosy/violaceous flush on the malar eminences with a contrasting pale central face. Caused by: reduced cardiac output + pulmonary hypertension → peripheral vasodilation → telangiectasia in the malar distribution. Classically associated with severe mitral stenosis but not pathognomonic — also seen in carcinoid, SLE, polycythaemia.
- Corneal arcus (arcus senilis): white/grey ring at the corneal periphery from lipid deposition. Normal in those >60 years. In those <45 years: suggestive of hypercholesterolaemia / FH.
- Xanthelasma: yellowish, slightly raised plaques around the medial canthi of both eyes. Associated with hypercholesterolaemia in 50% of cases — always check fasting lipids.
- Marfanoid facies: tall stature, long narrow face, high-arched palate, lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), arachnodactyly. Associated with: aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse.
- Down syndrome features: epicanthic folds, up-slanting palpebral fissures, flat nasal bridge, single palmar crease. Always examine for AVSD (most common CHD in Down syndrome — characteristic ECG: LAD + RBBB + long PR).

## Neck — JVP and carotid pulsations at a glance

Assess the neck with the patient at 45° inclination. The neck gives two distinct vascular pulsations: the JVP (internal jugular, which reflects RA pressure) and the carotid pulse (arterial). Distinguishing them is the most commonly tested bedside skill in cardiology:

| Feature | JVP | Carotid pulse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visible waveform | Biphasic (a + v waves) — two peaks per cycle | Single peak per cycle |
| Palpable | Not palpable (venous, soft) | Palpable |
| Effect of pressure | Disappears with gentle pressure at base | Not abolished by gentle pressure |
| Effect of inspiration | Normally decreases on inspiration | No change |
| Effect of position | Falls when patient sits upright further | No change |
| Effect of abdominal pressure (AJR) | Rises temporarily | No change |

sections.body:
Dynamic auscultation is the art of deliberately changing loading conditions while listening — turning the stethoscope into a haemodynamic instrument. Valsalva, squatting, inspiration, and isometric handgrip each stress the heart in a specific way, and the murmur's response is as diagnostic as its character at rest.

## The physiological principles — why maneuvers work

Mental model: The two key variables:
Preload (ventricular volume): maneuvers that ↓ preload (Valsalva strain phase, standing, dehydration) → smaller LV cavity. Maneuvers that ↑ preload (squatting, passive leg raise, isometric handgrip) → larger LV cavity.
Afterload (systemic vascular resistance): maneuvers that ↑ afterload (isometric handgrip, squatting) → more resistance against which the heart must eject. Maneuvers that ↓ afterload (amyl nitrite inhalation, hot environment) → less resistance.
The two murmurs most affected by these variables: HOCM (↓ preload → worse obstruction → louder murmur) and MVP (↓ preload → earlier prolapse → click moves earlier, murmur lengthens). All other murmurs respond in the opposite direction to ↓ preload (get softer).

## Valsalva maneuver — phases and effects

Technique: ask the patient to blow hard against a closed glottis (or blow steadily against a manometer to 40 mmHg) for 15 seconds. Four phases: Phase I (compression, brief) → ↑ BP; Phase II (strain) → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ CO → ↓ BP; Phase III (release) → transient ↓ BP; Phase IV → overshoot ↑ BP. Clinically use the Phase II strain phase:

| Murmur | Response to Valsalva strain (↓ preload, ↓ CO) | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HOCM | LOUDER (increases) | ↓ LV cavity → LVOTO worsens → more obstruction → louder dynamic murmur |
| MVP | Click moves earlier; murmur lengthens | ↓ LV cavity → leaflets prolapse earlier in systole |
| AS | Softer (decreases) | ↓ preload → ↓ flow through stenotic valve → softer |
| MR | Softer (decreases) | ↓ LV filling → ↓ regurgitant volume |
| AR | Softer (decreases) | ↓ diastolic filling → ↓ regurgitant volume |

## Squatting — the opposite of Valsalva

Squatting → (1) kinking of the femoral arteries → ↑ SVR (↑ afterload); (2) compression of lower limb veins → ↑ venous return → ↑ preload → ↑ LV volume. Net effect: ↑ preload + ↑ afterload.

| Murmur | Response to squatting |
| --- | --- |
| HOCM | SOFTER (↑ LV volume → less obstruction → better leaflet coaptation) |
| MVP click | Click moves later; murmur shortens (↑ LV volume → leaflets prolapse later) |
| AS, MR, VSD | Louder (↑ preload → ↑ flow → louder) |

## Inspiration — the right heart maneuver

Inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure → ↑ venous return to the right heart → ↑ RV filling → ↑ RV stroke volume. This selectively increases RIGHT-SIDED murmurs and sounds.

| Finding | Response to inspiration |
| --- | --- |
| TR murmur (Rivero-Carvalho sign) | LOUDER on inspiration |
| PS murmur | Louder on inspiration |
| Pulmonary ejection click (PS) | SOFTER on inspiration (paradoxical) |
| TS murmur | Louder on inspiration |
| S3 of RV origin | Louder on inspiration |
| Physiological S2 splitting | Wider split on inspiration (A2–P2 gap increases) |
| Fixed split S2 (ASD) | Split remains fixed (no change) |

## Isometric handgrip

Ask the patient to squeeze your fingers (or a rubber ball) as hard as possible for 20–30 seconds. Effect: ↑ SVR (afterload) + mild ↑ HR + ↑ CO. Net effect: increases pressure load on the LV.

- MR: louder (↑ afterload → more gradient from LV into LA → ↑ regurgitant volume)
- AR: louder (↑ aortic diastolic pressure → ↑ regurgitant gradient)
- HOCM: softer (↑ afterload → larger LV cavity → less LVOTO)
- AS: variable (↑ afterload may reduce forward flow slightly)
- VSD: louder (↑ systemic resistance → greater L-R gradient → ↑ shunt)

## The maneuver summary table — the examination cheat sheet

| Maneuver | HOCM | MVP | AS | MR | AR | TR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Valsalva (strain) | ↑↑ | Click earlier, murmur ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ |
| Squatting | ↓↓ | Click later, murmur ↓ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ |
| Standing | ↑↑ | Click earlier | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ |
| Inspiration | No change | No change | No change | No change | No change | ↑↑ |
| Isometric grip | ↓ | Click later | ↓ or N | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ |

sections.body:
The examination of a patient with heart failure is an integrated assessment of two dysfunctional systems: the failing pump (left heart signs — dyspnoea, S3, crepitations) and the congested venous reservoir (right heart signs — elevated JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly). Recognising which system is predominating shapes both the diagnosis and the urgency of treatment.

## Left heart failure — signs of pulmonary congestion and reduced forward output

- Displaced apex beat: the volume-overloaded, dilated LV pushes the apex laterally and inferiorly. In HFrEF with DCM: apex often displaced to the 6th ICS, anterior axillary line. Character: hyperdynamic (volume-loaded) or diffuse and poorly localised (severe DCM).
- Third heart sound (S3): heard with the bell at the apex in left lateral decubitus. The pathological S3 in HFrEF is caused by abrupt deceleration of the large early diastolic filling wave hitting a non-compliant, already-overloaded ventricle. A pathological S3 is one of the most specific signs of elevated LV filling pressure.
- Pulmonary crepitations (crackles): fine, late-inspiratory crackles at the lung bases (coarser with frank pulmonary oedema). Caused by the reopening of collapsed alveoli during inspiration — the wet, fluid-laden alveolar walls stick together and snap open. In chronic stable HFrEF: may be absent even with mildly elevated PCWP (due to increased lymphatic drainage). Fresh-onset acute decompensation → bilateral crepitations to the mid/upper zones.
- Pleural effusion: in advanced or acutely decompensated HF — reduced breath sounds and stony dull percussion at the lung bases (right-sided more common than left in heart failure; bilateral in severe HF).
- Cheyne-Stokes respiration: periodic breathing pattern — crescendo-decrescendo hyperpnoea followed by apnoea — in severe HFrEF with low cardiac output. The prolonged circulation time from heart to brain delays the feedback signal for CO₂ regulation → oscillating respiratory pattern. Sign of severely reduced CO and poor prognosis.
- Pulsus alternans: seen in severe LV dysfunction (see Chapter 2). Always indicates severe HF requiring urgent reassessment.

## Right heart failure — signs of systemic venous congestion

- Elevated JVP: the most sensitive clinical sign of elevated RA pressure. Always measure and report the JVP height in a HF patient — it drives diuretic titration decisions. JVP >3 cm above the sternal angle = elevated.
- Positive abdominojugular reflux (AJR): confirms elevated filling pressures even when resting JVP is borderline. Sustained JVP rise >3 cm for the full 15 seconds of abdominal pressure = positive.
- Peripheral oedema: pitting oedema (press firmly for 5 seconds over the tibia or medial malleolus — a pit that slowly fills = pitting oedema). Grading: 1+ (trace, medial ankle); 2+ (to the ankle); 3+ (to the knee); 4+ (to the thigh). Bilateral symmetrical lower limb oedema in a patient with elevated JVP = right heart failure (or biventricular failure). Asymmetric oedema → consider DVT, local causes.
- Hepatomegaly: tender, smooth hepatomegaly from hepatic venous congestion. In acute right heart failure: acutely tender liver that may be dramatically enlarged. Chronic right heart failure: the liver may become fibrotic (cardiac cirrhosis) and tender on palpation diminishes. Assess: size (percussion + palpation), tenderness, pulsatility.
- Pulsatile liver: in severe TR, each systolic regurgitant jet into the RA transmits back through the hepatic veins into the liver → palpable systolic liver pulsation. Distinguishing from aortic pulsation: liver pulsation expands outward in all directions (expansile) vs aortic pulsation which is more anteroposterior. Pulsatile liver = severe TR until proven otherwise.
- Ascites: late sign of chronic right heart failure / cardiac cirrhosis. Shifting dullness (fluid level changes with position) and fluid wave (positive fluid thrill). Cardiac ascites: high-protein (unlike hepatic cirrhosis from portal hypertension, which also has high-protein ascites — SAAG helps distinguish).
- Parasternal heave: from RV hypertrophy or dilation in right heart failure (any cause).
- Loud P2: in right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension — the pulmonic valve closes more forcefully. Palpable P2 at the LUSB = always pathological.

## Cardiac cachexia — a sign of advanced failure

Severe, unintentional weight loss (>5% body weight over 12 months in the absence of oedema) in the context of heart failure. Driven by: ↑ TNF-alpha, ↑ IL-6, reduced gut absorption from mesenteric congestion, reduced appetite, increased energy expenditure from breathlessness. Signs: temporal wasting, bitemporal wasting, interosseous muscle wasting, cachexia paradox in volume-overloaded patients (they look edematous but have severe muscle wasting underneath). Poor prognostic sign — 1-year mortality >50% in cardiac cachexia.

sections.body:
Each valvular lesion generates a constellation of signs that, taken together, are more specific than any individual finding. Knowing the full sign set for each valve lesion — from the inspection of the hands to the character of the last Korotkoff sound — is the hallmark of the complete cardiovascular clinician.

## Aortic stenosis (AS) — the complete examination

| Examination component | Sign in severe AS | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pulse | Slow-rising, plateau pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) | Narrowed valve limits ejection velocity |
| Pulse pressure | Narrow pulse pressure (<40 mmHg) | Reduced stroke volume through stenotic valve |
| Apex beat | Sustained, heaving (pressure-loaded) | LV hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload |
| Thrill | Systolic thrill at RUSB and carotids in severe AS | High-velocity turbulent jet |
| S1 | Normal or soft (if long PR interval) | Usually unaffected |
| S2 | Soft or absent A2; paradoxical splitting in severe AS | Calcified immobile AV; delayed LV emptying → A2 comes after P2 |
| S4 | Prominent S4 gallop at the apex | Forceful atrial kick against hypertrophied, stiff LV |
| Murmur | Harsh, crescendo-decrescendo ESM at RUSB, radiates to carotids | Turbulent flow through stenotic AV orifice |
| Severity clues | Later peak of murmur; longer duration; softer A2; paradoxical split S2 — all suggest greater severity | Higher gradient → later peak; stiffer valve → less A2 |

## Aortic regurgitation (AR) — the peripheral signs

AR generates dramatic peripheral findings from the combination of high stroke volume (↑ systolic pressure) and rapid diastolic runoff (↓ diastolic pressure) → wide pulse pressure + collapsing pulse:

| Sign | Technique | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corrigan's pulse | Visible prominent carotid pulsation in the neck | Large stroke volume → forceful carotid distension |
| de Musset's sign | Head nodding rhythmically with each heartbeat | Large stroke volume → head moves with each cardiac cycle |
| Quincke's sign | Visible capillary pulsation in the nail bed when gentle pressure applied to the fingertip | Wide pulse pressure transmitted to capillary bed — alternating blanching and flushing |
| Duroziez's sign | Place the stethoscope over the femoral artery and apply partial occlusive pressure proximally → a systolic murmur is normal; with AR → an additional diastolic murmur appears (to-and-fro murmur) | Diastolic retrograde flow in the femoral artery from the wide pulse pressure |
| Traube's sign | "Pistol shot" sounds heard over the femoral artery with the stethoscope placed on the artery without pressure | The large arterial pulse against the artery wall creates an audible "shot" |
| Hill's sign | Popliteal SBP >20 mmHg more than brachial SBP (normal: popliteal is only 10–20 mmHg more) | Wave amplification of the collapsing pulse in the lower limb arteries; indicates severe AR |

## Mitral stenosis (MS) — the complete examination

- Malar flush: bilateral high cheekbone reddish-violaceous flush — ↓ CO + ↑ venodilation from pulmonary hypertension
- Pulse: small volume, may be irregularly irregular (AF — very common in MS); if in sinus rhythm, a normal rate pulse
- JVP: elevated if pulmonary hypertension has caused RV failure; prominent a wave if sinus rhythm + RV hypertrophy from PH
- Apex: tapping (palpable loud S1) — not displaced (unless there is also MR); parasternal heave if RV enlargement from PH
- Auscultation: loud S1 → opening snap → mid-diastolic low-pitched rumble (presystolic accentuation in SR) → loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension → Graham Steell murmur if severe PH
- Severity indicators: shorter S2-OS interval → more severe; longer diastolic rumble → more severe; absent OS (heavily calcified MV) → severe but calcified

## Mitral regurgitation (MR) — the complete examination

- Pulse: hyperdynamic (large volume), regular or AF in chronic MR
- Apex: displaced laterally and inferiorly (volume-loaded LV dilation); hyperdynamic/thrusting character
- S1: soft or absent (MV leaflets cannot close properly — low-energy closure)
- S3: common in significant MR (large diastolic filling from the regurgitant volume returning from the LA)
- Murmur: pansystolic, blowing, high-pitched, best at apex, radiates to left axilla (posterior leaflet MR) or LUSB (anterior leaflet MR or chordal rupture)
- Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture post-MI): murmur may be SHORT (not pansystolic) — the acutely non-compliant LA rapidly equalises pressure with the LV → the pressure gradient driving regurgitation disappears before S2. The hyperdynamic EF on echo (ejecting into low-resistance LA) is a clue.

title: Valvular heart disease — the complete sign set

sections.body:
Congenital heart disease in adults and children presents with a characteristic examination pattern for each lesion. The combination of cyanosis (or its absence), splitting of S2, the character of murmurs, and the pattern of heaves and pulses — assembled systematically — points to the correct anatomical diagnosis before any imaging is performed.

## Atrial septal defect (ASD)

| Sign | Finding | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cyanosis | Absent (left-to-right shunt — oxygenated blood flows right) | LA→RA → ↑ pulmonary blood flow → fully oxygenated blood in systemic circulation |
| Pulse | Normal or small volume | Small-to-moderate shunt: normal systemic CO |
| Apex | Normal or mildly hyperdynamic | Mild LV volume loading from increased pulmonary venous return |
| Parasternal heave | Present — RV volume overload from shunt | RV handles ↑ volume → ↑ RV size → heave |
| S2 | Fixed wide splitting — the DIAGNOSTIC sign | The atrial-level communication equalises RA pressure between inspiration and expiration → P2 delay is fixed regardless of breathing |
| Murmur | Ejection systolic murmur at LUSB (pulmonary flow murmur — from ↑ flow across the PV, NOT from the ASD itself) | Increased pulmonary blood flow → relative PS |
| Diastolic | Mid-diastolic tricuspid flow murmur at LLSB (if Qp:Qs >2:1) | Increased TV flow from extra RA volume |

## Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

- Murmur: harsh, loud pansystolic murmur at the LLSB (3rd–4th left ICS). Thrill almost always palpable. Grade 4–5/6 in moderate VSD. "Maladie de Roger" — a small VSD with a very loud murmur (Vin ordinaire with much turbulence through a tiny hole).
- S2: normal splitting (unless pulmonary hypertension develops — then P2 becomes loud; in Eisenmenger: single or reversed splitting)
- Apex: hyperdynamic (LV volume overload from pulmonary-to-systemic recirculation)
- Cyanosis: absent initially (L-R shunt); with Eisenmenger → central cyanosis + loud P2 + murmur shortens/disappears

## Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

- Pulse: collapsing/bounding (wide pulse pressure — similar to AR, from diastolic runoff into the pulmonary circuit)
- Murmur: continuous "machinery" (Gibson) murmur — occupies all of systole and all of diastole; best heard at the left infraclavicular area or upper left sternal border; a thrill may be palpable
- Differential cyanosis: in Eisenmenger PDA — cyanosis in the lower limbs only (right-to-left ductal shunting → deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta below the subclavian arteries → lower limb cyanosis; upper limbs receive oxygenated blood from the aortic arch above the duct)

## Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

- Central cyanosis + clubbing: from birth or early life; degree of cyanosis correlates with severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction
- Parasternal heave: RV hypertrophy (infundibular hypertrophy in TOF)
- S2: single (P2 is soft or absent — reduced pulmonary blood flow → soft pulmonic component)
- Murmur: ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal border (from the RVOTO/PS component — NOT from the VSD which is non-restrictive). With increasing obstruction → louder and longer RVOTO murmur initially, but in severe obstruction → less blood can get through → murmur shortens (less flow = less turbulence). During a tet spell: the murmur becomes very soft or disappears (RVOTO is so severe that little blood reaches the pulmonary artery).

## Eisenmenger syndrome

- Central cyanosis (right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood): blue-purple discolouration of lips, tongue, oral mucosa. Distinguish from peripheral cyanosis.
- Clubbing: in all longstanding Eisenmenger lesions. Differential clubbing (only lower limbs) in PDA-Eisenmenger.
- Polycythaemia: compensatory erythrocytosis from chronic hypoxaemia. Haematocrit may reach 60–70%.
- Loud P2: always present in Eisenmenger — the suprasystemic PA pressure snaps the pulmonic valve shut with great force. Often palpable at the LUSB.
- Murmur: the original murmur shortens dramatically or disappears as pulmonary pressure equalises with systemic. With equal pressures: no pressure gradient → no turbulence → no murmur. The disappearance of the murmur in a previously-known VSD patient is a sign of Eisenmenger.
- Peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly: from right heart failure, which develops late in Eisenmenger. Also associated with haemoptysis (pulmonary vascular disease), paradoxical emboli (right-to-left shunting → clots/air from venous system reach the systemic circulation).

Exam tip: The S2 splitting as the master CHD clue:
• Fixed wide splitting: ASD (pathognomonic)
• Wide non-fixed splitting: RBBB, PS
• Paradoxical (reversed) splitting: LBBB, severe AS
• Single S2: TOF (absent P2), severe AS (absent A2), Eisenmenger (equal pressures)
• Loud P2: pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger, severe MS
Always assess S2 before attributing a murmur to a specific lesion — the S2 character often clinches the anatomy.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
The peripheral vasculature is the final common pathway of cardiovascular function — it is where the heart's output meets the tissues' demand. Peripheral arterial disease, venous insufficiency, and the acute presentations of limb ischaemia each have clinical signs that must be systematically sought in every cardiovascular patient.

## Peripheral pulse examination — systematic approach

Examine all major peripheral pulses bilaterally and simultaneously where possible: radial, brachial, carotid (one side at a time — bilateral carotid pressure → ↓ cerebral perfusion → syncope), femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis. For each: presence, volume, and character.

| Pulse | Location | Technique |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Radial | Lateral aspect of the wrist | Two or three fingertips over the radial styloid |
| Brachial | Medial aspect of the antecubital fossa | Thumb on the lateral side, fingertips pressing medially |
| Carotid | Medial to the SCM at the level of the thyroid cartilage | One side at a time; never both simultaneously. Use fingertips, NOT thumb (can create carotid sinus pressure effect) |
| Femoral | Mid-inguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) | Firm pressure; in obese patients, deeper palpation required |
| Popliteal | Popliteal fossa behind the knee | Flex the knee to 30–45°; both hands around the knee, thumbs anteriorly, fingertips pressing into the popliteal fossa from behind |
| Posterior tibial | Posterior to the medial malleolus | Press fingertips into the groove behind the medial malleolus |
| Dorsalis pedis | Dorsum of the foot between 1st and 2nd metatarsals | Light fingertip pressure in the groove between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals |

## Acute limb ischaemia — the 6 Ps

Sign: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia — a surgical emergency
Pain: severe, sudden, unrelenting. Early: well-localised. Late: diffuse from tissue necrosis.
Pallor: the limb appears white or ashen — no blood reaching the tissue distal to the occlusion.
Pulselessness: absent pulses distal to the occlusion (may be absent at multiple levels).
Paraesthesia: tingling, numbness — early sign of nerve ischaemia (earliest structure to be ischaemia-sensitive). If paraesthesia is present → limb viability is threatened → surgical urgency.
Paralysis: inability to move the limb — late sign indicating motor nerve and muscle ischaemia. Limb is no longer viable → emergency revascularisation.
Perishing cold: the ischaemic limb is strikingly cold compared with the contralateral side and the patient's proximal limb.
Paraesthesia and paralysis indicate the limb is immediately threatened — time to operating theatre or angiography should be minutes to <6 hours.

## Chronic limb ischaemia — signs of PAD

- Hair loss: below the level of arterial insufficiency
- Thin, shiny, atrophic skin: reduced blood flow → impaired skin nutrition
- Thickened nails: chronically ischaemic nail beds grow slowly → thickened, brittle nails
- Muscle wasting: chronically ischaemic muscles lose bulk
- Dependent rubor: the ischaemic foot becomes intensely red/purple when hanging down (vasodilated capillaries still fill by gravity); becomes pallid when elevated above heart level (insufficient arterial pressure to fill against gravity). Buerger's test: (1) elevate the leg to 45° for 2 minutes — normal stays pink; PAD → pallor appears. (2) Hang the leg over the side of the bed — normal: colour returns in <5 seconds; PAD: colour return >15 seconds + dependent rubor.
- Ulcers: arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, with pale/grey base, occur on the tips of toes, pressure points, dorsum of foot. Venous ulcers: painless or mildly painful, irregular margins, pigmented (hemosiderin), above the medial malleolus, associated with lipodermatosclerosis.

## Allen's test — pre-radial artery cannulation

Before radial artery cannulation (arterial line, ABG, radial artery graft harvest): (1) ask the patient to make a tight fist while you compress both radial and ulnar arteries; (2) ask them to open the hand — it should be pale/white; (3) release the ulnar artery only; (4) normal: colour returns to the palm within 5–7 seconds (positive Allen's = adequate ulnar collateral). If colour does not return within 10 seconds: negative Allen's = inadequate ulnar collateral → do NOT cannulate the radial artery (risk of hand ischaemia).

sections.body:
Every examination has a consistent set of errors that candidates make — not from ignorance of facts but from overlooked technique, incomplete sequences, or failure to integrate findings. This chapter systematically documents the 30 most common errors, paired with the correction. Reviewing this chapter the night before an examination or clinical posting is the highest-yield use of 30 minutes.

## Errors in preparation and positioning

Common mistake: MISTAKE 1: Not exposing the patient adequately. Examining through clothing or with the chest incompletely exposed.

Correct approach: The entire anterior chest must be exposed. For female patients: expose the chest and cover with a gown between examination steps — this is appropriate clinical technique. The apex beat, parasternal heave, and lower cardiac border cannot be properly assessed through clothing.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 2: Starting auscultation without palpation. Going directly from pulse to stethoscope.

Correct approach: Always inspect → palpate (apex, heave, thrill) → then auscultate. Palpation findings (displaced apex = LV enlargement; parasternal heave = RV enlargement; thrill = grade ≥4 murmur) inform and focus auscultation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 3: Not turning the patient to the left lateral decubitus position for apex beat assessment and S3/S4/MS rumble auscultation.

Correct approach: The left lateral decubitus position brings the apex closer to the chest wall — essential for: (1) accurate apex beat characterisation; (2) hearing the S3 and S4 gallops; (3) bringing out the mid-diastolic rumble of MS. Always complete this position change before concluding the cardiac examination.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 4: Not leaning the patient forward for AR murmur auscultation.

Correct approach: The early diastolic murmur of AR is best heard with the patient sitting up, leaning forward, breath held in full expiration, with the diaphragm pressed firmly at the left sternal border (3rd–4th ICS). This is the ONLY murmur that requires this specific position. Omitting it = missing a soft AR murmur.

## Errors in pulse examination

Common mistake: MISTAKE 5: Counting the pulse for 15 seconds × 4 in an irregular rhythm.

Correct approach: In any irregular rhythm (especially AF), count for a full 60 seconds. The 15-second extrapolation introduces up to 25% error in the rate estimate.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 6: Not comparing both radial pulses simultaneously.

Correct approach: Always palpate both radials simultaneously. Radio-radial delay (subclavian stenosis, aortic dissection) is only detectable when both are felt at the same time. Note this explicitly in every examination presentation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 7: Forgetting to lift the arm to elicit a collapsing pulse.

Correct approach: At heart level, a mild or moderate collapsing pulse in AR may feel nearly normal. Ask the patient's permission, grasp the forearm, and lift it above the shoulder. The collapsing quality is dramatically amplified by the gravity effect.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 8: Not checking for radio-femoral delay.

Correct approach: In any young hypertensive patient, or when coarctation is in the differential, always check radio-femoral delay. Palpate the right radial and right femoral simultaneously — the femoral should arrive with only an imperceptibly brief delay. A clearly felt delay = coarctation until proven otherwise.

## Errors in JVP assessment

Common mistake: MISTAKE 9: Using the external jugular vein (EJV) instead of the internal jugular vein (IJV).

Correct approach: The EJV has valves and may be kinked at the entry to the subclavian vein → falsely elevated. Always assess the IJV (the undulating pulsation visible behind/between the SCM heads). If only the EJV is assessable: state this explicitly and note that the reading may overestimate the true RA pressure.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 10: Measuring the horizontal distance rather than the vertical height of the JVP from the sternal angle.

Correct approach: The JVP height is the vertical distance from the sternal angle to the top of the JVP pulsation. Use a ruler or a card held horizontally at the sternal angle and vertically at the JVP level to ensure a true right-angle measurement. Measuring the slanted distance overestimates the JVP height.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 11: Saying "hepatojugular reflux" instead of "abdominojugular reflux" (AJR).

Correct approach: The correct term is abdominojugular reflux. The test works with pressure applied anywhere on the abdomen (including above the liver). "Hepatojugular" implies the response comes specifically from the liver — it does not. More importantly, in examinations this terminology error marks a candidate as imprecise.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 12: Not performing the AJR test in a patient with suspected heart failure.

Correct approach: AJR is a sensitive marker of elevated right heart filling pressure, often positive before the JVP is overtly elevated. Always perform it. Technique: sustained 15-second firm abdominal pressure, patient breathing normally (not breath-holding — Valsalva from breath-holding gives a false-positive result).

## Errors in auscultation

Common mistake: MISTAKE 13: Using only the diaphragm — missing S3, S4, and the MS diastolic rumble.

Correct approach: The bell of the stethoscope (applied with light pressure so the skin acts as a membrane) is essential for: S3, S4, the MS diastolic rumble. The diaphragm misses these. Develop the habit of listening with both diaphragm AND bell at each auscultatory area.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 14: Not auscultating in the axilla and carotids.

Correct approach: MR murmur radiates to the left axilla — auscultate there. AS murmur radiates to the carotids bilaterally — auscultate both carotids. These radiation patterns are frequently tested and frequently omitted by candidates.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 15: Failing to distinguish fixed splitting of S2 from physiological splitting by not comparing inspiration vs expiration.

Correct approach: Ask the patient to breathe normally. Listen to S2 on inspiration and on expiration. Fixed splitting (ASD) = the gap between A2 and P2 does NOT change with respiration. Physiological splitting = gap widens on inspiration, disappears on expiration. This single observation can diagnose ASD on auscultation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 16: Confusing the opening snap of MS with P2 (concluding the patient has a wide split S2).

Correct approach: P2 is at the LUSB and changes with respiration. The opening snap is best heard at the LLSB/apex and does not change with respiration. Additionally: the S2-OS interval is shorter than the A2-P2 interval of wide splitting; the OS is followed by the diastolic rumble. If in doubt: assess respiratory variation (OS = fixed; P2 = moves with respiration).

Common mistake: MISTAKE 17: Not performing dynamic auscultation for HOCM and MVP.

Correct approach: Any ESM that does NOT radiate to the carotids (unlike AS), or any mid-systolic click, requires dynamic auscultation: ask the patient to stand, then squat, then strain (Valsalva). HOCM: louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting. MVP: click moves earlier on standing/Valsalva, later on squatting. This differentiates three diagnoses with overlapping murmur character at rest.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 18: Describing every systolic murmur as "ejection systolic" without checking if it truly starts after S1.

Correct approach: A pansystolic murmur (MR, TR, VSD) begins with S1 — there is no gap between S1 and the onset of the murmur. An ejection systolic murmur (AS, PS, HOCM, innocent) begins after S1 — there is a gap. This distinction changes the diagnosis fundamentally. Listen carefully to whether S1 is audible separately from the start of the murmur.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 19: Calling the Rivero-Carvalho sign as "inspiration increases all right-sided murmurs" without understanding the exception (pulmonary ejection click decreases on inspiration).

Correct approach: The pulmonary ejection click (in PS) is the only right-sided sound that paradoxically DECREASES (or disappears) on inspiration. All other right-sided murmurs/sounds increase. The pulmonary ejection click decreases because ↑ venous return on inspiration partially pre-opens the PV during atrial systole → the click is no longer needed at the start of RV systole. This reversal is pathognomonic of PS.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 20: Not listening for the murmur of AR with the patient in the specific "lean-forward-breath-held-expiration" position.

Correct approach: The AR murmur is the most commonly missed murmur due to position omission. A soft AR murmur (grade 1–2/6) may be inaudible in any other position. The correct position: patient sits up → leans forward → holds breath at end-expiration → firm diaphragm pressure at the 3rd–4th left ICS. If AR is suspected from the pulse character (collapsing) and wide pulse pressure, this position is mandatory.

## Errors in integration and presentation

Common mistake: MISTAKE 21: Presenting the examination findings without a summary or differential diagnosis.

Correct approach: A good clinical examination presentation ends with: "In summary, the findings suggest [primary diagnosis], with evidence of [severity/complications], consistent with [aetiology if known]." The examiner wants to see that you can synthesise individual findings into a clinical picture.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 22: Not noting the presence or absence of surgical scars before beginning.

Correct approach: A midline sternotomy scar changes the entire examination interpretation (prior cardiac surgery). Always inspect for scars before anything else. In an examination, a well-healed scar may be subtle — look carefully along the entire sternum and in the infraclavicular regions (pacemaker).

Common mistake: MISTAKE 23: Confusing the Austin Flint murmur of AR with mitral stenosis.

Correct approach: Austin Flint has no opening snap; no loud S1; the AR murmur and signs of wide pulse pressure are present. MS has an opening snap; loud S1; slow-rising pulse is absent; no collapsing pulse. The echo will always distinguish them — but on clinical examination, the Austin Flint murmur is softer, without the sharp OS, and in the context of severe AR signs.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 24: Missing differential cyanosis in PDA-Eisenmenger.

Correct approach: Always check the toenails in any patient with central cyanosis. In PDA-Eisenmenger, the right-to-left shunt enters the descending aorta below the subclavian arteries → lower limbs are cyanosed and clubbed; upper limbs (left arm may be slightly affected if left subclavian origin is near the duct) appear pink. This is diagnostic of PDA-Eisenmenger.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 25: Forgetting that an S4 gallop is IMPOSSIBLE in atrial fibrillation.

Correct approach: S4 requires organised atrial contraction (the late diastolic "kick" against a stiff ventricle). AF has no organised atrial contraction. If you hear what sounds like a four-sound complex in AF, it is a summation gallop (S3 + S4 fuse when heart rate is fast and diastole is short). Never report S4 in AF — correct it in the examination if you have already stated it.

title: The most common mistakes in clinical examination and OSCE settings

sections.body:
Clinical examination questions in the PPDS entrance examination test pattern recognition — the ability to map a set of physical findings to the correct diagnosis. The patterns are consistent, the traps are predictable, and the preparation is systematic.

## High-yield sign-diagnosis associations

| Sign | Diagnosis | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed wide splitting of S2 | ASD | Equalised RA filling → fixed P2 delay |
| Collapsing pulse + early diastolic murmur (lean forward) | Aortic regurgitation | Wide pulse pressure + AR jet |
| Malar flush + loud S1 + opening snap + diastolic rumble at apex | Mitral stenosis | All from MS and its sequelae |
| Paradoxical splitting of S2 | LBBB, severe AS, RV pacing | Delayed A2 comes after P2 |
| Pulsatile liver + giant v waves in JVP | Severe tricuspid regurgitation | Systolic regurgitant jet into RA/hepatic veins |
| Kussmaul's sign + elevated JVP + clear lungs + elevated JVP | RV infarction or constrictive pericarditis | Fixed pericardium or stiff RV cannot expand on inspiration |
| Mid-systolic click moving earlier with Valsalva/standing | Mitral valve prolapse | Smaller LV → earlier prolapse |
| Murmur louder with Valsalva, softer with squatting | HOCM | Dynamic LVOTO worsens with ↓ preload |
| Differential cyanosis (lower limbs only) | PDA-Eisenmenger | Right-to-left ductal flow into descending aorta |
| Continuous machinery murmur, infraclavicular | PDA | Continuous aorto-pulmonary pressure gradient |
| Single S2 + cyanosis + RV heave | TOF or severe PS | Absent/soft P2 from reduced pulmonary blood flow |
| Bisferiens pulse | Mixed AS+AR or HOCM | Two systolic peaks from anacrotic and tidal wave |
| Pulmonary ejection click louder in expiration | Pulmonary stenosis | Paradoxical — PV pre-opened by ↑ RV filling on inspiration |
| de Musset's sign + collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure | Severe aortic regurgitation | Large stroke volume → head nodding |
| S3 + displaced apex + elevated JVP + crepitations | Biventricular heart failure | Left and right heart failure signs combined |

## The 10 most frequently asked clinical examination question patterns

1. Which position enhances the AR murmur? → Lean forward, breath held in expiration, diaphragm at left sternal border
2. Which position enhances the MS rumble and S3? → Left lateral decubitus, bell of stethoscope at the apex
3. What happens to the HOCM murmur on Valsalva? → Increases (↓ preload → worsens LVOTO)
4. What happens to the MVP click on standing? → Moves earlier in systole (the murmur lengthens)
5. What is the Rivero-Carvalho sign? → TR murmur increases on inspiration (↑ RV filling → ↑ regurgitant volume)
6. Which S2 splitting pattern is pathognomonic of ASD? → Fixed wide splitting (does not change with respiration)
7. What is the significance of a palpable P2? → Always pathological — pulmonary hypertension
8. Can S4 be present in AF? → No — S4 requires organised atrial contraction
9. What is Kussmaul's sign and where is it seen? → JVP rises or fails to fall on inspiration; constrictive pericarditis, restrictive CMP, RV infarction, severe RHF
10. What is the significance of the Austin Flint murmur? → Mid-diastolic rumble in severe AR from functional MV obstruction by the AR jet — echoes like MS but no OS, no loud S1

## Quick reference — the OSCE cardiovascular examination sequence

Key concept: The complete 5-minute cardiovascular examination sequence for OSCE
1. General inspection: dyspnoea, cyanosis, pallor, cachexia, oedema visible
2. Hands: clubbing (Schamroth test), splinter haemorrhages, peripheral cyanosis, xanthomata, temperature
3. Radial pulse: rate, rhythm, character, volume; both radials simultaneously
4. Face: malar flush, corneal arcus, xanthelasma, conjunctival pallor/icterus
5. JVP: patient at 45°, measure height, waveform, AJR test
6. Carotid pulse: character (one side at a time), bruits
7. Blood pressure: both arms first visit; postural if indicated
8. Precordial inspection: scars, deformity, visible pulsations
9. Palpation: apex beat (location and character), parasternal heave, thrills (4 areas)
10. Auscultation — supine: 4 areas with diaphragm AND bell; S1, S2, murmurs, gallops
11. Auscultation — left lateral decubitus: apex with bell (S3, S4, MS rumble)
12. Auscultation — leaning forward: left sternal border with diaphragm (AR)
13. Dynamic auscultation: if HOCM or MVP suspected — Valsalva, squat/stand
14. Lung bases: auscultate posteriorly (crepitations, effusion)
15. Abdomen: hepatomegaly (size, tenderness, pulsatility), splenomegaly (IE), ascites
16. Legs: oedema (grade), peripheral pulses (all 8 pulses), venous changes
17. Thank and cover the patient; present findings with a summary and differential
