sections.body:
A prolonged QT is the electrical tripwire for torsades de pointes. Knowing how to measure it, which values are dangerous, and which conditions — inherited or acquired — create it determines whether your patient lives or dies from a preventable arrhythmia.

## Why the QT interval matters

The QT interval represents the total duration of ventricular electrical activity — depolarisation plus repolarisation. During the latter portion of the T wave, the ventricle is in its relative refractory period: some cells have recovered excitability and others have not. A stimulus arriving during this vulnerable window (an R-on-T phenomenon) can trigger re-entrant circuits that cannot be sustained normally — leading to torsades de pointes (TdP), which can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

A longer QT = a longer vulnerable window = more opportunity for a triggering beat to find the ventricle partially recovered and spark TdP.

Key concept: QTc >500 ms is the clinical danger threshold for torsades de pointes
QTc 440–460 ms = borderline prolonged (review drugs and electrolytes). QTc 460–500 ms = definitely prolonged (avoid all QT-prolonging agents, correct electrolytes, consider cardiology review). QTc >500 ms = high-risk TdP zone — immediate review of all medications, electrolytes, and consider telemetry monitoring. QTc >600 ms = imminent TdP risk — urgent intervention needed. Normal values: men <440 ms, women <460 ms (women have slightly longer QT at baseline due to hormonal effects on ion channels).

## How to measure QTc correctly

Common errors invalidate QTc calculations. Follow this process precisely:

1. Choose the right lead: V5 or II usually give the clearest T-wave endpoint. Avoid leads where the T wave is flat or blends into a U wave.
2. Identify the start of the QRS: the very first deflection from baseline — this may be a tiny Q wave, do not miss it.
3. Identify the end of the T wave: where the T wave returns to the TP baseline. Use the tangent method — draw a line along the steepest downslope of the T wave and extend it to the baseline. The intersection is the T-wave end. Do not include the U wave.
4. Measure the RR interval in seconds from one QRS onset to the next.
5. Apply Bazett's formula:

Equation: QTc = QT (in ms) ÷ √RR interval (in seconds)

Common shortcut: at HR 60 bpm (RR = 1.0 s), QTc = QT. At HR 75 bpm (RR = 0.80 s), QTc = QT ÷ 0.894. At HR 100 bpm (RR = 0.60 s), QTc = QT ÷ 0.775. Tachycardia shortens QT — if the measured QT looks short at HR 120, the QTc may still be prolonged when corrected.

Exam tip: The three most common QTc measurement mistakes: Including the U wave: Prominent U waves (common in hypokalaemia) follow the T wave and can be mistaken for T-wave prolongation. Measure only to where the T wave meets baseline — the U wave after it is separate.
Using a single-beat measurement: QT varies beat to beat in irregular rhythms (AF). Use 3–5 beats and average the QT, then correct using the mean RR.
Not correcting for rate: A QT of 440 ms at HR 50 bpm is actually prolonged (QTc ~500 ms). A QT of 380 ms at HR 100 bpm is actually prolonged (QTc ~490 ms). Never report the raw QT without correction.

## Congenital Long QT Syndrome (LQTS)

Congenital LQTS is caused by mutations in cardiac ion channel genes, producing abnormally prolonged repolarisation. There are >15 subtypes; three are clinically most important:

| Type | Gene / Channel | T-wave morphology | Classic trigger | Management pearls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LQT1 | KCNQ1 / IKs (slow K⁺ current) | Broad-based, smooth T wave | Exercise, swimming, emotional arousal | Beta-blockers highly effective (IKs normally shortens QT during exercise — blocking this protective current worsens QT, but overall BB reduces events) |
| LQT2 | KCNH2 / IKr (rapid K⁺ current) | Notched or biphasic T waves, low amplitude | Auditory stimuli (alarm clocks, doorbells), emotional startle, postpartum period | Avoid auditory triggers. BB effective. ICD for high-risk patients. Hypo-kalaemia worsens — keep K⁺ >4.5 mmol/L. |
| LQT3 | SCN5A / INa (late Na⁺ inward current) | Long isoelectric ST segment then late T wave (ST prolonged) | Bradycardia, sleep, rest | BBs less effective (sometimes worse). Mexiletine or flecainide (block late Na⁺). ICD indicated in most symptomatic patients. |

Key concept: LQT1 = exercise/swimming. LQT2 = sounds/alarm. LQT3 = sleep. Three triggers, three genes.
This is the most testable LQTS fact. A question describing: young patient, drowning or near-drowning during swimming → LQT1. Patient collapsing when the phone rings or alarm goes off → LQT2. Patient dying in their sleep, or SCD found in bed → LQT3. Beta-blockers are first-line for LQT1 and LQT2. LQT3 needs a different approach (mexiletine, ICD). This is clinically critical because giving a beta-blocker to an LQT3 patient (who has events at slow heart rates) can increase risk by slowing the heart further.

## Acquired long QT syndrome

Acquired long QT is far more common than congenital LQTS and is almost always drug- or electrolyte-related. The most important causes:

### Drug causes (partial list):

| Drug class | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Antiarrhythmics (Class IA) | Quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide |
| Antiarrhythmics (Class III) | Amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide |
| Antibiotics | Azithromycin, clarithromycin, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin), chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine |
| Antipsychotics | Haloperidol, droperidol, chlorpromazine, quetiapine, ziprasidone |
| Antidepressants | TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine), citalopram (dose-dependent) |
| Antiemetics | Domperidone, metoclopramide, ondansetron (high dose IV) |
| Antifungals | Ketoconazole, fluconazole (via CYP3A4 inhibition increasing other QT-prolongers) |

### Electrolyte causes:

- Hypokalaemia — potassium channels contribute to repolarisation; K⁺ depletion prolongs it. Keep K⁺ >4.5 in any patient with risk of TdP.
- Hypomagnesaemia — magnesium stabilises ion channels. Mg²⁺ depletion worsens QT prolongation. IV Mg²⁺ is also the treatment for TdP even when Mg²⁺ is normal.
- Hypocalcaemia — lengthens the ST segment (plateau phase) → long QT. Classic in hypoparathyroidism.

Warning: The deadly combination: hypokalaemia + QT-prolonging drug + bradycardia. Each factor alone carries modest risk. Together, they are synergistic: low K⁺ prolongs repolarisation → QT lengthens → drug blocks further repolarisation → QT very long → bradycardia means each cycle takes longer → further QT prolongation → R-on-T PVC → TdP → VF. Hospitalised patients commonly have all three simultaneously (diuretics causing K⁺ loss, antibiotics or antipsychotics for comorbidities, bradycardia from medications or vagal tone). Check QTc at baseline and again 4–8 hours after starting any QT-prolonging drug.

## Short QT syndrome

Rare, but testable. Short QT syndrome (QTc <320–340 ms) is caused by gain-of-function mutations in potassium channels (repolarisation accelerated) or loss-of-function mutations in calcium channels. ECG: very short QT with tall, narrow, peaked T waves (T wave immediately follows the QRS — almost no ST segment). Associated with AF, VT/VF, and sudden cardiac death. ICD is the primary treatment.

## Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT)

CPVT is not a QT disorder but is often grouped with channelopathies. Caused by mutations in the ryanodine receptor (RyR2) causing abnormal intracellular calcium release during adrenergic stimulation. The resting ECG is completely normal. The diagnosis is made by:

- Polymorphic VT or bidirectional VT (QRS axis alternates 180° beat to beat — highly characteristic) triggered by exercise or emotional stress
- Normal coronaries, normal echo, normal resting ECG and normal QTc
- Exercise ECG or adrenaline provocation reproduces the VT
- Family history of exercise-related SCD or unexplained syncope

Treatment: beta-blockers (mandatory), flecainide (additive benefit), ICD for high-risk patients. Avoid all sympathomimetics including decongestants and exercise in competitive settings.

Checkpoint: A 17-year-old girl with no structural heart disease collapses during a school swimming lesson. She is resuscitated. ECG at rest: QTc 510 ms, broad-based smooth T waves. Her brother had a similar event two years ago while swimming. What is the most likely diagnosis, what gene is involved, and what is the first-line treatment?
Congenital Long QT Syndrome Type 1 (LQT1). The three classical features: (1) QTc 510 ms — significantly prolonged; (2) broad-based smooth T waves — the LQT1 T-wave morphology; (3) event during swimming/exercise — LQT1's specific trigger (exercise increases sympathetic tone, normally IKs current shortens QT at fast rates, but this channel is defective in LQT1). Gene: KCNQ1 (loss-of-function mutation in the slow potassium current IKs). Family history confirms autosomal dominant inheritance. First-line treatment: beta-blockers (propranolol or nadolol — non-selective BB preferred over bisoprolol in LQTS) — reduce sympathetic-triggered events in LQT1 by ~80%. ICD for secondary prevention (resuscitated SCD is a Class I indication). All family members should be screened (ECG + genetic testing for the familial mutation).

sections.body:
Certain ECG patterns carry specific diagnoses that would otherwise be invisible on clinical examination. Some indicate a genetic syndrome. Some herald sudden death. Some are drug signatures. This chapter catalogs the patterns every cardiologist must recognise on sight.

## Brugada syndrome

Brugada syndrome is a genetic sodium channelopathy (SCN5A mutations in ~20–30% of cases) causing abnormal repolarisation in the RVOT, with a characteristic ST pattern in V1–V2 and a high risk of VF and sudden cardiac death — especially at rest or during fever.

### The three Brugada patterns

| Type | V1–V2 morphology | Diagnostic significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 (Coved) | Coved (convex-up) ST elevation ≥2 mm, gradually descending into an inverted T wave — "cobra head" appearance | Diagnostic. Type 1 alone = Brugada pattern. With symptoms (syncope, SCD, documented VF) or positive family/genetic history = Brugada syndrome. |
| Type 2 (Saddleback) | Saddleback ST elevation: the ST rises, then descends to ≥0.5 mm, then rises again before a positive/biphasic T wave — like a saddle | Suspicious but NOT diagnostic alone. Can convert to Type 1 with sodium channel blockers or fever. |
| Type 3 | Minor ST elevation <1 mm, non-specific | Not diagnostic. Historical classification — less used now. |

Key concept: Brugada Type 1 can be unmasked by fever — check the ECG when febrile
Many patients with Brugada syndrome have a normal ECG at rest. Fever, alcohol, cocaine, class IC drugs (flecainide, ajmaline), and some medications transiently unmask the Type 1 pattern by further blocking sodium channels. A patient who collapses during a febrile illness and is resuscitated from VF — check for Brugada pattern in V1–V2 during the fever, and again after it resolves. Provocation testing with IV ajmaline or flecainide can unmask the pattern in suspected Brugada when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic.

Warning: Always confirm V1 and V2 are correctly positioned before diagnosing Brugada. Placing V1/V2 one or two interspaces too high (2nd or 3rd ICS instead of 4th) can produce a coved ST pattern that mimics Type 1 Brugada. If the pattern disappears when leads are correctly repositioned → it was a lead placement artefact, not Brugada. If it persists → Brugada cannot be excluded. This is a life-changing diagnosis — do not make it from a single ECG with possible lead misplacement.

Management: ICD is the only proven effective treatment for Brugada syndrome. Quinidine (class IA antiarrhythmic, which also blocks Ito current — the problematic current in Brugada) may reduce VF burden and can be used as adjunct. Avoid all sodium channel blockers (flecainide, ajmaline, propafenone, TCAs), avoid fever without treatment (paracetamol proactively), avoid cocaine. Asymptomatic patients with only Type 1 pattern: risk stratify (EP study, genetics); ICD recommendation is debated in low-risk asymptomatic patients.

## WPW — the full pattern

Already covered in Chapters 4 and 5, but the resting pre-excitation ECG deserves detailed analysis here. In WPW, the accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) conducts from atria to ventricles before the AV node. The ECG shows a "fusion beat": part of the ventricle is activated via the accessory pathway (slow cell-to-cell conduction, producing the delta wave), while the rest activates via the His-Purkinje system.

Classic resting WPW pattern:

- Short PR (<120 ms) — the AV node delay is bypassed
- Delta wave — a slurred, slow upstroke at the beginning of the QRS (the accessory pathway activating its local ventricular territory before His-Purkinje completes conduction)
- Wide QRS (>120 ms) — fusion of normal and pre-excited conduction
- Secondary ST-T changes — discordant to the delta wave (T wave and delta wave in opposite directions), a secondary repolarisation change
- Pseudo-Q waves — downward delta waves in inferior leads can mimic inferior MI Q waves
- Pseudo-RBBB or LBBB pattern — depending on accessory pathway location

Exam tip: Localising the accessory pathway from the delta wave direction (high-yield for EP exams): Delta positive in V1 → left-sided pathway (pre-excites left lateral wall, vector moves anteriorly toward V1)
Delta negative in V1 → right-sided or posteroseptal pathway
Delta positive in inferior leads → anteroseptal or left lateral pathway
Delta negative in inferior leads → posteroseptal pathway
This localisation helps plan catheter ablation — the electrophysiologist can predict where to map before entering the lab.

## Digoxin — the reverse tick

Therapeutic digoxin produces characteristic ECG changes that are not signs of toxicity — they are expected pharmacological effects:

- "Reverse tick" or "scooping" of the ST segment — the ST segment sags down in a characteristic concave-up scoop, giving it the appearance of the letter "J" reversed (or a hockey-stick). Best seen in V5–V6, I, II.
- Shortened QT interval — digoxin accelerates repolarisation by enhancing K⁺ conductance
- PR prolongation — digoxin increases vagal tone at the AV node
- T-wave flattening or inversion

Digoxin toxicity ECG features (at toxic blood levels or with hypokalaemia): virtually any arrhythmia can occur — especially regularised AF (junctional tachycardia with block — the AF disappears and a regular narrow tachycardia appears, suggesting enhanced automaticity + AV block), bidirectional VT (classic for digoxin toxicity), PAT with block, complete heart block, ventricular bigeminy, multifocal PVCs.

Clinical link: Digoxin toxicity is dramatically worsened by hypokalaemia. Digoxin works by blocking Na/K-ATPase — when K⁺ is low, more Na/K-ATPase binding sites are available for digoxin, increasing its effect at any given blood level. A "therapeutic" digoxin level becomes toxic when the patient is hypokalaemic (from diuretics — the classic combination in heart failure). Treat digoxin toxicity: stop digoxin, correct K⁺, and consider digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) for serious arrhythmias or haemodynamic compromise.

## Hyperkalaemia — the ECG progression

Hyperkalaemia produces a predictable ECG sequence as potassium rises. Knowing this sequence allows you to estimate severity from the ECG alone:

| Serum K⁺ | ECG changes | Clinical action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5.5–6.0 mmol/L | Tall, narrow, peaked ("tented") T waves — symmetric, high amplitude, often >5 mm in precordial leads | Restrict K⁺, review medications, check renal function |
| 6.0–6.5 mmol/L | PR prolongation, P-wave flattening and widening | IV dextrose + insulin, salbutamol nebulisers; urgent dialysis discussion |
| 6.5–7.0 mmol/L | P waves disappear ("sinoventricular conduction" — the SA node still fires but the depressed atrial conduction produces no visible P wave) | IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% immediately (membrane stabilisation) |
| >7.0 mmol/L | QRS widening, RBBB or LBBB morphology, increasing QRS distortion | Cardiac arrest imminent — IV calcium, insulin-dextrose, emergency dialysis |
| >8.0 mmol/L | Sinusoidal pattern — QRS and T merge into a continuous wave, no distinct waveforms. VF and asystole. | Cardiac arrest — immediate resuscitation + emergency dialysis |

Key concept: First sign of hyperkalaemia on ECG: symmetric, tall, narrow, peaked T waves
The classic teaching is "tented T waves" — symmetric, narrow-based, high-amplitude T waves, like a tent or spike. Compare to hyperacute T waves of MI (which are broad-based and asymmetric). In a patient with renal failure, check for these T waves — even if the nurse says "the K⁺ result is still pending." Peaked T waves in a dialysis patient or AKI patient = treat empirically for hyperkalaemia while awaiting the result.

## Hypokalaemia — flat T waves and U waves

Hypokalaemia produces the opposite effect — repolarisation is prolonged (QT prolonged) and the T wave is reduced or replaced by a prominent U wave:

- Flat or inverted T waves
- Prominent U waves — in V2–V3, the U wave becomes taller than the T wave. When the U wave is taller than the T in the same lead → suspect K⁺ <3.0 mmol/L
- Apparent prolonged QT — if the U wave is included in the measurement (common mistake)
- ST depression — secondary to repolarisation changes

Hypokalaemia combined with QT-prolonging drugs is particularly dangerous — TdP risk is greatly amplified. Correct K⁺ to >4.0–4.5 mmol/L in any patient on QT-prolonging drugs or with known LQTS.

## Hypothermia — Osborn waves (J waves)

Hypothermia (core temperature <35°C) produces characteristic ECG changes, most notably the Osborn wave (J wave):

- A positive notch or hump at the J-point (the junction between the QRS and ST segment), most prominent in V3–V6 and inferior leads
- Height and width correlate with severity of hypothermia — the colder the patient, the larger the Osborn wave
- Bradycardia — sinus bradycardia, AF, or junctional rhythm
- Prolonged all intervals (PR, QRS, QT) — hypothermia slows all conduction
- Risk of VF, especially during rewarming

Mental model: The Osborn wave looks like a "camel hump" after the QRS — a small positive bump sitting at the junction between the QRS end and the ST segment. Its presence in a bradycardic patient with altered consciousness and low body temperature is essentially diagnostic of significant hypothermia. Treat the patient, not just the ECG — rewarm carefully, monitor continuously, have a defibrillator ready (VF threshold is very low in hypothermia).

## Paced rhythms — reading pacemaker ECGs

Pacemaker spikes appear as sharp, narrow vertical lines (artefact) on the ECG — either before the P wave (atrial pacing), before the QRS (ventricular pacing), or both. Key concepts:

- RV apical pacing (most common): pacing spike → wide QRS with LBBB morphology + extreme left axis deviation (because the RV apex activates first, then LV via slow conduction)
- Biventricular pacing (CRT): pacing spike → QRS that is narrower than intrinsic LBBB, often RBBB-like morphology — both ventricles activated simultaneously
- Failure to capture: pacing spike not followed by a P or QRS — the stimulus did not depolarise the chamber
- Failure to sense: pacemaker fires when it should not — a spike appears during an intrinsic QRS or P wave (the pacemaker did not detect the intrinsic beat)
- Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia (PMT): a re-entrant circuit using the atrial lead retrograde and triggering repetitive ventricular pacing — regular tachycardia at upper rate limit of the pacemaker

Exam tip: STEMI in paced rhythms uses the same Sgarbossa criteria as LBBB — because RV pacing produces a paced LBBB pattern (see Chapter 11). Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm, concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3, or modified Smith ratio ≥0.25. New acute chest pain in a paced patient requires immediate scrutiny of the QRS-ST relationship — do not assume "it's just the pacemaker."

## Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress cardiomyopathy)

Takotsubo causes transient apical LV ballooning triggered by catecholamine surge (emotional or physical stress). The ECG mimics anterior STEMI and then evolves characteristically:

- Acute phase: ST elevation in V3–V6 (sometimes anterior leads) — resembles LAD STEMI
- Within 24–48 hours: ST normalises but deep, diffuse T-wave inversions develop — particularly in V1–V6, often deeper than in typical ischaemia reperfusion
- QTc often markedly prolonged — from the diffuse T-wave changes; can be >500 ms
- QRS relatively spared — unlike large anterior STEMI, the QRS voltages are maintained (the wall is stunned, not dead)

The ECG evolution — acute ST elevation → marked T inversions and prolonged QT within 24–72 hours — in a patient with stress trigger, clean coronaries, and apical ballooning on echo is the classic picture. Recovery typically complete within 4–8 weeks.

Checkpoint: A 55-year-old woman with known chronic kidney disease on amlodipine and furosemide is found confused at home. HR 48 bpm, BP 95/60. ECG shows absent P waves, wide QRS at 160 ms, and large symmetric T waves in all leads. What is the most urgent ECG diagnosis, and what is the first drug to give?
Severe hyperkalaemia with sinoventricular conduction and widened QRS. The ECG sequence — absent P waves (atrial suppression) + very wide QRS (160 ms, marked conduction slowing) + peaked T waves — corresponds to serum K⁺ likely >7 mmol/L. This is imminent cardiac arrest. First drug: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution over 3 minutes (or calcium chloride 6.8 mL of 10%). Calcium does not lower K⁺ — it membrane-stabilises by raising the threshold potential, immediately reducing arrhythmia risk. Effect onset: 1–3 minutes. Duration: 30–60 minutes. Give as a bridge while other K⁺-lowering measures are initiated (insulin 10 units IV + 50 mL 50% dextrose, salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised, sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, arrange emergency dialysis). ECG monitoring is mandatory throughout — repeat calcium if the QRS remains wide.

A perfect knowledge of every individual finding means nothing without a system that ensures you find them. This chapter gives you a reproducible reading sequence and the exam strategy to convert pattern recognition into correct answers under time pressure.

## The 9-step systematic ECG reading sequence

Read every ECG in this order — every time, without exception. The system exists so that no finding is ever missed due to distraction by an obvious abnormality.

| Step | What to assess | Key questions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Rate | Ventricular rate (QRS rate) and atrial rate (P rate) separately | How fast? Are they the same? Use the 300-rule or count-10 method as appropriate. |
| 2. Rhythm | Regular or irregular? What is the pacemaker? | Is there a P before every QRS? A QRS after every P? Are P waves normal (positive in I and II)? |
| 3. Axis | Frontal plane QRS axis using leads I and aVF | Both positive (normal) / I positive aVF negative (LAD) / I negative aVF positive (RAD) / both negative (extreme) |
| 4. Intervals | PR interval, QRS duration, QTc | PR >200 ms? QRS ≥120 ms? Calculate QTc — is it >460 ms? |
| 5. P waves | Morphology, width, height | P-pulmonale (RAE)? P-mitrale (LAE)? PR depression (pericarditis)? |
| 6. QRS complex | Width, morphology, R-wave progression, Q waves | BBB? LVH voltage? Pathological Q waves (territory, width, height)? Poor R progression? |
| 7. ST segment | Elevation or depression, morphology, leads involved | Territory? Morphology (coved, convex, concave, horizontal, downsloping)? Concordant/discordant in BBB? |
| 8. T waves and U waves | Polarity, symmetry, height, U wave presence | Hyperacute T? Deep symmetric inversions? T-QRS concordance normal? Prominent U waves? |
| 9. Compare | Compare to any previous ECG available | What is new? What is old? Interval change is often more diagnostically important than an isolated finding. |

Key concept: Always complete the whole sequence before concluding — the second finding changes the interpretation of the first
Classic mistake: you see ST elevation in V1–V2 and immediately think "posterior MI." But step 4 reveals QRS ≥120 ms with rSR' in V1 — it's RBBB, and those are secondary ST changes. If you jump to a conclusion at Step 7 before completing Steps 4–6, you will make this error. The system protects against it. The thirty seconds it adds are worth every one.

## Reading ECG MCQs — the exam approach

ECG questions in cardiology exams take one of three formats:

1. "What does this ECG show?" — pure pattern recognition. Apply the 9-step sequence mentally. State the most important finding first.
2. "What is the most appropriate management?" — pattern recognition plus clinical reasoning. Identify the diagnosis from the ECG description, then apply management principles.
3. "Which ECG pattern is associated with condition X?" — requires knowing both the clinical condition and its ECG signature.

Exam tip: For ECG MCQs with a described pattern: Do not read the answer options first. Read the ECG description, mentally apply your 9-step sequence, form your diagnosis, then look at the options to find your answer. Reading the options first biases you toward the most familiar-sounding diagnosis — which is how the "attractive wrong answer" works.

## The 10 most commonly tested ECG patterns — high yield summary

| Pattern | Key ECG features | The exam trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inferior STEMI | ST elevation II, III, aVF; reciprocal depression I, aVL | Missing V4R elevation (RV infarct) → giving nitrates |
| Anterior STEMI | ST elevation V1–V4; reciprocal depression inferior leads | Not recognising cardiogenic shock signs (tachycardia + hypotension) |
| Posterior MI | ST depression + tall R in V1–V3 (mirror image) | Calling it NSTEMI; not placing V7–V9 |
| Atrial fibrillation | Irregularly irregular, no P waves | Forgetting EF before choosing rate-control drug |
| Complete heart block | P waves and QRS fully dissociated, different rates | Confusing with Wenckebach; missing escape rate clue (narrow vs wide) |
| Mobitz II | Fixed PR, sudden dropped QRS without warning | Treating as benign; it always needs pacing regardless of symptoms |
| LBBB (new) | Wide QRS, QS in V1, broad R in I/aVL, no Q in I | Missing STEMI below the LBBB; not applying Sgarbossa |
| VT | Wide complex tachycardia, AV dissociation | Treating as SVT with aberrancy; giving verapamil → death |
| WPW + AF | Irregular wide complex tachy, varying morphology, very fast rate | Giving adenosine/digoxin/verapamil → VF |
| Hyperkalaemia (severe) | Absent P, wide QRS, sinusoidal pattern | Not recognising urgency; not giving calcium gluconate first |

## The five "do not miss" ECG diagnoses

These five patterns are examiner favourites because they are life-threatening and involve a specific dangerous error if missed:

1. Wellens' syndrome — biphasic or deeply inverted T waves V2–V3 in a pain-free patient. Do not exercise-test. Urgent angio.
2. RV infarction — inferior STEMI + ST elevation V4R. Do not give nitrates. Give fluids.
3. WPW + AF — irregular wide complex tachycardia. Do not give adenosine, digoxin, or verapamil. Cardiovert.
4. Mobitz II AV block — fixed PR, sudden dropped beats. Do not discharge. Permanent pacemaker.
5. De Winter T waves — upsloping ST depression + tall T waves V1–V6. Proximal LAD occlusion. Treat as STEMI.

## Common ECG traps and how to avoid them

Trap 1: The wide complex tachycardia: You see a fast wide complex rhythm. The patient looks OK. You consider adenosine. Stop. Apply the Brugada algorithm. AV dissociation = VT. Wide complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise. Adenosine in VT → haemodynamic collapse. Treat as VT (amiodarone or cardiovert).

Trap 2: The pain-free patient with abnormal T waves: Pain resolved, troponin minimal, the patient wants to go home. But V2–V3 show biphasic T waves. Stop. This is Wellens'. The LAD is critically stenosed and will re-occlude. Admit, urgent angiography. Stress-test in clinic is the wrong answer.

Trap 3: The rate at exactly 150 bpm: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm. You think AVNRT or sinus tachycardia. Consider flutter first. Atrial flutter with 2:1 block = 300 atrial / 2 = 150 ventricular. Look for hidden sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF or between QRS complexes. Give adenosine diagnostically to slow the ventricular rate and unmask the flutter waves.

Trap 4: The "normal" ECG in LBBB: LBBB on the ECG. Acute chest pain. "The ECG can't be interpreted for ischaemia in LBBB." This is outdated. Apply Sgarbossa criteria. Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm = STEMI until proven otherwise. New LBBB with chest pain = STEMI equivalent. Activate the cath lab.

## Building pattern recognition — deliberate practice guide

Pattern recognition is a skill, not knowledge. It must be built through repetition with feedback. The most effective approach:

1. Look first, then label: For every practice ECG, spend 30 seconds applying the 9-step sequence mentally before reading any description or question. Form your interpretation, then compare to the key.
2. Explain each finding out loud: After identifying a pattern, state why it appears. "The rSR' in V1 is from late right ventricular activation because the right bundle is blocked." This converts recognition into understanding, which generalises to variant presentations.
3. Use flash cards for the critical patterns: The 10 patterns in the table above should be drillable in <2 seconds each. One ECG lead pattern per card. If you hesitate, the pattern is not fluent yet.
4. Read at least one real clinical ECG per day in practice — and actively apply the 9 steps, even when the clinical context makes the diagnosis obvious. You are training the habit, not just learning the fact.
5. Review your errors specifically: Every wrong interpretation reveals a gap — either in pattern recognition (you did not see it), knowledge (you did not know it), or systematic (you skipped a step). Different remedies for each.

Checkpoint: Final synthesis question: A 62-year-old man presents with 40 minutes of chest pain and diaphoresis. ECG: HR 90, PR 160 ms, QRS 148 ms with rSR' in V1 and wide S in I and V6, ST elevation 2.5 mm in II, III, aVF (convex, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL), ST depression 1 mm in V1–V2. QTc 440 ms. What are the ECG abnormalities in order, what is the most important immediate diagnosis, and what is the one investigation that must happen before giving GTN?
Systematic reading:
1. Rate — 90 bpm (normal range). 2. Rhythm — sinus (P before every QRS, P positive in II). 3. Axis — need to assess (ST changes visible). 4. Intervals — PR 160 ms (normal), QRS 148 ms (wide → BBB), QTc 440 ms (normal). 5. P waves — normal. 6. QRS — rSR' in V1 + wide S in I/V6 = RBBB. 7. ST segment — ST elevation II, III, aVF (convex) = inferior STEMI; reciprocal depression I, aVL confirms; ST depression V1–V2 may be posterior involvement or RBBB secondary change. 8. T waves — not specifically abnormal beyond ST changes. 9. Compare — not available.
Key diagnoses: (1) Acute inferior STEMI — the dominant finding requiring immediate action. (2) RBBB — new RBBB in the context of inferior STEMI often means the block is proximal to the RCA/LAD bifurcation or there is concomitant septal involvement; note this but it does not change the initial management. (3) Consider posterior MI (ST depression V1–V2 could be posterior mirror — check V7–V9).
The one test before GTN: Right-sided V4R lead. Inferior STEMI carries ~30–40% risk of concomitant RV infarction. If V4R shows ST elevation ≥1 mm — nitrates are absolutely contraindicated (preload-dependent RV infarction → GTN causes venodilation → loss of preload → cardiac output collapses). Apply V4R, read it, only then decide on GTN. If V4R negative, GTN can be given. Activate cath lab immediately — do not delay PCI for this test, which takes 30 seconds at the bedside.

The 12 leads are not 12 independent measurements — they are 12 different camera angles looking at the same electrical event. Understanding which direction each lead faces lets you localise any abnormality instantly.

## How only 10 electrodes produce 12 leads

The standard ECG uses 10 electrodes — 4 limb electrodes and 6 precordial electrodes — to produce 12 leads. This works because some leads are mathematical combinations of other electrodes, not separate physical connections.

- 4 limb electrodes: Right arm (RA), Left arm (LA), Left leg (LL), Right leg (RL — grounding only, not used in calculations)
- 6 precordial electrodes: V1 through V6 placed on the chest

The 12 leads produced are:

- Bipolar limb leads: I (LA − RA), II (LL − RA), III (LL − LA)
- Augmented unipolar limb leads: aVR (RA vs average of LA+LL), aVL (LA vs average of RA+LL), aVF (LL vs average of RA+LA)
- Precordial (unipolar) leads: V1–V6 (each chest electrode vs a central reference — Wilson's Central Terminal)

Key concept: Each lead looks at the heart from a specific anatomical direction
This is not abstract — it is geometry. Lead I looks horizontally from right to left. Lead II looks from upper right to lower left (approx 60°). Lead aVF looks straight up from below. V1 looks at the heart from the right chest. V6 looks from the left axilla. When you see a change in a specific lead or group of leads, you immediately know which wall of the heart is affected — because you know which direction that lead faces.

## The frontal plane leads — the Einthoven triangle

The limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) measure electrical activity in the frontal plane — the plane that divides the body into front and back, as if you were looking at the patient face-on. Together they form the hexaxial reference system with leads arranged at 30° intervals around a circle.

Diagram: Hexaxial reference system — frontal plane leads at 30° intervals (drawing not carried over)

## The precordial leads — the horizontal plane

The precordial leads (V1–V6) measure electrical activity in the horizontal plane — as if you were looking down at the heart from above. They sweep from right (V1) to left (V6).

| Lead | Position | What it faces | Clinical significance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | Right sternal border, 4th intercostal space | RV free wall, interventricular septum | RBBB (rSR'), posterior MI (tall R), P wave (RA enlargement — peaked P) |
| V2 | Left sternal border, 4th ICS | Septum | Brugada (coved ST elevation), posterior MI mirror, septal infarction |
| V3 | Between V2 and V4 | Anterior wall (transition) | De Winter T waves, poor R-wave progression |
| V4 | Midclavicular line, 5th ICS | Anterior wall (apex) | LAD territory, apex of LV, PVC morphology |
| V5 | Anterior axillary line, same level as V4 | Lateral wall | LCx territory, LV strain, LVH voltage |
| V6 | Midaxillary line, same level as V4–V5 | Lateral wall | LCx territory, lateral ischaemia |

## ECG territory groupings — memorise this table

| Leads | Territory | Artery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II, III, aVF | Inferior wall | RCA (85%), LCx (15%) |
| V1–V2 | Septal | LAD (proximal septal branches) |
| V3–V4 | Anterior wall | LAD |
| V5–V6, I, aVL | Lateral wall | LCx or diagonal of LAD |
| V7–V9 (posterior, non-standard) | Posterior wall | RCA (right-dominant) or LCx |
| V3R–V4R (right-sided, non-standard) | RV free wall | Proximal RCA |
| aVR | Cavity / upper right / left main territory | Left main or proximal LAD (when ST elevated) |

Key concept: Contiguous leads = neighbouring leads sharing a wall
"Contiguous leads" means leads that are anatomical neighbours. Inferior group: II, III, aVF. Anterior group: V1–V4. Lateral group: I, aVL, V5–V6. ST changes must appear in at least 2 contiguous leads to qualify as a STEMI territory. A single-lead change can be artefact or a positioning error. Two contiguous leads mean the territory is real.

## Lead placement errors — the hidden trap

Incorrect electrode placement is one of the most common sources of ECG error. These errors produce patterns that mimic real pathology:

- Left-right arm reversal (RA and LA swapped): Lead I appears inverted (P waves negative in I, positive in aVR). Looks like extreme left axis deviation. Check: is P wave positive in I and aVF? If not, check for lead reversal.
- V1 and V2 placed too high (2nd ICS instead of 4th): Common in daily practice. Causes apparent RBBB, Brugada pattern, or anterior T-wave inversions that disappear when leads are correctly repositioned.
- Precordial leads placed from right to left instead of left to right: Very rare but causes reversed R-wave progression mimicking anterior infarct.

Warning: Before diagnosing Brugada syndrome from an ECG: Always confirm V1 and V2 are correctly positioned. The Brugada pattern (coved ST elevation in V1–V2) can be produced by high precordial lead placement. In Brugada, the pattern disappears when V1/V2 are moved one interspace down to a standard position — in true Brugada, it remains. Always check lead placement before labelling a potentially life-changing genetic diagnosis.

Checkpoint: An ECG shows ST elevation in II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. Which wall and which artery? What additional leads would complete the assessment?
ST elevation in II, III, aVF = inferior wall STEMI. The reciprocal depression in I and aVL is the mirror image of the inferior elevation — confirming it is a true STEMI, not artefact. The most likely artery is the RCA (80–85% of inferior MIs). Additional leads: V4R (right-sided V4) to screen for RV infarction — ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is diagnostic. Also consider V7–V9 (posterior leads) — the posterior wall is often co-involved in inferior STEMI because the posterior descending artery branches from the RCA. If V4R shows ST elevation, nitrates are contraindicated.

title: The 12 leads — geometry of the body

sections.body:
P wave, PR interval, QRS, ST segment, T wave, QT interval — each one represents a specific electrical event. When you know exactly what each one means, every abnormality becomes a statement about which step in the cardiac electrical sequence has gone wrong.

## The annotated normal ECG

Diagram: One complete cardiac cycle — all waves, segments, and intervals labelled with their normal values (drawing not carried over)

## Each wave and interval — in full detail

### P wave

The P wave is caused by atrial depolarisation spreading from the SA node through both atria. Normal P wave: duration <120 ms (3 small squares), amplitude <2.5 mm (2.5 small squares), and must be positive in lead II and aVF (because the normal atrial depolarisation vector sweeps from upper right toward lower left — toward those leads).

A P wave before every QRS confirms that the rhythm is being driven by the SA node (sinus rhythm). If P waves are absent, the rhythm is not sinus (AF, junctional, ventricular, or flutter).

Key concept: Normal P wave: positive in II and aVF — this one test tells you sinus rhythm
The SA node fires from the upper right atrium. Depolarisation spreads downward and leftward. Lead II faces downward-left (60°). Lead aVF faces straight down (90°). Both face toward the normal P-wave vector → P must be positive in both. If the P wave is negative in II, the rhythm is either not sinus or the lead is reversed. An inverted P in II suggests the pacemaker is at the bottom of the atrium (low atrial rhythm) or AV junction — where the wave spreads upward, away from II.

### PR interval

The PR interval measures from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS. It represents the time from atrial depolarisation onset to ventricular depolarisation onset, and is mostly accounted for by the AV node delay (~100 ms of physiological delay built in to allow atrial emptying before ventricular contraction).

Normal PR: 120–200 ms (3–5 small squares).

- Short PR (<120 ms): AV node bypass (WPW — delta wave + short PR), enhanced AV conduction, or rhythm originating near the AV node (junctional).
- Long PR (>200 ms): first-degree AV block — delayed conduction through the AV node (vagal tone, inferior MI, medications, intrinsic AV nodal disease).
- Varying PR: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) — PR lengthens progressively then drops; or variable rhythm.
- PR depression: pericarditis — atrial repolarisation (Ta wave) displaced by atrial inflammation. Seen in multiple leads simultaneously.

### QRS complex

The QRS represents ventricular depolarisation. It is composed of up to three deflections:

- Q wave: initial septal depolarisation spreads from left to right (right bundle branch delivers first), producing a small downward deflection in left-facing leads (I, aVL, V5–V6). Pathological Q waves are >1 mm (0.04 s) wide or >25% of the R wave height — indicating prior transmural infarction (necrotic myocardium produces no electrical signal, leaving an unopposed vector from the opposite wall).
- R wave: main ventricular depolarisation, sweeping from base toward apex. Height varies by lead — tallest in V5–V6 in LVH.
- S wave: late depolarisation of the posterolateral LV and RV base, moving away from left-facing leads.

Normal QRS duration: <120 ms (3 small squares). A QRS ≥120 ms means ventricular depolarisation is abnormally slow — either from a bundle branch block (BBB) or an abnormal origin (ventricular ectopic, VT, pacemaker).

Key concept: R-wave progression — V1 to V6 tells you the horizontal axis transition
In normal ECGs, the R wave is small in V1 and grows progressively toward V4–V5 (the "transition zone"). The S wave is large in V1 and shrinks toward V6. The point where R equals S amplitude is the "transition zone" — normally V3–V4. Poor R-wave progression (R waves fail to grow normally from V1 to V4) suggests anterior infarction, LBBB, or incorrect precordial lead placement. Early transition (R > S in V1 or V2) suggests posterior MI, RVH, or WPW.

### ST segment

The ST segment represents the plateau phase of the ventricular action potential — the period when all ventricular cells are depolarised but repolarisation has not yet begun. In a healthy heart, all cells have the same membrane potential during this plateau, so there is no current flowing and the ST segment lies flat on the baseline (isoelectric).

Any displacement of the ST segment from baseline is abnormal and indicates that some cells have a different membrane potential from others during the plateau — caused by injury, ischaemia, or abnormal repolarisation.

- ST elevation: injured myocardium is unable to maintain normal resting potential → current flows between normal and injured zones → ST elevation in leads facing the injury. Causes: STEMI, vasospasm, pericarditis, Brugada, early repolarisation, LV aneurysm.
- ST depression: opposite vector — ischaemia of the subendocardial layer, posterior MI (mirror of posterior ST elevation), digoxin effect (scooping), LVH strain.

Normal ST segment: flat or with minor concave-up variation. Elevation >1 mm in limb leads or >2 mm in V2–V3 (≥1.5 mm in women) in two contiguous leads is the diagnostic threshold for STEMI.

### T wave

The T wave is caused by ventricular repolarisation. As explained in Chapter 1, repolarisation runs epicardium to endocardium — the opposite direction of depolarisation — which is why the T wave normally points the same way as the QRS in most leads.

Normal T wave: same polarity as QRS in I, II, V4–V6; can be inverted in aVR (normal), V1 (normal), III and aVL (sometimes normal). T waves in V1–V3 are often flat or mildly negative in women.

- Tall, peaked T waves (hyperacute T waves): earliest sign of MI — occurring within minutes of occlusion, before ST elevation develops. Also seen in hyperkalaemia.
- T-wave inversion: ischaemia (especially anterior ischaemia when >1 mm deep in V1–V4), RBBB (V1–V3), LVH strain (V5–V6), Wellens' syndrome (deep symmetric V2–V3 inversion), PE (V1–V4 + III — "right heart strain"), right ventricular strain, HCM, cardiomyopathy.
- Biphasic T waves: ischaemia (Wellens' type A — upstroke positive, downstroke negative in V2–V3).

### QT interval and U wave

The QT interval measures from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave. It represents the total duration of ventricular electrical activity (depolarisation + repolarisation). Because the QT interval shortens at fast heart rates and lengthens at slow rates, it must be corrected for rate: QTc (corrected QT).

Equation: Bazett's formula: QTc = QT / √(RR interval in seconds)

Normal QTc: <440 ms in men, <460 ms in women. QTc >500 ms is high-risk for torsades de pointes.

The U wave is a small deflection after the T wave, best seen in V2–V3 at slow heart rates. Its origin is debated (possibly Purkinje fibre repolarisation or mid-myocardial cell repolarisation). Prominent U waves suggest hypokalaemia. Inverted U waves may indicate ischaemia.

Exam tip: How to measure QT manually: Find a lead with a clear T wave end (usually V5 or II). Measure from start of QRS to end of T wave (where the T wave returns to baseline — not where the U wave begins). Count small squares × 0.04 s. Then calculate RR interval (start of one QRS to start of next, in seconds) and apply Bazett's formula. Pitfalls: Long U wave mimics long QT; measuring to end of U wave overestimates QT. Normal T-wave end can be hard to identify in tachycardia when T waves merge into the next P wave.

Checkpoint: An ECG shows: HR 80 bpm, PR 240 ms, QRS 90 ms, QT 440 ms (measured), ST isoelectric, T waves upright in II and V4-V6. What single abnormality is present and what does it mean clinically?
The PR interval is 240 ms (normal <200 ms) — this is first-degree AV block. The QRS is normal (90 ms <120 ms), so the delay is entirely in the AV node, not the bundle branches. QTc at HR 80 (RR = 0.75 s): QTc = 0.440/√0.75 = 440/0.866 = 508 ms. Wait — QTc >500 ms warrants further investigation. Let me recalculate: QT 440 ms, RR = 60/80 = 0.75 s. QTc = 440/√0.75 = 440/0.866 = 508 ms — borderline prolonged QTc. Two abnormalities: first-degree AV block AND prolonged QTc. First-degree AV block: usually benign, often vagal or drug-related (BB, digoxin, CCB) or inferior MI. QTc 508 ms: review all QT-prolonging medications and electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺).

sections.body:
Every rhythm analysis starts with one question: is this sinus? If yes, is the rate normal? This chapter gives you the fast and accurate tools to calculate both, and to recognise every deviation from normal sinus rhythm.

## Calculating heart rate

There are three methods, each suited to a different situation:

### Method 1 — The 300 rule (regular rhythms, fastest)

Count the number of large squares between two R waves. Divide 300 by that number.

Equation: HR ≈ 300 / (number of large squares between R waves)

1 large square = HR 300. 2 large squares = 150. 3 = 100. 4 = 75. 5 = 60. 6 = 50. Memorise: 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 — each is 300 divided by 1–6.

### Method 2 — The 1500 rule (regular rhythms, more precise)

Equation: HR = 1500 / (number of small squares between R waves)

### Method 3 — Count-and-multiply (irregular rhythms)

Count the number of QRS complexes in a 6-second strip (30 large squares = 6 seconds at 25 mm/s) and multiply by 10. This is the only valid method for irregular rhythms like AF.

Key concept: For irregular rhythms, you must use the count-and-multiply method — the 300 rule is meaningless
In atrial fibrillation, the RR interval varies beat to beat. Quoting "HR 150" from a single RR interval is misleading — that same strip might contain beats at HR 80 and HR 200 in different RR intervals. Always count multiple beats in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10 for mean rate in AF.

## Normal sinus rhythm — the criteria

Normal sinus rhythm (NSR) requires all of the following:

1. P wave before every QRS — SA node is the pacemaker
2. QRS after every P wave — every atrial impulse conducts to the ventricles
3. P wave positive in I and II — the atrial vector points normally (leftward and downward)
4. Regular rhythm — RR interval varies by <10%
5. Rate 60–100 bpm — at rest

Sinus tachycardia (>100 bpm): Regular, normal P morphology, rate >100. Causes: exercise, pain, anxiety, fever, anaemia, PE, hyperthyroidism, hypovolaemia, drugs (stimulants, bronchodilators, vasopressors). Sinus tachycardia is a response to something — find and treat the cause. Slowing the rate with beta-blockers in compensatory sinus tachycardia (e.g., haemorrhagic shock) is dangerous.

Sinus bradycardia (<60 bpm): Regular, normal P morphology, rate <60. Causes: athletic training (normal), sleep, vagal tone, inferior MI (RCA supplies SA node in 55%), hypothyroidism, hypothermia, medications (BB, digoxin, CCB). Treat only if symptomatic (atropine first, then pacing if atropine fails or the block is infranodal).

## Sinus arrhythmia

In sinus arrhythmia, all the criteria for sinus rhythm are met except regularity — the rate varies by >10% (often >120 ms RR variation). This is usually respiratory: rate increases on inspiration (decreased vagal tone) and decreases on expiration. This is completely normal in young healthy people. In older adults or those with cardiac disease, prominent respiratory variation may occasionally indicate autonomic dysfunction.

## Sinus node dysfunction

When the SA node itself is diseased, several patterns can occur:

- Sinus pause/arrest: a P wave fails to occur when expected. The pause is not a multiple of the normal PP interval (distinguishing it from SA exit block, where it would be an exact multiple).
- SA exit block: the SA node fires but the impulse cannot exit. Type I (Wenckebach): PP interval shortens progressively before a dropped P. Type II: PP interval constant, then abrupt pause that is exactly double the normal PP.
- Sick sinus syndrome (SSS): a combination of sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, and often alternating with tachyarrhythmias (AF or flutter). The "bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome." Patients need a pacemaker to protect against the bradycardia, and anticoagulation for the AF component.

Clinical link: Sick sinus syndrome is a common indication for permanent pacing. The typical patient is elderly with symptomatic bradycardia (dizziness, presyncope, fatigue) or sinus pauses >3 seconds, often with intermittent AF. The reason for pacing: rate-control drugs for AF make the bradycardia worse; you need a pacemaker "safety net" before you can safely treat the tachycardia. This is why many SSS patients end up with a pacemaker + anticoagulation.

## Ectopic beats — PACs and PVCs

Premature atrial contractions (PACs): an impulse fires from somewhere in the atria outside the SA node, before the next expected sinus beat. On ECG: early P wave that looks different (different morphology) from sinus P waves, followed by a narrow QRS (normal conduction), and a brief compensatory pause. Usually benign, but frequent PACs can trigger AF in susceptible individuals.

Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs): an impulse fires from somewhere in the ventricles, bypassing normal His-Purkinje conduction. On ECG: early wide QRS (>120 ms), bizarre morphology, no preceding P wave, followed by a fully compensatory pause (the sinus node timing is not reset). The T wave is opposite to the QRS direction (discordant).

Key concept: Wide + early + no P wave + compensatory pause = PVC
The fully compensatory pause occurs because the PVC does not reset the SA node. The next sinus P fires on schedule but finds the ventricle refractory (still repolarising from the PVC) — it does not conduct. The beat after that conducts normally. So the total pause from the last normal beat to the first normal beat after the PVC = exactly two normal RR intervals. This "compensatory" pause distinguishes PVCs from PACs (which have non-compensatory pauses — they do reset the SA node).

Exam tip: PVC burden and cardiomyopathy: Frequent PVCs (>10–15% of all beats, or >10,000–20,000/day on Holter) can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy even without another cause. EF improves after PVC ablation or suppression. Exam pattern: unexplained cardiomyopathy + frequent PVCs on ECG or Holter → consider PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, refer for electrophysiology study and ablation.

Checkpoint: An ECG shows regular narrow QRS complexes at 70 bpm with P waves that are positive in aVR and negative in II. What is the rhythm, and where is the pacemaker?
A P wave positive in aVR and negative in II means the atrial depolarisation vector points upward and rightward — the exact opposite of normal sinus rhythm. This means the pacemaker is firing from the lower atrium or AV junction, producing retrograde atrial activation (depolarisation spreading upward from below). This is a low atrial or junctional rhythm. It can occur in inferior MI (RCA ischaemia affecting the SA node), medications, or as a normal variant in athletes with high vagal tone. The narrow QRS confirms normal infranodal conduction — the problem is only in the pacemaker source.

title: Rate, rhythm and the sinus node

sections.body:
Any tachycardia originating above the bundle of His is supraventricular. The key clinical question is not just naming it, but whether it is narrow or wide, regular or irregular — because those two questions determine immediate management.

## The two-question triage

When you see a tachycardia, ask in order:

1. Is the QRS narrow (<120 ms) or wide (≥120 ms)?
2. Is the rhythm regular or irregular?

Diagram: Tachycardia triage — narrow vs wide, regular vs irregular determines the differential (drawing not carried over)

## Atrial fibrillation (AF)

AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia. Multiple chaotic re-entrant wavelets circulate through atrial tissue, preventing organised atrial contraction. There is no single dominant pacemaker — just chaotic electrical activity producing fibrillatory baseline.

ECG features of AF:

- Absent P waves — replaced by fibrillatory baseline (best seen in V1 as fine rapid oscillations)
- Irregularly irregular RR intervals — the defining feature. No two consecutive RR intervals are the same.
- Narrow QRS — unless aberrant conduction (RBBB or LBBB) or pre-excitation (WPW)
- Variable ventricular rate — depends on AV nodal conduction; uncontrolled AF typically 120–160 bpm

Key concept: Irregularly irregular = AF until proven otherwise
No other common arrhythmia is truly irregularly irregular. Regular tachycardias, Wenckebach (group beating — regular-irregular), and ectopics all have some pattern. Pure random irregularity = AF. If someone asks you "what is the rhythm?" and the answer is "irregularly irregular with no P waves" — the answer is atrial fibrillation.

The 3 management questions for every AF patient:

1. Rate or rhythm control? New-onset AF <48 h (or confirmed no clot by TOE) → cardioversion considered. AF >48 h → anticoagulate ≥3 weeks first (or TOE to exclude LA thrombus). Paroxysmal symptomatic AF → rhythm control (EAST-AFNET 4 trial: early rhythm control reduces cardiovascular events).
2. Anticoagulation? CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women → DOAC (preferred over warfarin). Score of 0 (men) or 0-1 (women) → anticoagulation not routinely needed.
3. Rate control drug? Normal EF: beta-blocker or non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil). Reduced EF (<40%): beta-blocker or digoxin — never diltiazem or verapamil.

Warning: AF in WPW — the most dangerous combination in arrhythmology: If a patient with WPW develops AF, the accessory pathway can conduct impulses to the ventricles at 300–400 bpm, causing VF and sudden death. ECG shows: irregularly irregular rhythm, very fast rate, wide complexes (pre-excited), varying morphology. NEVER give adenosine, digoxin, or non-DHP CCBs — all block the AV node and force conduction through the accessory pathway. Treatment: IV procainamide, IV flecainide, or immediate DC cardioversion.

## Atrial flutter

Atrial flutter is a single, large re-entrant circuit circling the right atrium, typically around the tricuspid annulus (cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter = "typical flutter"). The atrial rate is 250–350 bpm, most commonly 300 bpm.

ECG features:

- Sawtooth flutter waves — regular, continuous waves, best seen in II, III, aVF (inverted sawtooth — negative flutter waves between QRS complexes). The isoelectric line disappears — there is no flat baseline between flutter waves.
- Regular ventricular response — usually 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 block. 2:1 flutter (atrial 300 → ventricular 150 bpm) is the classic presentation. A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm should raise immediate suspicion for flutter with 2:1 block.
- 1:1 conduction (atrial = ventricular rate, both at 300 bpm) can occur with accessory pathways or class IC drug administration — causes extremely fast, haemodynamically unstable tachycardia.

Key concept: Regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm → atrial flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise
The most common flutter rate is 300/min. 2:1 block gives a ventricular rate of exactly 150 bpm — a number that is suspiciously precise and falls between sinus tachycardia and AVNRT. The sawtooth may be hidden within QRS complexes or T waves. Use vagal manoeuvres or adenosine to transiently slow the ventricular rate — the flutter waves become visible as the conducting is momentarily slowed, revealing the underlying sawtooth. This is both diagnostic and avoids treating flutter with the wrong agent.

## AVNRT — AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia

AVNRT is the most common paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). It involves a re-entrant circuit within the AV node, using a "fast pathway" (fast conduction, long refractory) and a "slow pathway" (slow conduction, short refractory). The circuit goes: down the slow pathway → back up the fast pathway. This produces simultaneous or near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation.

ECG features:

- Narrow QRS tachycardia, rate 140–220 bpm, regular
- P waves hidden in or just after QRS — retrograde P waves buried in or immediately following the QRS (RP < PR). Pseudo-S waves in II, III, aVF; pseudo-R' waves in V1 — these are retrograde P waves distorting the terminal QRS.
- Onset and offset sudden — "paroxysmal." Starts and stops like a light switch.

Clinical link: AVNRT terminates with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine because the re-entrant circuit depends on AV nodal conduction. Carotid sinus massage, Valsalva manoeuvre, or IV adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg → 12 mg (3 doses) will terminate in >90%. If adenosine does not terminate it, reconsider the diagnosis — flutter, AT, or fascicular VT may not respond. Long-term prevention: verapamil, beta-blockers, or curative catheter ablation (of the slow pathway, >95% success rate, <1% AV block risk).

## AVRT — AV re-entrant tachycardia (WPW)

AVRT uses an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) as part of the re-entrant circuit. Two types:

- Orthodromic AVRT (most common, 90%): conducts down the AV node → up the accessory pathway. Narrow QRS (normal conduction through His-Purkinje). P waves visible after QRS (RP > 70 ms). Delta wave disappears during the tachycardia.
- Antidromic AVRT (10%): conducts down the accessory pathway → up the AV node. Wide QRS (all conduction bypasses His-Purkinje). Mimics VT. Treat as WPW — avoid AV nodal agents.

Exam tip: WPW signs at rest (pre-excitation pattern): Short PR (<120 ms), delta wave (slurred initial upstroke of QRS — the first part of the QRS is widened by the accessory pathway conducting before the AV node), wide QRS (>120 ms), secondary ST-T changes (discordant to the delta wave direction). The delta wave only appears during sinus rhythm — when the accessory pathway and AV node conduct simultaneously (fusion beat). During tachycardia (orthodromic), the delta wave disappears because the ventricle is activated entirely via His-Purkinje (the accessory pathway conducts retrogradely).

## Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)

MAT: multiple ectopic atrial foci firing chaotically. ECG: ≥3 different P-wave morphologies, irregular rhythm, rate >100 bpm. The irregularity resembles AF but P waves are present and vary in shape. Almost exclusively seen in severe COPD, hypoxia, or electrolyte abnormalities. Treatment: treat the underlying cause (bronchodilators, oxygenation, correct K⁺/Mg²⁺). AV nodal agents (verapamil, metoprolol) may slow the rate but do not cure MAT.

Checkpoint: A 35-year-old woman presents with palpitations. ECG shows a narrow QRS tachycardia at 185 bpm, regular, with no clearly visible P waves but small pseudo-S waves visible in lead II and III. What is the rhythm, how do you terminate it acutely, and what long-term option is curative?
This is AVNRT — the pseudo-S waves in II and III are retrograde P waves buried just after the QRS (the fast pathway conducts retrograde rapidly, producing near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation). Acute termination: Valsalva first (ask her to bear down, or "Modified Valsalva" — Valsalva + passive leg raise has 40% success, higher than standard Valsalva). If that fails: IV adenosine 6 mg rapid bolus with immediate flush → repeat 12 mg twice if needed. AVNRT depends on AV nodal conduction — adenosine terminates it by blocking the node transiently. Long-term curative option: catheter ablation of the slow pathway — outpatient procedure, >95% success rate, low recurrence. Beta-blockers or verapamil are reasonable alternatives if she prefers medication.

sections.body:
Ventricular arrhythmias are the primary cause of sudden cardiac death. Recognising them quickly and correctly distinguishing VT from SVT-with-aberrancy is one of the highest-stakes skills in clinical ECG reading.

## The cardinal rule

Key concept: Wide complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise
In any adult with structural heart disease (prior MI, cardiomyopathy, LVH), a wide complex tachycardia is VT in 80–90% of cases. Treating VT as SVT with aberrancy is dangerous — AV nodal agents (adenosine, verapamil) in VT can cause haemodynamic collapse and VF. Treating SVT with aberrancy as VT is safe — amiodarone terminates most SVT too. When in doubt, treat as VT.

## Ventricular tachycardia (VT)

VT is defined as ≥3 consecutive ventricular beats at rate >100 bpm. Types:

- Monomorphic VT: all QRS complexes have the same morphology — the same ectopic focus fires repeatedly, producing the same abnormal conduction pattern each time. Associated with structural heart disease (scar from prior MI is the most common substrate).
- Polymorphic VT: QRS morphology changes from beat to beat — multiple circuits or foci, or changing activation patterns. Associated with acute ischaemia, long QT syndrome (torsades), Brugada, catecholaminergic VT (CPVT).
- VT storm: ≥3 separate VT episodes within 24 hours, each requiring termination. Medical emergency. IV amiodarone, BB, treat ischaemia, consider catheter ablation.

## How to distinguish VT from SVT with aberrancy — the Brugada algorithm

Four criteria, applied in order. If any one criterion is met → VT. Only if all four are absent is SVT with aberrancy the preferred diagnosis.

| Step | Ask | VT diagnosis if… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Is there an RS complex in any precordial lead? | If NO RS anywhere (all positive or all negative in all precordial leads) → VT |
| 2 | Is the RS interval (onset of R to nadir of S) >100 ms in any precordial lead? | If YES → VT |
| 3 | Is there AV dissociation? | If YES → VT (P waves at a different rate from QRS = the ventricle is independent of the atria) |
| 4 | Are there morphology criteria for VT in V1 and V6? | If YES → VT (see below) |

Morphology criteria (Step 4):

- RBBB-like VT (monophasic R or Rr' in V1; QS or rS in V6): "rabbit-ear" with the left ear taller — in true RBBB, the right ear (first peak) is taller. If left ear is taller → VT.
- LBBB-like VT (broad R in V1 >30 ms; notched or slurred S downstroke in V1; R to nadir of S in V1 >70 ms; any Q in V6)

Key concept: AV dissociation is pathognomonic of VT
In VT, the ventricles are activated by an ectopic ventricular focus. The SA node continues to fire at its own rate, but P waves cannot conduct to the (refractory) ventricles. So: P waves at one rate, QRS complexes at a different (faster) rate, completely independent of each other. Look for P waves "marching through" the QRS complexes at a different rate. This is definitive — no SVT mechanism produces AV dissociation. Additional signs: fusion beats (a QRS midway between normal and VT morphology — the sinus impulse partially conducts into the ventricle while the VT fires simultaneously) and capture beats (a normal narrow QRS in the middle of VT — a sinus impulse that captured the ventricle before the VT).

## VT management

| Haemodynamic status | Rhythm | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered consciousness, pulmonary oedema) | Any VT or pulseless VT | Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (200 J biphasic). If pulseless → unsynchronised shock (defibrillation). Start CPR if pulseless. |
| Stable with structural heart disease | Monomorphic VT | IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min infusion. Alternative: IV lidocaine 1 mg/kg. Can cardiovert electively if drug fails. |
| Stable without structural heart disease | RVOT VT (LBBB + inferior axis) | Adenosine (often terminates idiopathic RVOT VT). Verapamil for fascicular VT. Catheter ablation curative. |
| Torsades de pointes | Polymorphic VT + long QT | IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 2 min. Correct K⁺/Mg²⁺. Overdrive pacing. Isoprenaline to shorten QT temporarily. Never amiodarone. |

## Ventricular fibrillation (VF)

VF: completely chaotic ventricular electrical activity. No coordinated contraction. No cardiac output. ECG: rapid, irregular, polymorphic deflections with no recognisable QRS complexes — a completely chaotic, undulating baseline.

VF = pulseless cardiac arrest. Begin CPR immediately. Defibrillate as soon as available. Every minute without defibrillation reduces survival by ~10%. No drug terminates VF faster than electricity. After defibrillation and ROSC: IV amiodarone 300 mg bolus if VF/pulseless VT recurs, IV lidocaine as alternative. Treat reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts).

## Torsades de pointes (TdP)

TdP is a specific polymorphic VT where the QRS axis continuously changes, producing a characteristic twisting of the QRS complexes around the baseline ("twisting of the points" in French). It occurs in the context of a prolonged QT interval — either congenital (LQTS) or acquired (drugs, electrolytes).

ECG features:

- Polymorphic wide complex tachycardia
- QRS amplitude alternates, axis rotates — "spindle" appearance
- Preceded by long QT on baseline ECG
- Often initiated by a late PVC that falls on the T wave (R-on-T phenomenon)
- Often self-terminating but can degenerate into VF

Warning: Amiodarone is contraindicated in TdP — it further prolongs QTc. The correct immediate treatment is: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g bolus (even if serum Mg²⁺ is normal — it works by stabilising the membrane). Then identify and remove all QT-prolonging drugs. Check and correct K⁺ (keep >4.5 mmol/L) and Mg²⁺. If recurrent TdP: overdrive pacing at rate 90–100 bpm (faster rate shortens the QT) or IV isoprenaline. If TdP degenerates to VF: unsynchronised shock.

Checkpoint: A patient with a history of LVEF 25% (dilated CMP) is brought in unconscious. ECG monitor shows a regular wide complex tachycardia at 160 bpm. A colleague suggests giving IV verapamil for rate control. What do you do?
Do not give verapamil. In a patient with structural heart disease (LVEF 25%), a wide complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. The patient is unconscious = haemodynamically unstable. The correct action is: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (200 J biphasic, or 120–150 J with manufacturer's recommended settings). Do not delay for a drug trial when the patient is unstable. Verapamil in VT causes further vasodilation, negative inotropy, and haemodynamic collapse → VF → death. After successful cardioversion: IV amiodarone infusion to prevent recurrence, find and treat the trigger (electrolyte imbalance, ischaemia, medication non-compliance).

sections.body:
Not all AV blocks are equal. A first-degree block is a footnote. Mobitz II can kill without warning. Complete heart block in the wrong patient needs a pacemaker within hours. The key is knowing where the block is — and what might be coming next.

## The hierarchy of danger

AV blocks are classified by how completely conduction through the AV node (or infranodal conduction system) is impaired. The danger of a block is primarily determined by its location — not just its degree.

Diagram: AV block patterns — ECG appearance and clinical significance (drawing not carried over)

## First-degree AV block

Every P wave conducts to the ventricle — but the PR interval is prolonged (>200 ms). Every beat has a corresponding QRS, just with a longer-than-normal delay through the AV node. No beats are dropped.

Causes: vagal tone (athletes), inferior MI, medications (BB, digoxin, non-DHP CCB, amiodarone), myocarditis, intrinsic AV nodal fibrosis (elderly). Usually benign. Does not require treatment. However, a very long PR (>300 ms) can occasionally cause symptoms (pacemaker syndrome-like), and first-degree block in acute inferior MI can progress.

Key concept: In first-degree AV block, count beats: same number of P waves as QRS complexes — just with a long PR
The hallmark is 1:1 conduction with prolonged PR. Every P conducts, every QRS is preceded by a P. Nothing is dropped. This distinguishes it from all other blocks. If the PR is long but every P still conducts → first-degree. If any P fails to conduct → second-degree or higher.

## Second-degree AV block

Some P waves conduct and some do not. There are two fundamentally different types:

### Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)

The PR interval progressively lengthens over successive beats until one P wave fails to conduct (no QRS). After the pause, the PR resets to its shortest value and the cycle begins again. The group of beats before the pause is called a "Wenckebach period." Typical ratio: 3:2 or 4:3 (3 P waves for 2 QRS complexes, etc.).

Location: almost always within the AV node itself. The AV node is "tiring" with successive stimulations (fatigue of the slow calcium-dependent conduction). The AV node recovers during the pause. This is generally benign — the AV node is the block site, junctional escape (40–60 bpm) is reliable. Often caused by inferior MI, vagal tone, or drugs. Rarely requires pacing unless symptomatic.

### Mobitz Type II

The PR interval is constant and fixed — then without warning, one P wave fails to conduct. The next conducted beat has the same PR as all previous beats. There is no warning that the next beat will drop.

Location: below the AV node — in the His bundle or bundle branches. This is infranodal block. If the block occurs lower down, the escape pacemaker is also lower — ventricular escape at 20–40 bpm, unreliable, can fail suddenly without warning. Mobitz II almost always requires a permanent pacemaker. Can progress to complete heart block without warning.

Warning: Mobitz II is a pacemaker indication regardless of symptoms. The reason is unpredictability. The block is below the AV node, and the next step down the hierarchy (ventricular escape at 20–40 bpm) is unreliable. The patient can be walking normally, then suddenly have a 10-second pause → syncope → fall → injury. Do not discharge a patient with Mobitz II and "outpatient cardiology follow-up." Admit, monitor, arrange pacing. This is one of the most testable emergency pacing indications on cardiology exams.

### 2:1 AV Block — the one you cannot classify as Mobitz I or II

When every other P conducts (2:1 ratio), you cannot observe progressive PR lengthening (there are not enough consecutive conducted beats) or a fixed PR (you cannot compare two consecutive conducted PRs). This is a trap — 2:1 block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the 2:1 rhythm alone. Look at longer rhythm strips or shorter periods of block to determine the type. In general, narrow QRS 2:1 block suggests AV nodal (Mobitz I family). Wide QRS 2:1 block suggests infranodal (Mobitz II family) — treat more aggressively.

## Third-degree (complete) AV block

No P waves conduct to the ventricles. Complete electrical dissociation between atria and ventricles. The SA node fires at its own rate (usually 60–80 bpm). The ventricles are driven by an escape pacemaker below the level of block.

- Block at AV node level: junctional escape rhythm at 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS. More stable, better haemodynamics. Causes: inferior MI, vagal, congenital CHB, drugs.
- Block below AV node (His-Purkinje): ventricular escape at 20–40 bpm, wide QRS. Unreliable, can fail suddenly. Causes: anterior MI (bilateral bundle branch disease), fibrosis (Lenegre disease), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, surgical complication.

Key concept: Complete heart block: count P waves separately from QRS complexes — they are independent
The P waves march through at one rate. The QRS complexes march at a slower rate. They are completely independent — the PR interval varies because P waves "wander" through the QRS. This independent regularity is the signature of complete dissociation. The P rate is faster. The QRS rate is slower. They never have a fixed relationship. Compare: in third-degree block with 50 bpm P rate and 30 bpm QRS, you'll have P waves falling at: 0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.6 s and QRS at 0.3, 2.3, 4.3 s — no consistent PR interval, P waves fall "randomly" relative to QRS.

Exam tip: The exam trap: inferior STEMI → complete heart block. The RCA supplies the AV node in ~85–90% of people. Inferior STEMI can produce complete heart block — often junctional escape with narrow QRS at 40–60 bpm. This is usually temporary, resolving with reperfusion. Temporary pacing threshold: symptomatic bradycardia, Mobitz II in the context of anterior MI, complete heart block with ventricular escape, or bifascicular block with new first-degree AV block (suggesting imminent complete block). After reperfusion of inferior STEMI, most CHB resolves — permanent pacemaker is not automatically needed.

Checkpoint: Strip shows: P waves at 70 bpm, QRS complexes at 35 bpm, completely dissociated, QRS wide at 160 ms. What is the rhythm, and what is the pacing urgency?
Complete (third-degree) heart block with wide complex ventricular escape rhythm. The wide QRS (160 ms) indicates the escape pacemaker is below the AV node and His bundle — in the bundle branches or ventricular myocardium. This is a ventricular escape at 35 bpm — inherently unreliable and can fail suddenly. This patient needs urgent temporary transvenous pacing (not just transcutaneous, which is a bridge only). If symptomatic (haemodynamically unstable, very slow rate), give atropine 0.5–1 mg IV as a bridge — but atropine works at the AV node, not below it, so may have limited effect with infranodal escape. Transcutaneous pacing as bridge. Then urgent permanent pacemaker implant — this is a Class I indication.
