sections.body:
RBBB and LBBB look complex but follow a simple logic — you just need to know what direction the conduction abnormality sends the electrical wavefront in each lead. Master V1 and I and you can identify both in 5 seconds.

## Why bundle branch blocks produce wide QRS

Normally, the His-Purkinje system delivers the electrical impulse rapidly and simultaneously to both ventricles, producing a coordinated narrow QRS (<120 ms). When one bundle branch is blocked, the ventricle on that side cannot receive the impulse through the fast Purkinje system. Instead, the impulse must "creep" across the interventricular septum via slow cell-to-cell conduction (like a signal travelling through cardiac muscle without the expressway). This takes much longer — hence the QRS widens to ≥120 ms.

Key concept: Any QRS ≥120 ms means conduction through one or both ventricles is abnormally slow
Wide QRS has three major causes: (1) bundle branch block — normal sinus depolarisation but aberrant conduction to one ventricle; (2) ventricular origin — impulse starts in ventricular myocardium (VT, PVC, pacemaker rhythm); (3) pre-excitation — accessory pathway activates part of the ventricle before the AV node (WPW). The QRS width alone does not tell you which — that requires morphology analysis.

## Right bundle branch block (RBBB)

In RBBB, the right bundle is blocked. The left ventricle activates normally (via the intact left bundle). The right ventricle activates late, via slow conduction from the LV through the septum to the RV free wall. This late RV activation appears as a late additional deflection in the leads that face the RV — primarily V1.

RBBB criteria (requires all):

1. QRS ≥120 ms
2. rSR' pattern in V1 — a "rabbit ears" or "M-shaped" pattern in V1. The initial r is septal activation (L→R), S is LV activation, R' is the late RV activation. Think: "rabbit ears in V1 facing right."
3. Wide S wave in I, V5–V6 — the delayed RV activation moves away from the left-facing leads, producing a broad terminal S wave.
4. T-wave inversion in V1–V2 (secondary repolarisation change — normal in RBBB, not a sign of ischaemia).

Diagram: RBBB vs LBBB — the key distinguishing features in V1 and lead I (drawing not carried over)

## Left bundle branch block (LBBB)

In LBBB, the left bundle is blocked. The right ventricle activates normally (via the right bundle). The left ventricle activates late via slow conduction from the RV through the septum to the LV free wall — the opposite direction from normal. This reversed septal activation and late LV activation produces characteristic findings.

LBBB criteria (requires all):

1. QRS ≥120 ms
2. Broad monophasic R wave in I, aVL, V5–V6 — no Q wave in these leads (normal septal Q disappears because septal activation is now R→L instead of L→R), no S wave (late LV activation moves toward left-facing leads).
3. QS or rS in V1 — the late LV activation moves entirely away from V1. Deep, broad negative deflection.
4. Discordant T waves — T waves in the opposite direction from the QRS in nearly every lead (T inverted in I, V5–V6; T upright in V1). This is a secondary repolarisation change and is expected in LBBB.

Warning: New LBBB is a STEMI equivalent until proven otherwise. A new LBBB in the setting of chest pain should be treated as a STEMI — urgent angiography. The reason: LBBB distorts the ST segment and masks ischaemia changes in almost all leads (the discordant T waves and ST changes are expected in LBBB, making new ischaemia invisible). Use the Sgarbossa criteria to detect STEMI in the context of LBBB (see Chapter 11). Never dismiss chest pain + new LBBB as "just LBBB" — this is one of the most fatal ECG misses.

## Fascicular blocks (hemiblocks)

The left bundle branch has two main fascicles — the left anterior fascicle (LAF) and the left posterior fascicle (LPF). Block of either fascicle causes a relatively narrow QRS (<120 ms, or 100–119 ms) with an abnormal axis, but no complete bundle branch morphology.

- Left anterior fascicular block (LAFB): LAF is blocked → early inferior activation dominates → then superior LV activates late → net vector shifts upward and leftward. ECG: marked left axis deviation (−45° to −90°), small Q in I/aVL, small R in II/III/aVF (qR in I, rS in II/III/aVF), QRS 100–119 ms. Most common fascicular block.
- Left posterior fascicular block (LPFB): LPF is blocked → early superior activation dominates → inferior LV activates late → net vector shifts downward and rightward. ECG: right axis deviation (>+90° or >+120°), small R in I/aVL, small Q in II/III/aVF, QRS 100–119 ms. Must exclude other causes of RAD first (RVH, lateral MI, normal in tall thin adults, lead reversal).

## Bifascicular and trifascicular block

Bifascicular block: two of the three main fascicles are blocked simultaneously:

- RBBB + LAFB: most common bifascicular combination. ECG: RBBB morphology + left axis deviation.
- RBBB + LPFB: ECG: RBBB morphology + right axis deviation (after excluding other RAD causes).
- LBBB itself = block of both left fascicles simultaneously.

Trifascicular block: all three fascicles are diseased — not necessarily blocked simultaneously. Clinical manifestation: bifascicular block + prolonged PR interval (the third fascicle conducts but slowly). This is a high-risk state — any transient deterioration in the partially-conducting fascicle causes complete heart block. Trifascicular block is generally a Class IIa indication for prophylactic pacemaker implantation, particularly if symptomatic (syncope, presyncope).

Exam tip: Quick BBB identification — 5-second method:
Step 1 — Is QRS ≥120 ms? If no, not a complete BBB.
Step 2 — Look at V1. Positive terminal deflection (R' or rSR') in V1 → RBBB. Negative terminal deflection (deep QS or rS) → LBBB.
Step 3 — Confirm with lead I. RBBB: wide S in I. LBBB: broad R, no Q or S in I.
That's it. Two leads, three criteria, 5 seconds.

Checkpoint: ECG: QRS 148 ms, rSR' in V1, wide S in V5–V6 and lead I, left axis deviation at −60°. What is the diagnosis?
RBBB + left anterior fascicular block = bifascicular block. The wide QRS (148 ms) confirms complete BBB. The rSR' in V1 and wide S in I confirm RBBB. The left axis deviation (−60°, beyond the normal −30° limit) confirms LAFB. This is the most common bifascicular combination. Clinical significance: suggests widespread conduction system disease. If this is acute in the setting of chest pain — admit for monitoring. If new and the patient has syncope — trifascicular block may be developing (check PR interval on a longer rhythm strip). If chronic and asymptomatic, typically does not need pacing unless symptoms develop. If the PR is also prolonged in this context (PR >200 ms) = trifascicular block → consider pacing referral.

sections.body:
Ischaemia produces three types of ECG change — and they correlate with how severe the imbalance is and which layer of the myocardium is affected. Understanding the physiology behind each change is more reliable than memorising appearances.

## The ischaemic cascade on ECG

When myocardial ischaemia develops, the ECG changes in a predictable sequence. The earliest changes occur within seconds to minutes of occlusion and progress through the following stages:

1. Hyperacute T waves — tall, peaked, broad T waves. Occur within the first few minutes. May be the only change in very early occlusion.
2. ST elevation — develops over minutes to an hour. Indicates transmural (full-thickness) injury current.
3. Q waves — develop over hours as myocardium necroses and loses electrical activity. May appear within 1–2 hours in large occlusions.
4. T-wave inversion — develops as reperfusion occurs or as the acute phase passes.
5. Persistent Q waves, T inversion — permanent finding in complete transmural infarction. Persistent ST elevation suggests LV aneurysm.

Key concept: Subendocardial ischaemia → ST depression. Transmural ischaemia/injury → ST elevation.
The inner layer (subendocardium) is most vulnerable to ischaemia. When only the subendocardium is ischaemic, the injury current vector points away from the ischaemic zone (toward the epicardium) → the leads facing the epicardium show ST depression. When the full thickness of the wall is ischaemic/injured (STEMI), the injury current vector points toward the ischaemic zone → leads facing that wall show ST elevation. This is not just a pattern to memorise — it follows directly from the vector theory of Chapter 1.

## ST depression — patterns and causes

ST depression must be ≥1 mm below the isoelectric line (TP baseline) in at least 2 contiguous leads to be significant. There are three morphological types:

- Horizontal ST depression — flat, runs parallel to the baseline. The most specific for ischaemia. Associated with demand ischaemia (exertion, tachycardia) or NSTEMI (subendocardial injury).
- Downsloping ST depression — slopes downward from J-point. Highly specific for ischaemia. Also associated with NSTEMI and digitalis effect.
- Upsloping ST depression — rises from J-point toward the T wave. Less specific — can occur normally at fast heart rates (rate-dependent repolarisation). Only considered significant if the slope is very steep and ST is still >1 mm depressed at 80 ms after J-point.

Diagram: Three types of ST depression — only horizontal and downsloping are highly specific for ischaemia (drawing not carried over)

## ST depression as a mirror image of posterior MI

This is the most commonly missed finding in ischaemia. The posterior wall of the LV is not directly viewed by standard leads V1–V6. When the posterior wall has a STEMI (transmural injury), the ST elevation in the posterior wall is seen as its mirror image (reciprocal) in the anterior leads V1–V3:

- ST depression in V1–V3
- Tall, broad R wave in V1 or V2 (the mirror of a Q wave)
- Upright T waves in V1–V3 (the mirror of inverted T waves)

This can be confused for anterior ischaemia or RBBB. The key: in posterior MI, the R wave in V1 is tall and broad, whereas in anterior ischaemia, the R wave is absent or small (poor R-wave progression).

Key concept: Posterior MI = ST depression + tall R wave in V1 — get posterior leads V7–V9
If you see horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with a tall R wave in V1 and the patient has chest pain, place posterior leads V7 (left posterior axillary line), V8 (left mid-scapular line), V9 (left of spine) — all at the same horizontal level as V4–V6. ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9 confirms posterior STEMI. Treatment: same as STEMI — urgent PCI. Without posterior leads, these patients are frequently discharged as "NSTEMI" or "demand ischaemia."

## T-wave changes in ischaemia

Hyperacute T waves (earliest ischaemia sign): tall, broad, peaked, often asymmetric. Appear in the territory of the occluded vessel within minutes of occlusion — before ST elevation develops. Important because they can be the only finding in the very early window. May be subtle and overlooked if only the classic "tombstone" STEMI pattern is sought.

T-wave inversions: multiple contexts:

- Deep symmetric T inversions in V1–V4: anterior ischaemia (LAD territory). Also Wellens' syndrome (critical LAD stenosis — see Chapter 11).
- T inversions in V1–V4 + III + right heart strain pattern: pulmonary embolism (acute RV pressure overload producing "right heart strain" on ECG — see RV strain pattern).
- T inversions in V5–V6 + I + aVL: LV strain from hypertension or AS (secondary to LVH).
- New T inversions in any territory after recent STEMI: part of the natural evolution — the hyperacute T wave becomes inverted as the ST normalises. Called "reperfusion T waves" — concave rather than symmetric inversions, and a good sign.

## Q waves — normal versus pathological

Q waves appear in many normal contexts. You must distinguish normal from pathological Q waves before diagnosing infarction:

| Q wave type | Characteristic | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal septal Q | <1 mm wide, <25% R height, in I, aVL, V5–V6 | Normal — septal depolarisation left to right |
| Normal Q in III | Isolated to lead III, disappears on inspiration | Normal positional change |
| Pathological Q | ≥1 mm (0.04 s) wide AND/OR ≥25% of R height, in 2+ contiguous leads | Prior transmural infarction — dead (electrically silent) myocardium |
| QS complex | Entirely negative, no R wave — the "hole" in the myocardium is so large there is no forward vector | Transmural infarction in that territory |

Clinical link: Q waves are permanent in most transmural MIs. A patient who had an anterior MI 10 years ago will still have Q waves in V1–V4. These are a scar marker, not acutely dangerous by themselves. However, new Q waves in a patient with chest pain confirm the MI has occurred (or is occurring). Q waves developing within 30 minutes of symptom onset suggests very large territory infarction — consider immediate intervention.

Exam tip: Stress ECG interpretation tip: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥1 mm during exercise is the positive criterion for exertional ischaemia. Upsloping ST depression is non-diagnostic. Additional high-risk markers on stress test: ST elevation during exercise (rare but indicates transmural ischaemia or vasospasm)
Positive at low workload (Stage 1 or 2 Bruce; HR <120 bpm)
ΔST depression >2 mm or in ≥5 leads
Failure to raise BP with exercise (suggest poor LV function)
Exercise-induced VT or VF
Duke Treadmill Score ≤−11 (high-risk)

Checkpoint: A 60-year-old man with chest pain for 2 hours. ECG shows horizontal ST depression 2.5 mm in V1, V2, V3. Tall R wave in V1 (R:S ratio >1). T waves upright in V1–V3. What is the likely diagnosis, and what do you do next?
Posterior STEMI (mirror image). ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R wave in V1 (mirror of posterior Q wave) and upright T waves (mirror of posterior T inversions) = classic posterior wall injury current seen as its reciprocal in anterior leads. This is a STEMI equivalent. Immediate action: place posterior leads V7–V8–V9 — if ST elevation ≥0.5 mm confirmed, activate the cath lab. Give aspirin 300 mg, heparin. Target: PCI <90 minutes from first medical contact. Do not mistake this for NSTEMI and delay angiography — the treatment urgency is the same as any other STEMI.

sections.body:
Every clinical decision in ACS — which drug, which timing, which intervention — follows from understanding what is happening at the plaque level. This chapter traces the chain of events from the first lipid deposit to the occluded artery.

## The substrate: atherosclerosis

Atherosclerosis begins decades before the first ACS event. The sequence:

1. Endothelial injury — the arterial endothelium is damaged by hypertension (mechanical shear stress), hyperglycaemia, smoking, dyslipidaemia, and circulating inflammatory mediators. Endothelial dysfunction precedes visible atherosclerosis by years.
2. LDL accumulation in the intima — damaged endothelium becomes permeable to LDL particles, particularly small dense LDL (sdLDL). LDL trapped in the subendothelial space undergoes oxidation (ox-LDL).
3. Macrophage infiltration and foam cell formation — ox-LDL is recognised by scavenger receptors on macrophages, which engulf it. Macrophages become lipid-laden "foam cells," accumulating to form the lipid core of the plaque.
4. Fibrous cap formation — vascular smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, proliferate, and secrete extracellular matrix (collagen), forming a fibrous cap over the lipid core. This cap is what keeps the plaque "stable."
5. Mature plaque — a stable plaque has a thick fibrous cap, a moderate lipid core, and limited inflammatory activity. These can cause angina by flow-limiting stenosis but rarely cause acute MI.

Key concept: The most dangerous plaques are NOT the most stenotic — they are the most vulnerable
A "vulnerable plaque" has: thin fibrous cap (<65 μm thick, vs 200+ μm in stable plaques), large lipid core (>40% of plaque volume), heavy macrophage infiltration at the shoulder regions, and neovascularisation within the plaque. These features make the cap prone to rupture. The coronary lesion causing a heart attack is often only 40–60% stenotic on prior angiograms — it was not haemodynamically significant and was therefore not revascularised. This is why stable CAD management cannot rely on anatomy alone.

## The trigger: plaque rupture or erosion

The acute event in ~70% of STEMI and most NSTEMI is plaque rupture — the fibrous cap tears, exposing the highly thrombogenic lipid core and underlying collagen to circulating blood. In ~30% of STEMI (more common in women and younger patients), the mechanism is plaque erosion — superficial endothelial loss without cap rupture, triggering thrombus on an intact but eroded surface.

Rupture triggers are both local (plaque instability) and systemic:

- Physical triggers — heavy exertion, Valsalva-like activity (lifting, straining), cold exposure, sexual activity. These cause sudden rises in heart rate, blood pressure, and shear stress across the plaque.
- Emotional triggers — anger, anxiety, acute grief. The catecholamine surge increases HR, BP, and coronary vasoconstriction simultaneously.
- Circadian pattern — MI incidence peaks in the morning (6 AM–12 PM) when cortisol and catecholamine levels rise with waking, platelet aggregability is highest, and fibrinolytic activity is lowest.

Mental model: Think of a vulnerable plaque as a pimple under thin skin. The skin (fibrous cap) is thin and inflamed at the edges. The contents (lipid core) are under pressure. It doesn't matter how large the swelling is — what matters is how thin and fragile the skin over it is. A tiny pimple with very thin skin ruptures more easily than a large one covered by thick skin. The plaque that ruptures isn't the biggest one on the angiogram — it's the one with the thinnest cap.

## The thrombotic cascade

Once the cap ruptures, a sequence of rapid thrombosis occurs:

1. Platelet adhesion — subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF) are exposed. Platelets adhere via GPIb (binds vWF) and GPVI/α2β1 (bind collagen).
2. Platelet activation — adherent platelets undergo shape change and release granule contents: ADP (binds P2Y12 receptor → amplifies activation), thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂, via COX-1 → vasoconstriction and further platelet activation), serotonin, platelet-activating factor. This "outside-in" signalling is the target of most antiplatelet drugs.
3. Platelet aggregation — activated platelets express GPIIb/IIIa receptors, which bind fibrinogen cross-linking platelets → platelet plug (primary haemostasis). GPIIb/IIIa is the final common pathway of platelet aggregation — its inhibition is the most powerful antiplatelet strategy.
4. Coagulation cascade — exposed tissue factor (TF, expressed by macrophages in the lipid core) activates the extrinsic pathway → thrombin generation → fibrin clot forms around the platelet plug → stable thrombus.

Diagram: The thrombotic cascade — from plaque rupture to coronary occlusion, with drug targets labelled (drawing not carried over)

## Why the thrombus determines the clinical syndrome

The nature of the thrombus determines whether the patient presents with STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina:

- Complete, persistent occlusion: Thrombus fully occludes the artery. All myocardium downstream is ischaemic. If not reperfused within 20–40 minutes, necrosis begins at the subendocardium and progresses outward (the "wavefront phenomenon"). After 6 hours, most of the jeopardised territory is dead. This is STEMI.
- Subtotal or intermittent occlusion: Thrombus partially obstructs or repeatedly occludes and spontaneously reperfuses. The downstream myocardium is ischaemic but may not die completely — or dies only in a subendocardial strip. Troponin leaks from injured/necrotic cells. This is NSTEMI.
- Transient severe ischaemia without necrosis: The thrombus causes critical ischaemia but spontaneously lyses before any cell death occurs. Troponin remains normal. Symptoms resolve completely. This is unstable angina.

Key concept: Troponin is the test of cell death — its rise marks the line between UA and NSTEMI
Troponin I and T are structural proteins of the cardiac myofilament. They are not released by ischaemia alone — they are released when the myocyte membrane ruptures (necrosis) or when there is severe enough injury to cause reversible membrane permeabilisation. A normal troponin means no myocardial necrosis has occurred. NSTEMI requires both: (1) clinical context of ACS plus (2) troponin rise above the 99th percentile. Without the troponin rise, it's unstable angina, not NSTEMI — despite identical symptoms.

## The wavefront phenomenon — why time matters so much

When the coronary artery is completely occluded, ischaemia begins immediately in the territory supplied. Necrosis (irreversible cell death) begins in the subendocardium first (most vulnerable, as we learned in the Cardiology Fundamentals guide), and spreads outward toward the epicardium like a wavefront. The progression:

- 0–20 minutes: reversible ischaemia only. No cell death. Full recovery possible with reperfusion.
- 20–40 minutes: first irreversible necrosis begins in subendocardium. Reperfusion here salvages substantial muscle.
- 1–3 hours: wavefront progresses outward. Each additional minute = ~2 million additional cardiomyocytes dead.
- 3–6 hours: most of the jeopardised territory is necrotic. Reperfusion benefit decreasing but still significant.
- 6–12 hours: limited additional salvage in completed infarction. Benefit is primarily in large STEMIs where the wavefront is still in progress or collateral vessels have slowed the progression.
- >12 hours: "late presentation" — reperfusion still indicated if ongoing ischaemia, haemodynamic instability, or uncertainty about time of onset.

Clinical link: "Time is muscle" is not a slogan — it is a quantifiable physiological reality. The GUSTO-I trial estimated that each minute of delay in STEMI reperfusion costs approximately 1.75 additional deaths per 1000 treated patients per year. For a typical STEMI patient losing 2 million cells/minute, a 60-minute delay means 120 million additional dead cardiomyocytes — the difference between mild LV dysfunction (EF 50%) and moderate-severe dysfunction (EF 35%). Every minute you shave off door-to-balloon time directly translates into preserved myocardium and improved survival.

Checkpoint: Why does aspirin need to be given immediately in ACS rather than at discharge? Trace the mechanism from plaque rupture to the specific step aspirin interrupts.
At plaque rupture, activated platelets release thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂) via the COX-1 enzyme pathway. TXA₂ does two things: (1) it further activates platelets via TP receptors, and (2) it causes coronary vasoconstriction, worsening luminal narrowing. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, blocking TXA₂ synthesis for the lifetime of the platelet (~7–10 days). This interrupts the amplification loop of TXA₂-mediated platelet activation and removes the vasoconstrictive signal. The earlier aspirin is given, the earlier this amplification loop is interrupted. A 300 mg loading dose (chewed, not swallowed whole — for faster buccal absorption) achieves near-complete platelet TXA₂ inhibition within 30 minutes. Waiting until discharge means the thrombus continues to grow with unopposed TXA₂ for hours.

sections.body:
NSTEMI management requires stratifying every patient into the right invasive timing category. Going too fast in low-risk patients wastes resources and adds procedural risk. Going too slow in high-risk patients is lethal. The key is understanding what drives each timing category.

## Four timing categories — when to go to the cath lab

| Category | Timing | Criteria (any one sufficient) | Clinical example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate (<2h) | As urgent as STEMI | Haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock; refractory chest pain despite medical therapy; life-threatening arrhythmias; mechanical complications | NSTEMI with new onset pulmonary oedema; NSTEMI with sustained VT; NSTEMI with SBP 75/50 despite resuscitation |
| Early (<24h) | Overnight if needed | GRACE >140; dynamic ST changes or new LBBB; significant troponin rise; Killip ≥2; EF <40% on echo | Elderly diabetic with large troponin rise, ST depression V1–V5; prior MI patient with troponin rise and Killip II HF signs |
| Delayed (<72h) | Within 3 days | GRACE 109–140; diabetes with any troponin rise; recurrent symptoms on medical therapy; PCI within previous 3 months; prior CABG with suspected graft failure | Middle-aged hypertensive with modest troponin rise and T-wave changes in V4–V6; no haemodynamic compromise |
| Non-invasive first | Elective workup | GRACE <109; No ECG changes; Normal serial troponins; Low clinical risk; Symptoms resolved | 55-year-old with single episode of chest tightness, normal ECG, negative troponins × 2 → exercise ECG or CT coronary angiography |

Key concept: The early invasive strategy (<24h) is NOT better than delayed invasive (<72h) in the majority of NSTEMI patients — timing matters at the extremes, not the middle
The ICTUS, RITA-3, FRISC-II, and TIMACS trials provide nuanced data: early angiography (<24h) vs delayed (<72h) shows equivalent outcomes in the average NSTEMI patient, but shows significant benefit of early strategy in high-risk subgroups (GRACE >140, dynamic ECG changes, elevated troponins). The key insight: the "urgent" signal is not simply "NSTEMI" — it's the specific risk features. A low-GRACE NSTEMI with minimal troponin elevation does not need a midnight cath lab call. A high-GRACE NSTEMI with significant ST depression does.

## The TICAGRELOR vs CLOPIDOGREL question in NSTEMI

In NSTEMI managed with an invasive strategy, ticagrelor is preferred over clopidogrel (PLATO trial). However, several situations favour clopidogrel:

- High bleeding risk (HAS-BLED ≥3) where ticagrelor's stronger platelet inhibition is dangerous
- Patient has intolerable dyspnoea from ticagrelor (15% of patients report transient dyspnoea — not bronchospasm, but can be distressing)
- CABG expected (clopidogrel held 5 days, ticagrelor held 3–5 days pre-CABG — comparable washout)
- Conservative (non-invasive) management: clopidogrel is acceptable; ticagrelor's superiority was shown predominantly in the invasive strategy arm of PLATO

## When NOT to give P2Y12 inhibitors upfront — the pre-treatment controversy

For NSTEMI patients going to immediate angiography, whether to give P2Y12 inhibitor before the procedure (pre-treatment) or at the time of PCI (if needed after seeing the anatomy) is debated:

- Arguments for pre-treatment: platelet inhibition begins before PCI, potentially reducing periprocedural MI; benefit if procedure is delayed >2h
- Arguments against: if the patient needs CABG (not PCI), P2Y12 inhibitor given 2h ago needs to be held 3–5 days before surgery — increases bleeding risk and delays surgery. The ISAR-REACT 5 trial showed prasugrel given at time of PCI (after anatomy known) was superior to ticagrelor pre-treatment in invasive NSTEMI management.
- Current practice: Pre-treatment with P2Y12 inhibitor in NSTEMI going to immediate angio (<2h) is reasonable with ticagrelor but contentious. For delayed strategy (>24h), pre-treatment is beneficial.

## Anticoagulation management around PCI in NSTEMI

This is a high-stakes practical issue that requires precision:

- If already on fondaparinux → add UFH 85 units/kg bolus IV at start of PCI (prevents catheter thrombosis, as discussed in Chapter 7)
- If already on enoxaparin → last subcutaneous dose <8h ago: no additional anticoagulation needed. >8–12h ago: additional IV enoxaparin 0.3 mg/kg bolus. Avoid switching between UFH and enoxaparin (additive bleeding risk without additive benefit — "don't cross the streams")
- If starting fresh (no prior anticoagulant) → UFH (70–100 units/kg IV) or bivalirudin at start of PCI

Exam tip: The "conservative strategy" is not the same as "no angiography." It means "non-invasive risk stratification first." In low-risk NSTEMI/UA (GRACE <109, negative troponins, no ECG changes), the appropriate management is: optimal medical therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 + anticoagulation) → exercise ECG or CT coronary angiography → stress imaging if positive or equivocal → invasive angiography if high-risk features identified on non-invasive testing. This is not "discharge home without anything." Patients in this group still need thorough evaluation before being cleared.

Checkpoint: A 66-year-old man is admitted with NSTEMI. GRACE score 160. ECG: T-wave inversions V4–V6. hs-TnT at 0h: 185 ng/L, at 3h: 280 ng/L. BP 130/85, HR 75, Killip I. Medications started: aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC. What angiography timing category is this patient in, and what practical step is required when he goes to the cath lab?
Early invasive (<24 hours): GRACE score 160 (>140 threshold), significant troponin rise (185 → 280 ng/L delta), dynamic T-wave changes in lateral leads. These are all high-risk features meeting the ≤24h invasive criteria. He is haemodynamically stable (BP 130/85, Killip I), so this is not "immediate" — but should happen overnight or first thing the next morning, not delayed to 72h. Practical step at cath lab: add IV UFH 85 units/kg bolus at the start of the procedure because he received fondaparinux (which carries catheter thrombosis risk if used alone during PCI). This is mandatory — fondaparinux alone is inadequate anticoagulation during catheter-based procedures. Then proceed with radial access angiography; if culprit lesion identified, ad-hoc PCI is appropriate.

sections.body:
Cardiogenic shock in ACS carries a 40–80% mortality despite modern treatment. Understanding the haemodynamic spiral that makes it so deadly — and the escalating interventions that can break it — is the key to managing it effectively.

## Definition and diagnosis

Cardiogenic shock is defined by the coexistence of:

- Systolic BP <90 mmHg for ≥30 minutes (or requiring vasopressors to maintain SBP ≥90), despite adequate filling
- Evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion: altered consciousness, cold/clammy extremities, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr), elevated lactate (>2.0 mmol/L), rising creatinine
- Haemodynamic criteria (when Swan-Ganz available): cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m² AND pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) >15 mmHg ("cold and wet" Forrester profile)

Key concept: The cardiogenic shock death spiral: pump failure → hypotension → coronary underperfusion → more ischaemia → more pump failure
Once cardiogenic shock begins, a self-amplifying cycle accelerates. The failed LV produces low CO → systemic hypotension → reduced coronary perfusion pressure → worsened ischaemia of the already infarcted zone AND the surviving myocardium → further pump failure → deeper hypotension → cardiac arrest. Breaking this cycle requires simultaneous: (1) immediate reperfusion (PCI) to stop the ischaemia driving the spiral; (2) haemodynamic support (vasopressors and/or MCS) to maintain coronary perfusion pressure while reperfusion is being achieved.

## The Forrester haemodynamic profiles

Forrester classified post-MI patients into four groups based on cardiac output and filling pressures. This maps directly to clinical signs:

| Profile | CI | PCWP | Clinical signs | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I — Warm and dry | Normal | Normal | No congestion, no hypoperfusion | Optimize medical management |
| II — Warm and wet | Normal | High (>18) | Pulmonary oedema, clear peripheries | Diuresis + vasodilators |
| III — Cold and dry | Low (<2.2) | Low (<15) | Hypoperfusion, cool extremities, flat JVP | Fluid challenge first; consider RV failure |
| IV — Cold and wet | Low (<2.2) | High (>18) | Both congestion AND hypoperfusion — cardiogenic shock | Vasopressors + inotropes + MCS + urgent PCI |

## Medical management of cardiogenic shock in ACS

### Vasopressors

- Norepinephrine (noradrenaline): First-line vasopressor. Primarily α1 agonist → vasoconstriction → increases SVR and MAP. Some β1 activity → mild inotropy. The SOAP-II trial showed norepinephrine had lower arrhythmia incidence than dopamine in cardiogenic shock. Start norepinephrine at 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min via central line.
- Dopamine: Dose-dependent effects (dopaminergic at low dose, β1 at mid dose, α1 at high dose). Higher rates of arrhythmia than norepinephrine. Second-line or historical.

### Inotropes

- Dobutamine: β1 agonist → increases contractility and HR. Reduces SVR (β2 effect). Useful to add when norepinephrine maintains MAP but CI remains low. Risk: tachycardia and arrhythmia. 2–20 mcg/kg/min IV.
- Milrinone: PDE3 inhibitor → increases cAMP → inotropy + vasodilation. Does not require β-receptor. Useful in catecholamine-resistant shock or post-β-blocker overdose. Half-life much longer than dobutamine — more caution with titration.
- Levosimendan: Calcium sensitiser + K-ATP channel opener. Inotropy without major tachycardia, some vasodilatory properties. Evidence in cardiogenic shock is mixed but used in some European centres and Indonesia for acute decompensated HF.

## Mechanical circulatory support (MCS)

When vasopressors and inotropes cannot maintain end-organ perfusion, mechanical support devices take over the haemodynamic burden:

| Device | Mechanism | CO support | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IABP (Intra-aortic balloon pump) | Balloon inflates in diastole (↑ diastolic BP → ↑ coronary perfusion); deflates in systole (↓ afterload) | ~0.5 L/min | STEMI with cardiogenic shock when Impella/ECMO unavailable; MR or VSD as bridge to surgery |
| Impella (CP or 5.0) | Axial flow pump across aortic valve — sucks blood from LV and ejects into aorta | 2.5–5.0 L/min (device-dependent) | Cardiogenic shock, preferred over IABP in many centres (PROTECT-II, ISAR-SHOCK data); bridge to recovery or LVAD |
| VA-ECMO | Extracorporeal pump + oxygenator. Drains venous blood, oxygenates, returns arterialised blood to aorta | 3–6 L/min | Refractory cardiogenic shock; cardiac arrest with ECPR; bridge to decision |

Clinical link: IABP-SHOCK II trial changed practice: Despite widespread use, IABP in STEMI cardiogenic shock did not reduce 30-day mortality vs medical therapy alone (37% vs 40%, p=0.69). The IABP is now Class IIb (downgraded from Class I) in STEMI shock. However, the IABP remains valuable as a bridge device and in specific situations (acute MR, VSD) where it buys time while a definitive intervention is arranged. The negative trial result does not eliminate its use — it means it is not the "fix" by itself. The fix is urgent PCI.

Warning: Routine MCS implantation before PCI in STEMI shock (prophylactic Impella) is NOT standard — the CULPRIT-SHOCK and IMPRESS trials showed no mortality benefit. The correct approach: start vasopressors, perform urgent PCI, and then escalate to MCS if haemodynamic stability is not achieved post-PCI. MCS is a rescue strategy, not a pre-emptive one, except in highly selected patients or planned high-risk PCI. Aggressive upfront MCS without PCI delays reperfusion and does not stop the ischaemic spiral.

Checkpoint: A 70-year-old man has an anterior STEMI. On arrival: BP 80/55, HR 125, cold extremities, altered consciousness. SpO₂ 88%. ECG: ST elevation V1–V5. He is being prepared for primary PCI. What is the concurrent haemodynamic management while PCI is being set up?
This is cardiogenic shock at presentation (Killip IV) — Forrester Profile IV (cold and wet). Concurrent haemodynamic management while PCI is prepared: (1) Oxygen — SpO₂ 88%, give high-flow O₂ or CPAP/NIV if pulmonary oedema is causing the desaturation; consider early intubation if deteriorating. (2) Norepinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV via central line — first-line vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg. (3) Dobutamine 5–10 mcg/kg/min IV if CI appears very low and norepinephrine maintains MAP — adds inotropy. (4) DAPT loading: aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg (or consider IV GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor if oral absorption unreliable). (5) Anticoagulation: UFH 70–100 units/kg IV. Do NOT delay PCI for any of this — all concurrent. Target: PCI as fast as possible. Post-PCI: reassess for MCS escalation if haemodynamics do not improve. Echo to assess wall motion and EF. This patient will likely need ICU admission with invasive haemodynamic monitoring (arterial line, central line minimum; Swan-Ganz or PICCO in selected cases).

sections.body:
RV infarction is the most consistently mistreated complication of inferior STEMI. The haemodynamic logic is simple once you understand why the RV is different from the LV — but the temptation to give the "reflex" drugs (nitrates, diuretics, morphine) kills these patients.

## Why RV infarction occurs

The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall of the LV and, in most patients (right-dominant circulation, ~85%), also the posterior descending artery (PDA) and the RV marginal branches that supply the RV free wall. A proximal RCA occlusion — before the RV marginal branch origin — causes both inferior STEMI and RV infarction simultaneously.

The LCx supplies the RV free wall in left-dominant patients (~15%). In these patients, inferior STEMI from LCx occlusion may also be complicated by RV infarction, though less commonly.

Key concept: RV infarction = proximal RCA occlusion = inferior STEMI + right heart failure
This is the key anatomical fact. A "just inferior STEMI" is unlikely to have significant RV involvement unless the RCA is occluded proximal to the RV marginal branch. ECG: V4R (right-sided V4) is the most sensitive and specific test — ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is >90% sensitive for RV infarction within the first 10 hours of STEMI. After 10 hours it often normalises. Get V4R in every inferior STEMI before giving any vasoactive drug.

## The RV haemodynamic logic

The RV is fundamentally different from the LV in its physiology:

- The RV is a volume pump — it works against low pulmonary vascular resistance, needs high preload (filling volume) to function
- The normal RV is thin-walled and tolerates high pressure poorly but handles high volume well
- When the RV infarcted is unable to contract → it cannot push blood into the pulmonary circulation → pulmonary blood flow falls → left heart preload falls → LV cannot fill adequately → CO falls → systemic hypotension
- The infarcted RV is entirely preload-dependent — it needs maximum venous return to generate any output at all

Mental model: Think of the infarcted RV as a flaccid bag that can no longer contract. To squeeze blood through it, you need to fill it under pressure — from the venous side. If you reduce venous pressure (with nitrates, diuretics, or morphine-related venodilation), the bag collapses and output stops entirely. The treatment is to keep filling the bag (IV fluids) and relieve the obstruction (PCI to restore RV wall motion).

## Clinical and ECG features

Clinical triad of RV infarction (Cohn's triad):

- Hypotension (systolic <90 mmHg)
- Elevated JVP (venous congestion because RV cannot forward blood)
- Clear lung fields (because pulmonary blood flow is reduced — no pulmonary oedema)

This is also the haemodynamic picture of obstructive shock (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive PE). Differentiate with ECG + V4R leads + echo (which shows dilated, poorly contracting RV with paradoxical septal motion).

ECG findings:

- ST elevation II, III, aVF (inferior STEMI)
- ST elevation V4R ≥1 mm (most sensitive and specific for RV infarction)
- May also show ST elevation V1 (early, before resolves)
- Complete heart block or Mobitz II (RCA supplies AV node — AV block is common)

Warning: The four drugs that kill patients with RV infarction: Nitrates (GTN) — venodilation reduces venous return → RV preload collapses → output ceases → sudden cardiovascular collapse
Diuretics (furosemide) — same mechanism via volume depletion
Morphine — venodilatory effect (central nervous system-mediated venodilation) reduces venous return
ACEi/ARB in the acute phase — arterial vasodilation in a patient who is completely dependent on a high SVR to maintain BP → dangerous hypotension
All four are reflexively given in "inferior STEMI with hypotension" without checking V4R. ALWAYS check V4R before ANY vasoactive or diuretic drug in inferior STEMI.

## Management of RV infarction

1. IV fluid boluses (250–500 mL normal saline) to optimise RV preload. Target: JVP normalises and BP improves. Stop when: pulmonary oedema develops or JVP remains elevated without BP improvement (the RV may be beyond fluid-responsiveness)
2. Urgent PCI — reperfusion of the proximal RCA is the definitive treatment. RV function recovers dramatically with reperfusion (unlike LV infarction where scar is permanent, RV stunning is often reversible with restored flow)
3. Temporary pacing if complete heart block or haemodynamically significant AV block develops — atropine only transiently useful (acts at AV node, not below it)
4. Vasopressors if fluids alone do not restore MAP — norepinephrine preferred. Dobutamine to augment RV contractility in severe failure
5. Maintain sinus rhythm — RV depends on atrial kick (AV synchrony). AF with loss of atrial kick in RV infarction can cause catastrophic haemodynamic collapse → immediate DC cardioversion if AF develops

Exam tip: The RV recovers — and that's the key to reassuring the patient. Unlike LV infarction where dead myocardium is replaced by non-contractile scar, the RV free wall often recovers substantial function after reperfusion because: (1) the RV is thin-walled and has lower oxygen demand per gram, making it more resistant to permanent necrosis; (2) much of the early RV dysfunction is "stunning" (reversible ischaemic dysfunction) rather than true necrosis. Patients who survive the acute haemodynamic crisis of RV infarction with successful PCI often have near-normal RV function on echo at 3–6 months.

Checkpoint: A 60-year-old man develops inferior STEMI. Immediately post-GTN spray (administered in the ambulance for chest pain), BP drops from 90/60 to 55/30. Paramedics are unsure what to do. He arrives at hospital diaphoretic, confused, with clear lungs and elevated JVP. V4R: ST elevation 2 mm. How do you immediately rescue this haemodynamic collapse?
This is GTN-induced haemodynamic collapse in the context of RV infarction. The GTN caused venodilation → preload loss → RV output ceased → systemic collapse. Immediate rescue: (1) Trendelenburg position / passive leg raise immediately — use gravity to increase venous return back to the RV without waiting for IV access. (2) IV normal saline 250–500 mL bolus as fast as possible — restore venous preload. Repeat if BP responds. (3) If BP remains critically low despite fluids: IV norepinephrine via peripheral line initially (central line placement should not delay resuscitation). (4) Do NOT give any more nitrates, diuretics, or morphine — these are now absolutely contraindicated. (5) Urgent primary PCI — the proximal RCA needs to be opened to restore RV wall motion. Recovery after successful PCI is often dramatic. (6) If complete heart block develops: temporary pacing. Document V4R findings on the medical record clearly — all future caregivers must see this contraindication.

sections.body:
The mechanical complications of acute MI — free wall rupture, ventricular septal rupture, and papillary muscle rupture — are dramatic, rapidly fatal, and entirely preventable with timely reperfusion. This chapter ensures you recognise them before they kill.

## The three mechanical catastrophes

Mechanical complications of acute MI occur because necrotic myocardium loses structural integrity. They typically present 3–7 days after MI — occasionally as early as 24 hours, and may be the first presentation in patients who did not seek initial care. All three are surgical emergencies.

### 1. Left ventricular free wall rupture

The LV free wall — usually the anterolateral wall from LAD territory infarction — ruptures into the pericardial space. This causes immediate haemopericardium and tamponade.

- Presentation: sudden catastrophic cardiovascular collapse, often with acute chest pain, rapid loss of consciousness, and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest. The ECG shows organised electrical activity without a pulse — the heart is still generating electricity but the pericardium is full of blood and no cardiac output is possible.
- Subacute rupture: in some patients, a pseudoaneurysm forms — the pericardium seals the rupture, creating a blood-filled sac connected to the LV cavity. This is less immediately fatal but will rupture if not surgically repaired. Echo shows the pseudoaneurysm (a narrow neck connecting LV to sac — distinguishing it from a true aneurysm which has a wide neck).
- Management: PEA from free wall rupture → CPR + emergency pericardiocentesis as a bridge → emergency surgery. Without surgery, survival is near zero.

Key concept: PEA cardiac arrest post-MI = think free wall rupture until proven otherwise
PEA (pulseless electrical activity) in the context of recent MI has a specific differential that differs from general PEA. The "4Hs and 4Ts" of PEA apply, but in post-MI PEA the leading diagnosis is haemopericardium from free wall rupture. During CPR: bedside echo to look for pericardial effusion. If confirmed: pericardiocentesis immediately + emergency CABG/surgery consult. Do not stop CPR for echo — do it during CPR. Pericardiocentesis decompressions the tamponade and can temporarily restore cardiac output while surgical backup is arranged.

### 2. Ventricular septal rupture (VSR / VSD)

The interventricular septum tears through the necrotic zone, creating a communication between the LV and RV — a newly acquired ventricular septal defect (VSD).

- Location: Anterior VSD from anterior MI (LAD territory); inferior/posterior VSD from inferior MI (RCA territory). Inferior VSDs are more complex and have worse prognosis.
- Presentation: new loud, harsh, pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border, often with a thrill. Rapid deterioration into cardiogenic shock. The LV pumps oxygenated blood into the RV (left-to-right shunt) → RV volume overload → pulmonary oedema + low systemic cardiac output.
- Diagnosis: echo (colour Doppler shows turbulent flow through the defect) + right heart catheterisation (step-up in O₂ saturation from RA to RV confirms the shunt).
- Management: Immediate stabilisation with IABP (reduces afterload, reduces left-to-right shunt) + vasodilators carefully (reduce shunt fraction). Definitive treatment: surgical repair or percutaneous closure device. Timing: ideally after 2–4 weeks (healed scar holds sutures better), but haemodynamic deterioration forces early intervention. Mortality: 50–80% even with surgery for large defects.

### 3. Acute mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle rupture)

The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied exclusively by the PDA (a posterior branch of the RCA in right-dominant circulation). When the RCA infarcted (inferior MI), this papillary muscle necroses and can rupture partially or completely, causing acute severe MR.

- Presentation: sudden severe pulmonary oedema 2–7 days post-MI, often in a patient who was previously stable. New soft (not loud — because the MR is into a non-dilated, compliant LA) systolic murmur at apex radiating to the axilla. Hypotension. The combination of pulmonary oedema + hypotension is the "cardiogenic shock" type of acute severe MR.
- Why the murmur may be soft: in acute severe MR, the LA was normal sized before the rupture. It cannot accommodate the sudden large regurgitant volume → LA pressure rises dramatically → pulmonary oedema. The pressure equalises quickly between LV and LA, reducing the pressure gradient across the MV during systole → the murmur becomes quieter. An acute MR murmur may be much softer than chronic MR — its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
- Diagnosis: echo (flail or torn papillary muscle, severe MR on colour Doppler). Swan-Ganz: large V-waves in PCWP tracing (the regurgitant jet into the LA creates a giant V-wave).
- Management: emergency stabilisation with vasodilators (nitroprusside — reduces SVR → reduces MR fraction), IABP. Definitive: emergency mitral valve surgery (repair or replacement). Without surgery: very high mortality. Carvedilol and other β-blockers are contraindicated acutely (negative inotropy worsens forward output).

| Exam tip: The clinical triad that distinguishes the three mechanical complications: Feature | Free wall rupture | Ventricular septal rupture | Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Presentation | Sudden PEA, shock | Progressive shock, new loud harsh PSM at LSB | Sudden pulmonary oedema, soft/absent murmur at apex |
| Murmur | None | Loud harsh PSM, thrill, at left sternal border | Soft or absent PSM at apex/axilla |
| Echo finding | Pericardial effusion, wall discontinuity | VSD on colour Doppler, step-up in O₂ from RA to RV | Flail mitral leaflet, severe MR on colour Doppler, V-waves on PCWP |
| Timing | Hours to 5 days | 3–7 days | 2–7 days |
| MI territory | Anterior (most common) | Anterior or inferior | Inferior (PM papillary muscle = RCA) |

## Post-MI arrhythmias

### Early arrhythmias (first 48 hours)

- Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR): wide complex rhythm at 60–100 bpm. A reperfusion arrhythmia — marker of successful thrombolysis or PCI. Completely benign and self-limiting. Do NOT treat.
- VF in the first 48h of STEMI: primary VF from acute ischaemia. Treat with immediate defibrillation. Does NOT necessarily indicate long-term arrhythmia risk — it is driven by acute ischaemia, not a scar-based substrate. ICD is generally not indicated for primary VF in the setting of acute STEMI (unlike late VF from scar).
- AF: occurs in 10–15% of MI patients. Associated with atrial ischaemia (RCA) or stretch from LV dysfunction. Rate control, consider anticoagulation (CHADSVASC), consider cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable.

### Late arrhythmias (after 48 hours)

- VT/VF after 48h: scar-related re-entrant circuit. Associated with reduced EF. These are the arrhythmias that drive ICD implantation — if sustained VT or VF occurs >48h post-MI and EF remains ≤35% at 90-day reassessment, ICD is indicated.
- AV blocks: may be permanent in large anterior MI (bilateral bundle branch disease) requiring permanent pacemaker. In inferior MI, AV block usually resolves after reperfusion.

## Dressler's syndrome (post-MI pericarditis)

Dressler's syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis occurring 1 week to months after MI. The immune system mounts a response against necrotic myocardial antigens (autoantigens exposed by cell death), causing pericarditis and occasionally pleuritis.

- Presentation: chest pain (pleuritic, positional), fever, pericardial friction rub, pericardial effusion on echo
- ECG: new or recurrent diffuse ST elevation (concave, pericarditis pattern) — distinct from the original infarct territory
- Treatment: aspirin (preferred over NSAIDs in post-MI patients) + colchicine 0.5 mg BD for 3 months. Avoid indomethacin and high-dose NSAIDs (impair infarct healing). Avoid corticosteroids (associated with scar thinning and rupture risk in early post-MI period)

Checkpoint: Five days after anterior STEMI, a 65-year-old man becomes acutely breathless with haemodynamic deterioration. BP 85/55, HR 115. Auscultation: harsh pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border, with a palpable thrill. No pulmonary oedema on CXR (lung fields clear). What is the diagnosis, which investigation confirms it, and what is the immediate management?
Ventricular septal rupture (VSR). The features: (1) Day 5 post-anterior MI — classic timing; (2) harsh PSM with thrill at left sternal border — the turbulent left-to-right shunt; (3) clear lungs despite shock — the shunt increases RV volume load and pulmonary blood flow is high, but the sudden LV-to-RV shunt may not immediately produce pulmonary oedema if the RV can partly compensate initially. Confirming investigation: bedside echocardiography with colour Doppler — shows the septal defect with turbulent flow from LV to RV. A right heart catheter would show a step-up in O₂ saturation from RA to RV. Immediate management: (1) IABP — reduces LV afterload, reduces the left-to-right shunt fraction; (2) careful vasodilators (nitroprusside IV) to reduce SVR and LV afterload — further reduces the shunt; (3) urgent surgical consult for VSR repair. Do NOT give diuretics as primary treatment — the shock is from LV forward output loss, not congestion (clear lungs confirm this). Emergency surgery: high-risk but the only definitive option. 30-day mortality even with surgery: 40–60% for large VSRs.

Surviving the acute event is only half the job. Secondary prevention reduces the 10-year risk of a second MI from ~40% to under 15%. Every drug in the post-ACS regimen has a specific trial, a specific mechanism, and a specific duration — this chapter makes those connections explicit.

## The five pillars of post-ACS secondary prevention

The evidence base for post-ACS secondary prevention is among the strongest in all of cardiology. Five drug classes provide mortality and event reduction:

### 1. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT)

DAPT (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) is the cornerstone of post-ACS antiplatelet strategy. Aspirin continues indefinitely. The P2Y12 inhibitor is given for a defined period, then reassessed:

- Standard duration after ACS/PCI: 12 months — based on CURE (clopidogrel), PLATO (ticagrelor), TRITON-TIMI 38 (prasugrel). At 12 months the ischaemic risk from the acute event decreases enough that dual therapy is no longer routinely required.
- Extended DAPT (>12 months): DAPT trial — 30 months of dual therapy after DES further reduces MI and stent thrombosis but increases bleeding. Appropriate for very high ischaemic risk (prior MI, DM, multivessel disease, chronic total occlusion), low bleeding risk. Ticagrelor 60 mg BD (lower maintenance dose) or clopidogrel are options for extended DAPT.
- Shortened DAPT (1–6 months): For high bleeding risk (HBR) patients (ARC-HBR criteria: age >75, CKD, anaemia, prior ICH, active cancer, oral anticoagulant use). 1-month DAPT then aspirin alone (or reverse — stop aspirin, continue P2Y12) — STOPDAPT-2, TWILIGHT trials.

Key concept: The most dangerous 30 days in post-ACS care are the first 30 days — when stent thrombosis risk is highest and DAPT must not be interrupted
Drug-eluting stents require 3–6 months for complete endothelialisation. In the first 30 days, any interruption of P2Y12 therapy risks catastrophic acute stent thrombosis (mortality 25–50%). DAPT interruption for non-cardiac surgery within 30 days of ACS or PCI should be avoided unless surgery is immediately life-saving. For elective surgery: delay ≥30 days (ideally ≥6 months). If surgery cannot be delayed: discuss with cardiology, continue aspirin perioperatively, restart P2Y12 as soon as haemostasis is secured. Never stop both antiplatelet agents simultaneously within 6 months of a DES.

Exam tip: DAPT score — helps decide extended DAPT at 12 months: Age <65 yr = 2 points; 65–74 = 1; ≥75 = −1
Cigarette smoker = 1; Diabetes = 1; Prior MI or PCI = 1
Paclitaxel-eluting stent = 1; Stent diameter <3 mm = 1
CABG-related MI = −2; CHF or LVEF <30% = 2
Score ≥2 = high ischaemic risk → favour extended DAPT. Score <2 = balance with bleeding risk. The DAPT score is the validated tool — commit the sign conventions (negative score = shorter, positive = longer) to memory.

### 2. High-intensity statins

High-intensity statin therapy is mandatory after ACS, regardless of baseline LDL. Target: LDL <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) and ≥50% reduction from baseline.

- Atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 40 mg — started during the index admission. PROVE-IT TIMI 22 trial: atorvastatin 80 mg vs pravastatin 40 mg after ACS — significant reduction in all-cause mortality and major cardiac events at 2 years with intensive statin. A-to-Z trial, similar results.
- If LDL target not achieved on high-intensity statin alone: add ezetimibe (IMPROVE-IT trial: ezetimibe + simvastatin vs simvastatin alone post-ACS — 6.4% relative risk reduction in cardiovascular events at 7 years). If still not at target: add PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab) — FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trials — large absolute risk reductions in very high-risk patients.
- Indonesian context (BPJS): Atorvastatin up to 40 mg and simvastatin are in FORNAS. Atorvastatin 80 mg and rosuvastatin may require referral or local institutional formulary coverage. Ezetimibe available but may require special approval. PCSK9 inhibitors currently not BPJS-covered for most patients.

### 3. ACEi or ARB (RAAS inhibition)

Mandatory post-MI in patients with EF ≤40% or anterior MI. Class IIa for all other post-MI patients (benefit from preventing LV remodelling).

- Start within 24 hours of STEMI (CONSENSUS, GISSI-3, ISIS-4, SAVE, AIRE trials)
- Agents: ramipril 5–10 mg OD, lisinopril 10–20 mg OD, perindopril 4–8 mg OD
- ARB (valsartan) is equivalent when ACEi-intolerant (VALIANT trial)
- Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi): the PARADISE-MI trial tested sacubitril/valsartan started within 7 days of STEMI vs ramipril — did not reach primary endpoint of superiority overall. In subgroups with new STEMI and EF <40%, ARNi showed benefit. Current use: transition from ACEi to sacubitril/valsartan at 4–6 weeks if EF remains ≤40% and patient tolerates (follows HFrEF GDMT principles).

### 4. Beta-blockers

- Start within 24 hours (oral, not IV routinely) if Killip I or II, HR >60, SBP >100
- Continue indefinitely post-MI if EF ≤40% (mortality benefit in HFrEF — CAPRICORN trial specifically in post-MI EF ≤40%: carvedilol vs placebo — 23% relative risk reduction in all-cause mortality)
- If EF recovers to >50% and patient is asymptomatic: can consider de-escalating at 12 months (CAPITAL-RCT, REDUCE trials suggest early discontinuation may be safe in recovered EF — evidence evolving)
- Agents: carvedilol 3.125–25 mg BD, bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg OD, metoprolol succinate 25–200 mg OD

### 5. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA)

Eplerenone or spironolactone add mortality benefit post-MI when:

- EPHESUS trial (eplerenone): patients with STEMI and EF ≤40% AND either HF symptoms OR diabetes. Eplerenone started 3–14 days post-MI → 15% relative risk reduction in all-cause mortality at 16 months.
- Start at low dose (eplerenone 25 mg OD, spironolactone 25 mg OD) once creatinine stabilised (avoid in eGFR <30 or K⁺ >5.0)
- Check K⁺ and creatinine at 1, 4, and 12 weeks after starting — hyperkalaemia is the key safety concern

## SGLT2 inhibitors — the newest pillar

SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) have entered the post-ACS prevention space based on cardiovascular outcomes trials (EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-REDUCED) and more recently post-ACS specific data (EMPACT-MI, DAPA-MI):

- DAPA-MI (2023): dapagliflozin started within 10 days of MI — significant reduction in composite of HF and death vs placebo in patients with EF <55%
- EMPACT-MI (2024): empagliflozin post-MI — reduced HF hospitalisation
- Current recommendation: consider SGLT2 inhibitor in post-ACS patients with EF ≤40% or type 2 diabetes, started during the index hospitalisation or early post-discharge
- Mechanism in HF/post-MI: beyond glycaemic lowering — natriuresis, volume reduction, cardioprotection via multiple mechanisms (ketone body utilisation, ion channel effects, direct myocardial protection)

## The "rule of halves" — the implementation gap

Despite overwhelming evidence, post-ACS secondary prevention remains underimplemented. Real-world data consistently shows:

- ~50% of eligible post-MI patients receive high-intensity statin therapy
- ~40% of post-MI patients with EF ≤40% receive ACEi + BB + MRA combination
- P2Y12 inhibitor adherence falls to ~60–70% at 12 months (patient-perceived side effects, cost, complexity)

Every inpatient discharge represents a critical opportunity. A discharge prescription that is complete and explained to the patient achieves better long-term adherence than a discharge letter that lists drugs without context. Take the time to explain the "why" of each drug at discharge.

## Non-pharmacological secondary prevention

- Cardiac rehabilitation: supervised exercise training + education + psychological support. Reduces cardiovascular mortality ~25%, improves quality of life, reduces rehospitalisation. Underutilised. Refer all eligible patients at discharge.
- Smoking cessation: the single most impactful lifestyle intervention. Halves cardiovascular event rate within 1 year. Pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion, NRT) + counselling.
- Blood pressure target: <130/80 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2017) or <140/90 (ESC 2021) — choose based on institutional guidelines.
- LDL target: <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) with ≥50% reduction from baseline for very high-risk post-ACS patients (ESC 2019/2021 Dyslipidaemia guidelines).
- HbA1c: <7% (53 mmol/mol) in diabetics — use SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA preferentially for glucose control post-MI (cardiovascular benefit).
- Activity and diet: Mediterranean diet, regular aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week moderate intensity, BMI <25 kg/m².

Checkpoint: A 60-year-old post-anterior STEMI patient (EF 38%) is ready for discharge on day 4. Current medications: aspirin 100 mg OD, ticagrelor 90 mg BD, bisoprolol 5 mg OD, ramipril 5 mg OD, atorvastatin 80 mg OD. His K⁺ is 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 80 µmol/L. What medication is missing from his discharge prescription and why?
The missing drug is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) — eplerenone or spironolactone. The EPHESUS criteria are met: anterior STEMI + EF 38% (≤40%). Eplerenone 25 mg OD should be added before or at discharge, given that: (1) K⁺ is 4.2 mmol/L (safe to start — would contraindicate if >5.0 mmol/L); (2) creatinine 80 µmol/L (eGFR adequate — would withhold if eGFR <30); (3) no concurrent K⁺-sparing diuretics that would add hyperkalaemia risk. Plan: start eplerenone 25 mg OD, check K⁺ and creatinine at 1 week and 4 weeks. Also consider: should SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin 10 mg OD) be added given EF <40%? The post-MI data and HFrEF GDMT data support this — strong consideration for co-prescription. The discharge regimen should be: aspirin + ticagrelor + bisoprolol + ramipril + atorvastatin + eplerenone + (dapagliflozin if appropriate). Cardiac rehabilitation referral should be documented.

sections.body:
Not all MI is caused by obstructive atherosclerosis. MINOCA, SCAD, vasospasm, and Takotsubo share the troponin rise of classic ACS but have different mechanisms, different treatments, and different prognoses. Recognising them prevents both under-treatment and dangerous mistreatment.

## MINOCA — MI with non-obstructive coronary arteries

MINOCA is defined as: acute MI (troponin rise with symptoms/ECG changes) in a patient with coronary arteries showing no stenosis ≥50% on angiography. It accounts for approximately 5–10% of all MI presentations and is disproportionately common in women (up to 30% of MI in women <60 years).

MINOCA is a working diagnosis at angiography, not a final diagnosis — it is the starting point for a structured investigation to find the underlying cause. The causes are diverse:

| Cause | Mechanism | Key investigation | Specific treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plaque rupture/erosion without obstructive stenosis | Small non-obstructive plaque ruptures and thromboses, causes ischaemia/MI, then spontaneously lyses before angio | OCT (optical coherence tomography) — visualises plaque morphology in the artery wall beyond angiographic resolution | DAPT + statin (as per standard ACS) |
| Coronary vasospasm (Printzmetal/variant angina) | Severe focal coronary vasoconstriction → transient total occlusion → ischaemia/MI. Often nocturnal, at rest. ST elevation during spasm, normal ECG between episodes. | Provocative testing (intracoronary acetylcholine or ergonovine during angiography — triggers spasm at the site) | Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, diltiazem) — first-line. Nitrates long-acting. Avoid beta-blockers (worsen vasospasm by unopposed α constriction). Aspirin alone (DAPT not clearly indicated). |
| Coronary microvascular disease (CMD) | Dysfunction of the small coronary arterioles (<500 µm) — impaired vasodilation response to demand. Normal epicardial arteries but impaired microvascular function → subendocardial ischaemia. | Coronary flow reserve (CFR) <2.0 or index of microvascular resistance (IMR) >25 by pressure wire or TIMI frame count | ACEi/ARB (improve microvascular function), ranolazine (reduces ischaemia), statin. Avoid dual antiplatelet unless plaque rupture confirmed. |
| Myocarditis mimicking MINOCA | Diffuse myocardial inflammation raises troponin and may cause regional wall motion abnormalities — clean coronaries at angio | Cardiac MRI (CMR) — midwall/epicardial LGE pattern (vs subendocardial/transmural in ischaemic MI). T2 mapping for oedema. | NSAIDs + colchicine (viral myocarditis); immunosuppression if giant-cell myocarditis or autoimmune. No DAPT unless concurrent plaque disease. |
| Takotsubo cardiomyopathy | Catecholamine-mediated apical stunning — mimics anterior STEMI acutely (ST elevation V3–V6, troponin rise) but echo shows apical ballooning without fixed coronary occlusion | Echo (apical ballooning, preserved basal function — "octopus trap" shape); CMR confirms no necrosis (no LGE in typical cases) | Supportive (ACEi, BB). No stent. Recovery expected in 4–8 weeks. |
| Type 2 MI | Demand ischaemia in the setting of clean coronaries — PE, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, hypotension in a patient without significant CAD | Clinical context; no angiographic culprit; treat the underlying cause | Treat precipitating condition. No DAPT unless plaque disease confirmed. |

Key concept: CMR is the key diagnostic step in MINOCA — it can identify the mechanism in 85% of cases
Cardiac MRI performed within 2 weeks of MINOCA provides: LGE pattern — ischaemic (subendocardial/transmural in a coronary territory) vs myocarditic (midwall, epicardial, patchy, multi-territory) vs no LGE (Takotsubo, CMD, vasospasm); T2 mapping — acute oedema indicating recent myocardial injury; Wall motion analysis — apical ballooning (Takotsubo), regional wall motion (ischaemic territory), global hypokinesis (myocarditis). Every MINOCA patient who is clinically stable should have CMR within 2 weeks. Without it, the cause — and therefore the correct long-term treatment — remains unknown.

## Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)

SCAD is a non-atherosclerotic, non-traumatic coronary dissection — a tear in the coronary artery wall creates a false lumen that compresses the true lumen, causing ischaemia or complete occlusion. It is responsible for approximately 25–35% of MI in women under 50 and is the leading cause of MI in pregnancy and the peripartum period.

### Who gets SCAD?

- Young women (<50 years) — 90% of cases are female
- Peripartum period (especially immediately post-delivery)
- Associated conditions: fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD — seen in 50–86% of SCAD patients on coronary angiography), connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), inflammatory conditions (SLE, IBD), extreme exertion
- Emotional stress and hormonal fluctuations (exogenous hormones, menstrual cycle)

### Angiographic appearance and diagnosis

- Long, smooth, tapering stenosis — unlike the focal lesions of atherosclerosis
- Double lumen appearance (true and false lumen both visible)
- The diagnosis can be missed if the dissection segment is long and only mild narrowing is apparent
- OCT or IVUS confirms the diagnosis by imaging the intramural haematoma

### Management — the opposite of atherosclerotic ACS

Warning: PCI is generally AVOIDED in SCAD unless the patient is haemodynamically unstable. Attempting to stent a SCAD lesion can extend the dissection further, cause iatrogenic propagation of the haematoma, and worsen the situation. Most SCAD lesions heal spontaneously — conservative management with aspirin alone (no DAPT unless stenting was required), beta-blocker (to reduce aortic stress), and in-hospital observation is the standard approach for haemodynamically stable patients. PCI reserved for: ongoing ischaemia, haemodynamic compromise, very proximal LMCA/proximal LAD involvement. CABG for LMCA/proximal LAD SCAD that cannot be managed conservatively.

## Coronary vasospasm (Printzmetal/variant angina)

Pure vasospasm without fixed atherosclerosis causes Prinzmetal (variant) angina — rest pain (typically nocturnal), transient ST elevation during the episode that fully resolves with GTN or spontaneously, normal angiography between attacks.

- ECG during attack: ST elevation in the territory of the spasming artery — can look identical to STEMI but resolves within minutes
- Triggers: smoking, cocaine, ergot derivatives, cold exposure
- Diagnosis: provocative testing (acetylcholine intracoronary) at angiography reproduces spasm
- Management: calcium channel blockers (diltiazem or amlodipine) are first-line — prevent vasoconstriction. Long-acting nitrates. Beta-blockers are contraindicated — they leave α-adrenergic receptors unopposed, worsening coronary constriction. Smoking cessation is the most important non-pharmacological intervention.

## Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — the complete picture

Takotsubo (stress cardiomyopathy, apical ballooning syndrome) is triggered by a massive catecholamine surge — emotional stress ("broken heart syndrome"), physical stress (surgery, critical illness), or medical procedures. The catecholamines cause direct myocardial toxicity and microvascular spasm, producing transient apical LV dysfunction while the basal segments (which have fewer β-receptors) are spared or even hypercontractile.

- Classic triad: (1) acute event resembling anterior STEMI (ST elevation or T inversions V3–V6, troponin rise); (2) apical ballooning on echo (apex doesn't move, base contracts normally); (3) clean coronaries on angiography (no culprit lesion)
- Risk of complications: most patients recover fully in 4–8 weeks. However, the acute phase carries risk: LVOTO (in the reverse or basal-type Takotsubo), mural thrombus in the akinetic apex → anticoagulate if thrombus seen, cardiogenic shock (5%), life-threatening arrhythmias, LV free wall rupture (rare)
- Treatment: supportive care (ACEi/BB), anticoagulation if apical thrombus, avoid catecholamines if possible. No coronary stent (no culprit lesion). Psychological support — the emotional trigger often needs addressing
- Recurrence: ~5% per year. Subsequent emotional or physical stressors may trigger repeat episodes

Exam tip: Takotsubo + LVOTO + cardiogenic shock — the trap within the trap: In Takotsubo, hypercontractile basal segments with an akinetic apex can create dynamic LVOTO (the basal myocardium moves so vigorously that it obstructs the outflow tract). This produces a paradoxical situation: the patient is in cardiogenic shock, but it is NOT from pump failure — it is from obstruction. Inotropes (dobutamine, norepinephrine) will worsen the obstruction by increasing basal contractility. The correct treatment for Takotsubo-induced LVOTO with shock: IV fluids (increase preload to reduce LVOTO), phenylephrine (pure α-agonist raises SVR without increasing contractility), and correct any precipitating arrhythmia. Never give dobutamine if echo shows LVOTO in the setting of Takotsubo.

Checkpoint: A 45-year-old woman with no cardiac risk factors presents 2 days after the death of her mother with chest pain and ECG showing deep symmetric T-wave inversions in V2–V6. Troponin I rises to 480 ng/L. Angiography shows no coronary stenosis. Echo shows apical ballooning and preserved basal function. What is the diagnosis, what do you look for on the echo to guide anticoagulation, and what is the key class of drug to avoid in this condition?
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress/broken heart syndrome). The triad is present: acute cardiac syndrome after major emotional stressor (death of mother) + ECG showing T-wave inversions V2–V6 (typical Takotsubo evolution: initial ST elevation then deep T inversions over 24–48h) + echo apical ballooning + clean coronaries. Echo assessment for anticoagulation guidance: look for an apical thrombus — the akinetic apex can serve as a site for thrombus formation (blood stagnates in the non-contracting apex). If visible thrombus → anticoagulate (LMWH or DOAC) for 3 months or until EF recovers and thrombus resolves. If no visible thrombus → aspirin alone is generally sufficient. Drug class to avoid: inotropes (dobutamine, norepinephrine) — if LVOTO is present (check on echo during systole), inotropes will increase basal contractility and worsen the obstruction. In uncomplicated Takotsubo, catecholamines are also theoretically harmful as the pathophysiology involves catecholamine excess. Recovery: full EF recovery expected in 4–8 weeks. Psychological support referral recommended.
